en: *Pinaiye*, Scroll One. "Pin" (鼻) means "to depart" in the language of Qin; "naiye" (奈耶) means "truth" (Sanskrit: *nayā*) in the language of Qin. Because one departs from various errors and proceeds toward truth, it is called "truth.

Because one subdues this mind, calms this mind, and maintains forbearance so that [defilements] do not arise, it is called "truth. Subduing is precept (*śīla*); calming is concentration (*samādhi*); forbearance is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
The Pārājika Dharma 1: Three Precepts—the unsurpassed precept of bodily conduct, the unsurpassed precept of mental conduct, and the unsurpassed precept of wisdom.
What is the unsurpassed precept of bodily conduct?

In this regard, a bhikṣu upholds the precepts; he adorns himself with liberation through the precepts, practices them until they become his established view, and feels fear at even the slightest transgression. He conforms to the precepts within the precepts; this is called the unsurpassed precept of precepts.
What is the unsurpassed precept of the mind?
For a bhikṣu, it is the removal of sexual desire and so forth, up to the meditative attainment of the fourth dhyāna through right contemplation; this is called the unsurpassed precept of the mind.
What is the unsurpassed precept of wisdom?

It is when a bhikṣu knows this truth of suffering, knows this truth of the origin of suffering, knows this truth of the cessation of suffering, and knows this truth of the path to the cessation of suffering; this is called the unsurpassed precept of wisdom.

By means of these three precepts, one establishes compliance with the Truth; the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—the Buddha-treasury, the Buddha-jewel, and the Buddha’s secret essentials—thereby instruct the three vehicles, the śrāvakas, and the pratyekabuddhas, leading them each to attain Samyak-saṃbuddhahood.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Stone Terrace Garden on the banks of the Monkey River (Markaṭahradatīra) in the city of Vaiśālī—which in the Qin language means "Vast and Broad"—not far from Vaiśālī, in the place called Kalandakanivāpa.

The son of Kalandaka, named Sudatta, resided there; his wealth was boundless, his estates were abundant, and his dwellings were fully established. Possessing elephants, horses, camels, oxen, and donkeys, as well as money, grain, treasures, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, shells, jade, amber, agate, musaragalva, and coral, he nevertheless renounced them all to approach the Tathāgata, so as to hear and receive the profound depths of the Dharma, thereby attaining a mind of faith and joy.

With this mind of faith and joy, he attained right concentration (*samādhi*), shaved off his hair and beard, left the household life for the sake of the path, and together with an infinite number of bhikṣus, went to the Bamboo Grove in the city of Kauśāmbī to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*).

At that time, grain was expensive and there was widespread famine; the crops had been destroyed by frost and hail, and even the small amount that survived was devoured by locusts, making it extremely difficult to obtain food through begging.
Thereupon, Sudatta, son of Kalandaka, thought to himself:

"At present, grain is expensive and there is famine; the crops have been destroyed by frost and hail, and those few that escaped have been devoured by locusts. Thus, it is extremely difficult to obtain alms."
"Venerable sirs, listen to what I have to say!
I have friends and kinsmen in the kingdom of Vethadīpa; their wealth and status are boundless, their money, property, and lands are immeasurable, and they abound in precious gems and various goods."
"We should go together to that place to bring blessings to our kinsmen; the bhikṣus will also find a place to rest, and it is timely for us to head toward the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
Once we have arrived there, the bhikṣus shall be provided with food, rice gruel, medicinal decoctions, and clothing."
Thereupon, Sudatta, son of Kalandaka, entered the retreat at the city of Kauśāmbī.

Having completed his retreat, he spent three months mending his robes; when one day remained until the end of the period, the robes were finished. He then put on his robes, took up his bowl, and set out for Vaiśālī.
Leading the assembly forward, he gradually arrived at Vaiśālī and proceeded to the stone terrace by the side of the Monkey River (Markaṭahrada) in Vaiśālī.
He prepared various kinds of food and offered them to the bhikṣus, serving them with his own hands.

At that time, Sudatta, the son of Kalandaka, having dressed and taken his bowl at the proper hour, went to the house of a relative in the country of Vaiśālī to beg for food; having finished his alms-round, he departed immediately.
At that time, a female servant of the Kalandaka family outside the gate saw Sudatta, the son of Kalandaka, entering his own kinsmen's house; she wondered why he had come out so quickly to return.
Seeing the wife of Kalandaka, she knelt and spoke these words:
"Just now, the noble Sudatta, son of Kalandaka, entered his kinsmen's house and returned very quickly."
"I hope you are free from illness and mental distress?
I trust you do not find the holy life (brahmacarya) unpleasant, nor have you broken the precepts, abandoned the Path, or turned back toward worldly ways?
Upon hearing these words, Sūradatta’s mother was filled with immeasurable joy, unable to contain herself.
He immediately went to where Sudatta was and said to him:
"Is your body light and healthy?
Is your mind free from other thoughts?"
"Does your mind harbor thoughts of violating the pure conduct?
Do you wish to break the precepts, abandon the Path, and return to the ways of the laity?
If such a thought exists, come quickly."
Sudatta! Although you have abandoned the precepts to follow worldly customs, this does not hinder your practice of giving or the performance of various meritorious deeds. Why is this?
"Among the assembly of the Buddha, it is extremely difficult to maintain the precepts, and it is also difficult to study the Path.
Having heard this, he immediately replied to his mother:
"I have no illness, nor do I have any other thoughts; I have not violated the Brahma-faring, nor does my mind intend to violate the precepts by abandoning the Path to follow worldly ways."
The mother replied again:
"Sudatta! You should understand this intention."
"Your former wife was peerlessly beautiful; if you do not wish to abandon the path for worldly life, you may remain here to continue the lineage and ensure our family line flourishes."
"Once there is no successor, all the money, wealth, and treasures will be seized by the King of Kosala. Sudatta replied,
"If you permit me to enter the religious life, this matter may be settled accordingly."
At that time, Sudatta’s mother said to Sudatta’s wife, "I now command you:
after three days have passed since your menses, put on your bridal garments, adorn yourself well, and come to inform me."
Sudatta’s wife followed his instructions; three days after her menstrual period had ended, she put on the garment her husband had previously venerated and went to Sudatta’s mother.
She then reported the matter exactly as it was:
"Her menstrual period has lasted three days; now is precisely the right time.
Thereupon, Sudatta’s mother took the woman to Sudatta and said to him:

"You should know that this woman is peerlessly beautiful; she can continue the lineage and ensure its succession. Do not allow my clan to be cut off, nor let our wealth and treasures be seized by the King of Kosala."
Having detained his wife, he immediately withdrew and departed.

At that time, Sudatta went forward, embraced his wife, and engaged in unchaste conduct with her in a secluded place; this occurred three times in a short while. At that very moment, Śakra descended from heaven and entered her womb.
At that time, within the eighth month and before the ninth month of her pregnancy, Sudatta’s wife gave birth to a son whose countenance and features were peerlessly handsome.
Regarding what had been previously said about continuing the lineage, the mother named him "Continuator of the Lineage" (Sudatta).
At that time, having committed such an evil deed, Sudatta felt ashamed and was humiliated by others.
Then Sudatta, who shared the same precepts and the same status as the bhikṣus, sat in formal assembly with them; now that the assembly had just concluded, he came to inquire after him, saying:
"Is your mind patient? Is your constant composure unimpaired? Are your strength and vigor light and robust?"
"Was the midday meal offering sufficient?
Did the bhikṣu who went out for alms have no illness, was his mind free from distress, and was he without distracting thoughts? Sudatta replied:

"Venerable friends, you should know that there is a state of mental forbearance wherein one remains fully satisfied while sitting in retreat, neither going out to beg for alms nor suffering from illness;
yet, within the mind, there arises the thought of another."
The bhikṣus replied:
"If you have a mind of forbearance, and the retreat has concluded successfully and fully, and you are free from illness,
why do you harbor thoughts of others?"
Sudatta went before the bhikṣus and related in full all that he had previously transgressed.
Immediately, those bhikṣus collectively rebuked Sudatta most severely, saying:

"The World-Honored One has, through countless skillful means, spoken of the foul impurity of sexual desire; yet you directed your thoughts toward sex, contemplated sex, and your lustful intent was fervent."

"The World-Honored One has described the foulness of sexual desire as such: one turns toward it, transgresses against it, contemplates it with integrity, and the intent for sexual desire becomes intensely blazing.

After the bhikṣus had thus severely rebuked themselves, they went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground, sat to one side, and reported in detail to the World-Honored One the transgression they had committed.
The Buddha, knowing this, addressed Sudatta:
"Have you truly committed this offense?
He replied:
“I have examined the offense,
World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One said:

"By various skillful means, I have taught the foulness of sexual desire to those deluded people; yet they continue to direct their thoughts toward sex and their lustful intentions remain intense, even as I thus describe the foulness of sexual desire."
The Buddha, through various skillful means, established the precepts for the śramaṇas:
"One should observe the ten virtues of a bhikṣu before conferring the precepts.
What are these ten qualities of the assembly?"
First, upholding all virtues and cultivating the path that nurtures all virtues;
second, teaching those who do not believe in the precepts so that they may enter into faith;
third, constantly feeling shame and remorse while reflecting upon one's own shortcomings.
1. To teach those who have committed errors so that they may enter the right path;

2. To cause those who are already correct to further deepen their correctness; 3. To manifest one's body to study the Path and extinguish the fetters, desiring to ensure that there are no fetters in future lives; 4. [Number four is implied by the context of the list]; 5. To desire to cause those who are correct to become doubly correct; 6. To manifest one's body to study the Path and extinguish the fetters, desiring to ensure that there are no fetters in future lives.
Seventh, in one's final existence, one desires that the fetters be extinguished and not arise;
eighth, one practices various pure conducts;
ninth, having attained the holy life, one desires not to lose it.
"Desiring that the holy life (brahmacarya) endure for a long time— this is the tenth point—
the śramaṇas should all know it together.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this matter and for this reason, assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and established this precept:

"If a bhikṣu has violated the precepts, yet does not renounce them, nor does he abandon his feeble morality; if he does not repent and commits the act of sexual intercourse, which is contrary to pure conduct—this bhikṣu is *pārājika*, *aprativāsya*, *aprativāsa*. This means he is not to be accepted by the Saṃgha, nor may he dwell with them."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who was practicing the summer retreat in a park located not far from a city in the kingdom of Kośala.
Not far from the monastery, there lived a female monkey.

This female monkey frequently went to where the bhikṣu was, and the bhikṣu repeatedly gave food to her. In this way, the monkey did not fear or trouble the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu engaged in unwholesome sexual conduct with the monkey.
Among that great assembly of bhikṣus, there were fellow students and co-donors who had held the *varṣā* retreat in the kingdom of Kośala.
Having completed their retreat and mended their robes, they prepared a robe on a single day; then, wearing the robe and carrying the alms bowl, they came to where this bhikṣu was and said to him:
"Have you been here since the summer retreat? Are you free from any suffering or hardship?"
"When going out for alms, does the mind of a bhikṣu have various perceptions?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Venerable sirs!"
"Having a mind of patience, he suffered no affliction or distress during the summer retreat, nor did he have any distracted thoughts.

Then a monkey came from outside and went straight to this bhikṣu; it crouched before him and stared intently at the bhikṣu. Having stared at the bhikṣu, it turned its face to look at another bhikṣu; having looked at the other bhikṣu, it turned its face back to look at this bhikṣu. Thereupon, it turned its body away from the bhikṣu and backed up behind him.
This bhikṣu felt ashamed that the other bhikṣus did not follow the monkey, nor did he look back at it.

Seeing that the bhikṣu did not look back, the monkey gave rise to an evil intent; turning its body around, it seized and clawed the bhikṣu’s head and face, wounding and disfiguring them, and then departed.
The great bhikṣus said to this bhikṣu:
"Just now a monkey came here; it first raised its eyes to look at you, then looked at us, and immediately turned its body away from you."
"Seeing that you did not speak to me nor look at me, I immediately gave rise to a mind of anger; I seized and clawed at your head and face until they were broken, and then I left.
The great bhikṣus rebuked him severely.
Having been rebuked by the bhikṣus, he immediately confessed his fault.
The bhikṣus said to him:
"How could you, O bhikṣu, have done this when the World-Honored One has not failed to explain, through countless skillful means, that sexual misconduct is a foul and impure thing?"
You direct your thoughts toward sexual desire, and your lustful intent is intense.
The World-Honored One has fully explained the foul impurities of sexual desire; you direct your thoughts toward sexual desire, and your lustful intent is intense.
Why do you not contemplate this course of sexual conduct, yet instead engage in such evil deeds?
After these great bhikṣus had thus rebuked and censured this bhikṣu, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
That assembly of bhikṣus reported everything they had seen to the Buddha as before.
Knowing this, the Buddha addressed those bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so, or not?"

The bhikṣu was filled with shame; his face lost its color as if covered in dust. He knelt on his right knee, bared his right shoulder, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, the World-Honored One:
"It is indeed true."
"World-Honored One!
At that time, the World-Honored One said to this bhikṣu: "How is it, bhikṣu?

Have I not, for the sake of foolish people, used countless skillful means to speak of the foul impurity of sexual desire—how one directs the mind toward sex, contemplates sex, and how the intent for sex becomes fiercely blazing?"
"I have thus fully described the foul impurities of sexual desire.

For this matter and for this purpose, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, using countless skillful means, spoke of sexual desire; he assembled the Saṃgha and observed ten benefits, up to the long endurance of the holy life (*brahmacarya*). The World-Honored One then established this precept for the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu commits a breach of the precepts, and with a lustful mind does not return [the robes] nor relinquish the precepts, and while his precepts are weakened he does not repent, yet engages in impure conduct even down to the members of the animal kingdom that possess form—such a person who has committed this offense shall not be accepted and shall be expelled."
"What, then, is that which is called 'precept' (śīla)?
As for the name 'precept,' if a bhikṣu upholds the two hundred and fifty precepts—the unsurpassed precepts—this is what is called the precept."
What is meant by "not returning the precepts"?
Not returning the precepts refers to ignorance, a distracted mind, and painful affliction.
To abandon the precepts is to not return them; it is like facing one another while mute and deaf.
Returning the precepts does not constitute returning them if the sounds do not reach one another;
returning the precepts does not constitute returning them if one returns them alone.
If one returns the precepts before a Buddha-stūpa or before a śramaṇa’s stūpa, it does not constitute a valid return of the precepts.

If one distances oneself from the Buddha, from one's preceptor (upādhyāya) and his companions, and from one's ācārya and his companions—distancing oneself completely and no longer relying upon them—one thinks, "I do not abide within the Buddha-dharma."
He spoke to the bhikṣus, saying:
"I have now departed and shall no longer practice the Way. The bhikṣus said:
"Do you not practice the Way? He replied,
"I do not practice the Way."
This constitutes the forfeiture of the precepts.
Regarding sexual intercourse with a courtesan, it constitutes three grounds for expulsion (*pārājika*):

if it occurs near the birth canal, it is the first ground for expulsion; if it occurs near the anus, it is the second ground for expulsion; and if it occurs near the mouth, it is the third ground for expulsion.
There are two ways in which a man is abandoned:
being near the anus and being near the mouth; these are the two ways he is abandoned.
There are also two things by which one does not become a man:
There are males and females. Regarding those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), there are three that are the same as females.
There are two types of proximity to animals, excluding the mouth, which is the same as that of females.
If it is a male animal, one [hand] is discarded; if it is a female animal, the same applies.
Among animals, if there are those with both male and female forms, two [hands] are discarded.
Chickens and ospreys are as described in the two cases above.
The three locations for non-human females are the same as those for human women.
This constitutes the *abrahmacarya* (unholy conduct) of *parimāṇa*.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was at Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, his disciples numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty.
At that time, the bhikṣus gathered firewood and grass to construct huts.

Later, when the bhikṣus entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms, the men, women, and children of all ages within the city came out and demolished those huts, taking the materials away for their own use.
After the bhikṣus had returned from begging for alms, they saw that the huts had been destroyed by others; the bhikṣus then once again gathered firewood and grass to build huts in which to dwell.
The bhikṣus again entered Rājagṛha to beg for food, but the men, women, and children of Rājagṛha once more destroyed their huts and took them away.
This happened as many as three times.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they thought:
"The men and women, great and small, of the city of Rājagṛha frequently come out and destroy these huts.
Among that assembly was a bhikṣu named Dhanika, the son of a potter, who then gave rise to this thought:
"We gathered this firewood and grass to construct a hut; while we were away in the city begging for alms, the men and women of the city came out and destroyed our hut."
"I have a carpenter in the city who is a relative of mine; I shall go to him and beg for timber to use in building a house.
When it was time, the bhikṣu Dhanika put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha. He went to the carpenter's house and said to him, "Do you know this?"
"King Ajātaśatru has granted me timber;
you should provide me with carpenters. He replied:
"The King has granted you the privilege that you may take wood from this forest as you please.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu Dantika took wood for himself; he took all the best timber the officials desired, cut it down, and piled it together in one place.

A city inspector from the city of Rājagṛha was making a circuit of the city when he arrived at a place where timber was being gathered; there he saw logs of wood forbidden by the authorities piled together in one spot.
Having seen this, he immediately went to the carpenter’s place and asked:
"Carpenter! Who has taken the timber from the government storehouse, cut it into pieces, and piled them together in one spot?"
The carpenter replied immediately:
"The bhikṣu Dvija has come and commanded me, saying that since the officials have granted me timber, you should give it to me.
This bhikṣu is taking the wood and cutting it into sections, piling them together in one place."
At that time, the city guards became angry with King Ajātaśatru from afar; they went to where the king was and said to him:
"There are many excellent timbers that you do not use, yet you take fine timber to provide for a bhikṣu?"
The King replied, "I have given no such command.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru ordered an attendant to summon a carpenter; immediately following the King's instruction, the attendant ran to summon the carpenter.
"King Ajātaśatru has issued a summons for you.
The carpenter immediately followed his instructions and went to the king's location; on the way, he encountered the bhikṣu Daṇḍakin.
When the carpenter saw the bhikṣu Daṇḍakin, he immediately went forward to pay his respects and said,
"Because you are a venerable person, please take me to the king's presence.
The bhikṣu replied:
"Furthermore, I arrived after having previously searched for him.
At that time, the carpenter went to the king's presence.
Upon seeing the carpenter, the king immediately asked:
"You are no human being; why do you act with such autonomy as to take timber from the royal storehouse and give it to a bhikṣu?
The carpenter replied immediately:
"Your Majesty should know that the bhikṣu Dabba arrived at the timber yard and spoke these words:"
"The official bestowed timber upon me; you, Minister, should give it to me.
He then said to the bhikṣu, "If the King has indeed granted it to you, then take it as you please."
Before the King had finished speaking to the carpenter, the bhikṣu Daṇḍakin arrived at the King’s location.
Seeing the bhikṣu approaching from afar, the King immediately commanded his attendants to take the carpenter away temporarily to a lower room and lead the bhikṣu forward.
Having heard the king’s command, he took the carpenters and went before the bhikṣu.
The king asked the bhikṣu:
“Now that this is a time of utmost sincerity, why have you taken these fine timbers from the government and cut them into pieces, piling them together in one place?”
The bhikṣu replied to the king:
“The King granted me timber. [The king said:
“I do not recall giving such an order.”
The bhikṣu replied to the king:
"Do you not remember, O King, when you first became king? At that time, did you not offer the three things—firewood, grass, and water—as alms to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?"
When the king saw that the bhikṣu was speaking such deceptive words, he replied: "Bhikṣu!
That which I bestow extends even to those who have no owner; it does not exclude those who do have an owner."
"Let the bhikṣu go and receive the royal decree.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru’s wrath was burning fiercely; yet, recollecting the virtues of the World-Honored One, he remained silent for a moment without speaking, and then commanded the bhikṣu:
"Return to your quarters and do not do this again."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru’s attendants and the hundred officials all raised their voices and cried out:
"How strange!
This bhikṣu has escaped death!"
At that time, the bhikṣu Dārika returned to where the great assembly was and said to them:
"Virtuous ones, you should know that just now the Great King intended to have me executed, but he subsequently released me."
The bhikṣus asked, "What is the matter?
This bhikṣu Dvika then related the matter in detail to the assembly.
Among them were certain *dhūta* monks who lived on alms; hearing these words, they each felt ashamed and went to the World-Honored One to report what those monks had said.
At that time, the World-Honored One looked toward Ānanda and said:
"Go quickly, Ānanda!
Enter the city of Rājagṛha and stand at the intersection of the four main roads, and speak these words:
"If a bhikṣu steals five coins or more, or steals clothing worth five coins—
if one commits such an act, what punishment does Ajaśatru impose?"

At that time, Ānanda, having received the instruction of the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and entered the city of Rājagṛha together with two bhikṣus.
Arriving at the crossroads, he addressed the passers-by:
"If a bhikṣu steals five coins, or clothing worth five coins..."
"If someone were to steal this, what punishment would King Ajātaśatru impose?
At that time, the mendicants from the four quarters of the city of Rājagṛha replied to him, saying:
"If a bhikṣu steals five coins or clothing worth five coins, King Ajātaśatru has a decree stating that he is no longer a śramaṇa."
At that time, Ānanda immediately departed from Rājagṛha and returned to the place where the Buddha was staying. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I inquired among the passersby in the city of Rājagṛha, and they said that if a bhikṣu steals five coins or clothing worth five coins, King Ajātaśatru will declare him no longer a śramaṇa."

At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, assembled the harmonious Saṃgha; observing ten virtues, the World-Honored One formulated the precepts for the śramaṇas, so that the holy life (brahmacarya) might endure for a long time.

“O Śramaṇas, you should know this matter: if a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, takes what is not given from a village or town, and by means of such an act of taking what is not given, he is seized by a king or a royal minister, who beats him, binds him, and drives him out of the boundary, or speaks these words: ‘Ho, bhikṣu!’”
You are not a thief. You are not a child. You are not a fool.
If one commits taking what is not given by making such a representation, it is a *pārājika*.
"A bhikṣu shall not dwell in a house that has not been formally assigned.
In the region of Kosala, there was a place near a frontier pass.
The merchant arrived and said to the bhikṣu, "I will give you a small amount of goods so that I may pass through the customs checkpoint; this item shall be half for you.
After the bhikṣu had accepted these goods, he later regretted it.
“Have I not committed an offense of abandonment and non-acceptance?
That bhikṣu reported this matter to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One addressed that bhikṣu:

"If a bhikṣu crosses a frontier with goods, and the value reaches five coins or the equivalent of five coins' worth of goods, having accepted payment from a merchant, he commits an offense of 'defeat' (pārājika), and [the saṃgha] shall not accept him."
"To protect against thieves, famine, and treacherous paths.
At that time, the village enclosures, moats, and walls surrounded those herds of elephants, horses, camels, oxen, and donkeys, which were tethered together with ropes.
If a bhikṣu steals an animal from among the beasts, untying its rope and crossing over a fence or railing, it is a pārājika offense;
if he crosses over a moat and abandons it, or crosses over a wall and abandons it, it constitutes the offense of "abandonment and non-acceptance" (pārājika);
if he goes outside the wall, it constitutes the offense of "abandonment and non-acceptance."
If one drives [the animal] from an external wasteland into a wall, it constitutes the offense of *pārājika* (defeat) for not being accepted;
if it enters a moat, it constitutes the offense of *pārājika* for not being accepted;
if it enters within a palisade, it constitutes the offense of *pārājika* for not being accepted.

If one is destined to pass through several households before attaining the fruit of stream-entry, and if a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, diverts water, even down to the value of five māsakas, it constitutes the offense of pārājika (defeat).

Whether by hand or foot, or by means of wood or a spade, if one steals water by breaking an embankment, it constitutes the offense of *pārājika* (defeat), for which one is not to be accepted back into the community.
Suppose a bhikṣu is bathing in the water; before his bath is finished, he breaks a channel and lets the water flow out.
That householder spoke with anger, saying,
"This bhikṣu feigned bathing in order to break the dikes and release the water.
Each of those bhikṣus harbored doubts.
"Will we not be guilty of abandoning and refusing [the teachings]?
Those bhikṣus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"If one makes a decision with a mind of theft, and the value of the object determined is five *kārsāpaṇas* or less, it constitutes the offense of 'abandonment and non-acceptance.
Furthermore, regarding the water in a pond—whether it has an owner or not—if there are birds therein and a net is cast because of those birds..."

If a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, steals a bird—whether from within a net or outside a net—and its value is five coins or more, it constitutes the offense of *pārājika* (expulsion), provided the bird was inside a net that has an owner.
Regarding "outside the net," it means the pond has an owner.
These two matters both have owners.
As for the birds, they may either have an owner or be ownerless; if a bhikṣu takes a bird with a thieving mind, it constitutes the offense of *pārājika* (expulsion).

If a householder has placed a body-ornament or necklace out in the sun upon the roof, and there is a bird—whether it has an owner or not—that bird might brush aside the pearl necklace or other ornaments and carry them off.
If a bhikṣu takes it away, or if with the intent to steal he takes a bird belonging to another that is worth five māsakas or more, it constitutes an offense of pārājika (expulsion).
If a bhikṣu hangs newly dyed robes on the roof to dry and they are blown down to the ground by the wind...
If a bhikṣu takes something into a house and then regrets it, thinking,
"Have I not committed the offense of stealing that is not relinquished and not accepted?
that bhikṣu informs the Blessed One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If one acts with the intent to steal, it constitutes the offense of 'abandonment and non-acceptance.
If one does not act with the intent to steal, it does not constitute the offense of 'abandonment and non-acceptance.'"

If such a robe falls from an upper story to a lower floor, or moves from a lower floor to an upper story, or from an upper story to a higher story, and one does so with the intent to steal, it constitutes the offense of *pārājika* (defeat), for which the robe is forfeited and not accepted.

If one takes such things, as well as various other items—beginning with hemp, rice, beans, money, barley, wheat, black beans, and mustard seeds—with the intent to steal, and their value reaches five *kārsāpaṇas*, it constitutes the offense of *pārājika* (expulsion).
In that garden, among the fruit trees—primarily walnuts, pears, jujubes, peaches, and pears—if a bhikṣu takes some to eat, he then feels doubt, thinking:
"I have not encroached upon the property of the Saṃgha, nor have I taken what was not given; do I not incur the offense of *pārājika*?"
He reported the matter to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told him:
"It does not constitute a formal renunciation and non-acceptance."
"If it is not within a boundary established by the Saṃgha, there is no fault for a śrāmaṇera to take fruit.
Outside the Bamboo Grove of Siṃha, he killed a deer, ate its meat, drank its blood, and slept; the remainder was left behind.
If a bhikṣu takes food, and a lion, having awakened, seeks it but does not find it, it will search everywhere and roar.
Knowing this, the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"For what reason is the lion circling the garden and roaring?"
Ānanda related the matter in detail.
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu eats the leftovers of what a lion has eaten, even if their value is less than five coins, it constitutes the offense of *pārājika* (an act for which one is no longer accepted)."
It is the same for tigers;
as well as for bears, brown bears, monkeys, leopards, and other carnivorous beasts, and for those with two legs—headed by vultures, crows, cranes, hawks, and falcons—who seize and eat meat.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bird seizes food and takes it away, it constitutes the offense of *pārājika* (defeat).
If it flies away in alarm, desiring to protect itself so that it is not taken, it does not constitute the offense of *pārājika*."
"If a bhikṣu takes meat from a butcher who is a relative without it being given to him, he may then harbor doubt, thinking:
'Have I not committed the offense of *pārājika*?
He reported this matter to the World-Honored One."
The World-Honored One said:
"If one takes with the intent to steal, it constitutes the offense of *pārājika* (expulsion).
If one takes because of kinship, it does not constitute the offense of *pārājika*."

Having finished [the account] of Rājagṛha, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī together with a great assembly of bhikṣus; while traveling from Kośala to Śrāvastī, he encountered bandits in the vicinity of Sālapana Park.
Those thieves were captured either by the power of the king or by the power of the village; their robes and bowls were seized and returned to the bhikṣus.
Those bhikṣus each harbored doubts, thinking:
"Have I not committed the offense of *pārājika* (defeat)?"
He reported the matter to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One declared:
"If a bhikṣu, while among bandits, forcibly seizes their robes, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense, and he is no longer in communion."
If one is deprived [of requisites] by the power of a king or the power of a village, it does not constitute the offense of *pārājika* (defeat) because there was no verbal declaration [of refusal].
However, if one speaks and yet is deprived [of them], it constitutes the offense of *pārājika*. A certain bhikṣu came from Kosala; on the way, he was stripped of his belongings by bandits.
That bhikṣu, by means of the power of his relatives, recovered the thief’s robe and bowl.
Having recovered them, the bhikṣu then felt doubt, thinking:
"Have I not committed the offense of *pārājika*?"
That bhikṣu reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha told him:
"The thieves have already obtained it; it cannot be taken back by force."
"If one seizes by force or instructs another to seize it, it constitutes the offense of *pārājika* (defeat), and the object shall not be accepted.
However, if a bhikṣu ransoms it with its value, he may take it.
Thereupon, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Blessed One:
“If a bhikṣu takes what has not been given from the property of the Saṃgha, whose property is it that he has taken when it has not been given?
The Blessed One replied:
“If the property has already entered the mouth for the purpose of eating, and one carries it away, he commits the offense of *pārājika* (defeat).”
"If such property is to be divided, and one takes it for oneself, does this constitute 'abandonment through refusal to accept'? Venerable Upāli asked:
"If it is the property of the Saṃgha or what is required by the Saṃgha, and that bhikṣu takes it without it being given to him, whose abandonment through refusal to accept is it?"
The World-Honored One replied:
"The property of the Saṃgha is not to be given away as a gift. If a donor were to give wealth, that person's merit would be severed; therefore, it is rejected and not accepted."
Upāli again addressed the World-Honored One:
"If a bhikṣu takes by stealth the painted banners or canopies of a Buddha-stūpa or monastery, whose property is this that he has abandoned and does not accept?"
The World-Honored One said:
"If one takes property belonging to a Buddha-stūpa or monastery, it constitutes an offense of 'abandonment and non-acceptance.
The same applies to the stūpas of śrāvakas."

This refers to when a donor gives to a stūpa or monastery, thereby severing the merit of that donor; [if one takes it], it constitutes the offense of "rejecting and not accepting," and one who steals the property of a stūpa or monastery enters hell.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Keṇiya Garden in the kingdom of Nādikā; Keṇiya was the name of the garden’s owner.
There was a lay follower who, out of his own faith, self-reliance, compassion, and resolve, had constructed a lecture hall and privately offered it to the Venerable Rāhula.
After the Venerable Rāhula had accepted this lecture hall, he went away for two months.

When that upāsaka heard that the Venerable Rāhula had been at the lecture hall for two months, having heard this, the upāsaka took the lecture hall and offered it as a gift to the Saṃgha of the four quarters.

Thereupon, after two months had passed, the Venerable Rāhula returned to Nādikā. Having heard that a donor had offered a lecture hall to the Saṃgha of the Universal Community (Cātuddisa-saṃgha), he went to the Buddha’s dwelling; having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Venerable Rāhula reported the matter to the Blessed One.
The Buddha said to you, Rāhula:
"Go to that lay follower; having arrived there, speak as follows:"
"O upāsaka, have I done anything toward you that was improper, painful, unrighteous, impure, unworthy of a śramaṇa, or inconsistent with the Dharma?"
Thereupon, the Venerable Rāhula received what the Blessed One had spoken and took it up with great care; having done so, he rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha, and departed.
Then, when the night had passed, the Venerable Rāhula rose early, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Nādikā for alms.
Having finished his alms-round in Nādikā, he went to where that lay devotee was staying.
That worthy man saw Rāhula coming from afar; having seen him, he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes properly, and with palms joined in reverence, approached Rāhula and said: "Welcome, Rāhula!"
"Excellent, Rāhula!
It has been a long time since you last came;
take this seat. As directed, Rāhula sat upon it.
Having sat down, he addressed the upāsaka, saying: "Upāsaka!

Do I not engage in things that are improper for you, things that are painful, things that are wrong, things that are impure, things that are unbecoming of a śramaṇa, or things that are not in accordance [with the Dharma]?"
When he had spoken thus, the upāsaka said,
"You have done nothing improper toward me, nor anything even contrary to my wishes.
Having heard these words, Rāhula rose from his seat and returned to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and reported the matter to the Buddha exactly as it had occurred.
Thereupon, after the World-Honored One had convened an assembly of the Saṃgha for this matter, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are ten kinds of unlawful giving, unlawful receiving, and unlawful use."
Having given to one bhikṣu, to take it away and give it to two is an unrighteous gift, an unrighteous acceptance, and an unrighteous use.
Having given to two, to take from those two and give it to two others is an unrighteous gift, an unrighteous acceptance, and an unrighteous use.
To take from two and give to many is an unrighteous act of giving and receiving, and an unrighteous use [of wealth].
To give to many and then take it away to give to one is likewise an unrighteous act of giving, receiving, and using.

Having given to one, he seizes it and gives it to two; having seized much, he gives it to the Saṃgha; having given to the Saṃgha, he seizes it and gives it to another Saṃgha; having given to two Saṃghas, he seizes it and gives it to the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha; having seized it from the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, he gives it to another Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha. When the Saṃgha is divided into two factions and has not yet reconciled, he seizes one group and gives it to another group, either favoring one or not favoring the other. This is an illegal gift, an illegal acceptance, and an illegal use.
The former gift is a true gift; the latter gift is not a gift.
Although a donor has mastery over what they give, it can only be properly guarded [by another].
The king is the lord of the land, and thus the master of the bed and bedding.
"The robes and bowl belong to the bhikṣu; he should use these.
Thus the Buddha spoke, yet he had not yet laid down a precept for the śramaṇas regarding this matter.
Now, in a vineyard that had an owner, a bhikṣu climbed a tree to gather fruit without permission. He climbed the tree and took the fruit.
To take fruit [not given] is a *pāyattika*.
If one takes fruit worth five *kārsāpaṇas*, it constitutes the offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (abandoning what is not accepted).
This applies to all kinds of raw fruit and all kinds of raw flowers.
In a sugarcane grove that has an owner, if a bhikṣu cuts and carries away sugarcane without being given permission, it is a pāyattika offense.
If the fruit is worth five māsakas or more, it constitutes the offense of "abandonment due to non-acceptance" (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
Regarding lotus roots, whether they have an owner or not: if a bhikṣu digs up the earth to take one that has an owner, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
To cut it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If its value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it constitutes the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

In this manner, regarding all such matters, if a bhikṣu receives two portions at a place where food is being distributed, and the value of the lower portion is five māsakas or more, he commits the offense of *pārājika* (defeat); furthermore, both individuals involved commit the offense of false speech.
The same applies to requesting two portions of rice.
If he is near a border region, a bhikṣu who instructs kings to attack one another commits the offense of *pārājika* (expulsion).
If one personally leads [the army], it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
To raise an army for mutual assault constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If the value of what is obtained is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it constitutes an offense of "abandonment and non-acceptance" (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*).
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the village of Vāsavagrāmaka on the banks of the Kimikālā River—the Qin name for which is "Winding"—together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Contemplate the impurities; contemplate them thoroughly until you are weary from sitting."
One should never forget the contemplation of the impurity of food.
Why is this? Because one who contemplates the foulness of the body attains great fruits, merit, and blessings.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The World-Honored One has taught the practice of contemplating the foulness of impure secretions,
even up to sitting and contemplating the impurity of food."
Having practiced this contemplation on the impurity of conduct, one shall obtain great fruits and the retribution of great merit.
Venerable friends, you should all together exhort yourselves to contemplate the impurity of conduct, even to the point of sitting and contemplating the impurity of food.
"Having observed this practice, we shall obtain great fruit and the retribution of great merit.
These bhikṣus contemplated the practice of impurity, contemplated it intensely, and even sat contemplating the impurity of food.
When practicing this contemplation, one grows weary of this foul body where a multitude of afflictions converge; one feels self-reproach, asking: "For what purpose do I use this body?
When shall I be liberated from this suffering?"

For example, it is like a robust man, peerless in his handsome appearance, whose body is adorned with various precious jewels and necklaces; who bathes at the proper times and anoints his body with fragrant perfumes; who wears a jeweled crown and floral garlands upon his head; whose body is clothed in celestial robes that do not collect dust; whose hands and feet are soft and supple, and whose hair is a deep blue-black color; and whose beard and mustache are luxuriant, making him the most excellent among men.

If one were to take a dead snake, a dead dog, and a human corpse—blue-black, bloated, festering with pus, with portions of flesh not yet consumed scattered in various places, stained with blood, foul-smelling, and impure—and use these three corpses as a garland for this person’s neck, the person would find it utterly loathsome; a multitude of afflictions would gather, and he would feel self-reproach, wondering: "When shall I soon be freed from this calamity?"
In this way, those bhikṣus contemplated all manner of impurities, even sitting to contemplate the practice of the impurity of food; weary of this foul body, they thought to themselves:
"When shall I die?"

At that time, there was a bhikṣu among the assembly who, through the practice of contemplating impurity, became so weary and disgusted with himself that he left his original seat and went to where the śramaṇa Kūṭa—a hunter by birth—was staying.
He said to the śramaṇa Kūṭa, "Venerable Kūṭa, if you can kill me, I shall reward you with my three robes."
At that time, the śramaṇa Kokālika took a sharp blade in his hand and took the monk's life.
Having killed the monk, he went with the blade to the river Bahukā and sat there to wash the blood from it.
At that time, a Māra-deva standing upon the water manifested his supernormal powers above the surface and praised the śramaṇa Bhikṣu Kūṭa, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! O Worthy and Sublime One, you have accomplished great merit!"
"One who is capable of exerting diligence can deliver those not yet delivered, liberate those not yet liberated, and lead those not yet to parinirvāṇa to parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the śramaṇa Ghaṭīkāra thought to himself:

"It is truly as the deva says; I shall gain great merit by delivering those among the bhikṣus not yet delivered, liberating those not yet liberated, and leading those not yet to parinirvāṇa to parinirvāṇa."
"Since I have already been ordained as a śramaṇa, I shall additionally receive the three robes.
Thus he rejoiced within himself.
At that time, the śramaṇa Kokālika, having embraced this perverted view, took up the aforementioned knife and returned to the midst of the assembly, going from room to room to proclaim his command:
"I shall deliver those who have not been delivered, liberate those who have not been liberated, and cause those who have not attained parinirvāṇa to attain parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the bhikṣus practiced the contemplation of impurity, even to the point of becoming weary of their own foul bodies and loathing them as filthy and evil.
The bhikṣus from each of the cells came out, went to where the śramaṇa Kūṭa was, and spoke these words:
"If you can take us and sever our lives, we shall reward you with our three robes."
At that time, the śramaṇa Kokālika took up a sharp sword and killed one, two, three, four, five, and even up to sixty bhikṣus, severing their lives.

Then, on the fifteenth day, when it was time for the recitation of the precepts, the World-Honored One prepared a high seat and sat down amidst the great assembly. Having surveyed all the bhikṣus, he saw that those seated were few and insufficient to mention.
The World-Honored One, knowing [the reason for] the question, asked Ānanda: "How is it, Ānanda?
Why is the assembly of monks gathered so sparsely today for the recitation of the precepts?"

Then Ānanda, having received what the World-Honored One had spoken and having properly upheld it, knelt with his right knee on the ground, bared his right shoulder, adjusted his robes, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"The World-Honored One has instructed the bhikṣus to contemplate the practice of impurity, even to the point of practicing the contemplation of the foulness of the body’s odors; having sat and contemplated the perception of food, they shall attain great fruit and great merit."
At that time, the bhikṣus said to one another:
"Virtuous ones, you should know that when the World-Honored One spoke of contemplating impurity and practicing the path of impurity, he attained great fruits and great merit."
"We should together contemplate the practice of impurity; having practiced the contemplation of impurity, we shall obtain great fruit and great merit.
At that time, the bhikṣus contemplated the practice of impurity, and having practiced the contemplation of impurity, they grew weary of this foul body.

For example, suppose there were a strong man, peerlessly handsome, his body adorned with various precious jewels and necklaces; who bathes and perfumes his body at all times and anoints it with fragrances; who wears a jeweled crown and floral garlands upon his head, and is clad in celestial robes that gather no dust; whose hands and feet are soft and supple, and whose hair is a deep blue-black; and whose beard and mustache are luxuriant—such a person would be the most excellent among men.

If one were to take three corpses—a dead snake, a dead dog, and a dead human—swollen, blue-black, festering with pus, with portions of flesh not yet consumed scattered in various places, stained with blood and foul with impurities, and place these three corpses as a garland around this person's neck; the person would find it utterly loathsome and distressing, and would feel self-reproach, thinking: "When shall I soon be freed from this affliction?"
Thus, these many bhikṣus contemplated all manner of impurities, even sitting to contemplate food and the practice of impurity; weary of this foul body, they thought to themselves:
"When shall we die?"

At that time, there was a bhikṣu among the assembly who, through the practice of contemplating impurity, became so weary and disgusted with himself that he left his original seat and went to where the śramaṇa Kūṭa of the hunter clan was. He said to the śramaṇa Kūṭa:
"If the venerable Bhikṣu Eka could kill me, I would reward you with my three robes."
At that time, the śramaṇa Kokālika took a sharp knife in his hand and took the monk’s life.
Having killed this monk, he went with the sharp knife to the Bahukā River and sat there to wash the blood from it.
At that time, a Māra-deva standing upon the water praised the śramaṇa Kūṭadanta:
"Excellent, excellent! O Worthy and Sublime One!"

Having accomplished great merit, he is able to deliver those bhikṣus who have not yet crossed over, liberate those who have not yet been liberated, and cause those who have not yet attained parinirvāṇa to attain parinirvāṇa.
Then the śramaṇa Kūṭadanta thought to himself: "It is truly as the deva says;

I have attained great merit, for I have caused those bhikṣus who had not crossed over to cross over, those who were not liberated to be liberated, and those who had not attained parinirvāṇa to attain parinirvāṇa."
"Once I have ordained as a śramaṇa, I shall additionally receive the three robes.
Thus he congratulated himself with joy.
Then, having accepted this perverted view, the śramaṇa Kokālika took the aforementioned knife and returned to the assembly, going from room to room to issue a proclamation:
"I am able to deliver those who have not been delivered, to liberate those who have not been liberated, and to lead to parinirvāṇa those who have not attained parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the bhikṣus contemplated the practice of impurity, even to the point of becoming weary of their own foul, stinking, and loathsome bodies.
The bhikṣus from each of the rooms came out, went to where the śramaṇa Kūṭa was, and spoke these words:
"If you can take us and kill us, ending our lives, we shall reward you with our three robes."
At that time, the śramaṇa Kokālika took up a sharp sword and killed one, two, three, four, five, and even up to sixty bhikṣus, ending their lives.
For this reason, the bhikṣu-saṃgha rarely recited the precepts.
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will explain other skillful means so that these bhikṣus may attain the realization of immeasurable wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"One should train in mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), cultivating its practice extensively; one must not lose the practice of mindfulness of breathing even for the duration of a meal or a breath.
Why is this? By practicing mindfulness of breathing and cultivating its practice extensively, one will later attain great fruits and receive the retribution of great merit."
Among these bhikṣus, if a bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon a village or a town, he puts on his robes and takes up his bowl at the proper time and enters the village to beg for food.
One should protect the body and focus the six sense faculties so as not to lose the supreme practice.
If, when the eye sees forms, one does not give rise to thoughts of conceptualization or attachment, practicing in this manner, then the faculty of the eye is perfected.

In this way, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, he does not give rise to thoughts of conceptual attachment toward phenomena; when the mind is not distracted by them, it becomes the faculty of the mind (*manendriya*).

After begging for alms in a village, he takes up his robes and bowl and places them in his dwelling. First washing his feet, he lifts his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) onto his shoulder and seeks a secluded place—such as beneath a quiet tree, in an open space, a grass hut, outside a garden, on level ground, in a cemetery, a mountain valley, or a rock cave—and dwells there.
Whether one has gone to a secluded dwelling or beneath a tree, one spreads the *niṣīdana* and sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
Sitting upright without leaning or slouching, one binds the mindfulness to the tip of the nose.

While the bhikṣu is mindful of the breath, he is mindful as the breath goes out and mindful as the breath comes in; he knows when the breath going out is long and knows when the breath coming in is long; he knows when the breath going out is short and knows when the breath coming in is short; he fully perceives the breath going out from all the pores of his body and fully perceives the breath coming in from all the pores of his body.
If the mind is concentrated, one is aware of the exhaling breath as it ceases and aware of the inhaling breath as it ceases.

With body, speech, and mind, one is aware of the exhaling breath as it ceases and aware of the inhaling breath as it ceases; the exhaling breath is *praśrabdhi* (tranquility), and the inhaling breath is *praśama* (calm).

For example, it is like a spinning wheel or a whirling top; whether the whirling cord is long or short, one knows it as such, and this land also makes such wheels. In the southern lands, they call them *bubuo* (whirling tops), and the wheels in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* are the same as these.
When a bhikṣu thus practices the mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), extensively cultivating this practice until he brings to mind the cessation of the out-breath and in-breath;
by practicing and extensively cultivating this mindfulness of breathing in this way, he attains great fruit and the retribution of great merit.
At that time, the bhikṣus exhorted one another, saying:
"The World-Honored One, out of compassion for you all, has taught the mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), desiring that we cultivate its practice extensively."
Having extensively cultivated the practice of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), one attains great rewards and possesses great merit.
Come, all of you, go together to that place, extensively cultivate the practice of mindfulness of breathing, and do not lose mindfulness of breathing.
"Why is this? By practicing *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) and extensively cultivating that practice, one attains great rewards and possesses great merit.
At that time, the bhikṣus practiced *ānāpānasmṛti*, extensively cultivating that practice, attained immeasurable wisdom, and realized the path of Arhatship.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda approached the World-Honored One, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The World-Honored One has extensively explained the practice of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti), even up to the extensive cultivation of its practice.”
"The bhikṣus, following the holy teachings of the Buddha, practiced *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) and all attained immeasurable wisdom, realizing the path of Arhatship.

At that time, for these reasons and by means of these sublime practices, the World-Honored One assembled the Saṃgha of harmonious monks, endowed with the ten merits. The World-Honored One established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"Bhikṣus, you must guard against this matter."

If a bhikṣu, with his own hand, intentionally takes the life of a human being or one of human form—whether by wielding a blade himself, causing another to wield it, or exhorting another to die; [he commits an offense].
If one praises death, or speaks these words:
"Alas, this man! What is the use of this painful life?"
"Your life is not worth living;
death would be better for you. Thus, from that mind, the person forms this thought and, through countless means, encourages another to die or praises death.
"If such a person were to die [as a result], such a bhikṣu would be abandoned and not accepted.
If a bhikṣu, in a secluded place, takes up bows, swords, crossbows with triggers, traps, or pits for the purpose of killing a person, he commits a *pārājika* offense and is not to be accepted.
If a bhikṣu slanders an official to the authorities and causes a person to be killed by the power of that office, he commits a pārājika offense and is not to be accepted [as a monk].

If a bhikṣu is possessed by a vettālava spirit, causing it to rise up and kill someone, or if he performs incantations or uses medicinal drugs to kill someone, he commits a pārājika offense and is not to be accepted.
If a bhikṣu sets a snare to kill a person by strangling their neck, he commits a pārājika offense and is not to be received back into the community.

If a bhikṣu prepares emetic or purgative medicines, or administers them via nasal drops or enemas, or performs bloodletting by acupuncture, or applies medicinal ointments to the eyes, or administers powders and other substances with the intent to kill a person, he commits a pārājika offense and is not to be received back into the community.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, with the intent to kill, presses a pregnant woman’s abdomen with his hand or instructs another to do so,
and if the child or the woman dies, he commits a pārājika offense and is not to be reinstated.
Whether it be a single death or two deaths, both constitute a *pārājika* offense and one does not receive [the precepts].

If a bhikṣu, harboring a murderous intent, instructs another to throw themselves into fire, enter water, or leap from a cliff—should he kill a person in this manner, it is a *pārājika* offense and one does not receive [the precepts]. Because such instances are frequent among non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), this rule was established as a precept.
If a bhikṣu, harboring a murderous intent, secretly composes a letter of slander and instructs the messenger to say that the recipient has committed a grave offense, thereby causing him to be killed—
if he is killed, [the instigator] commits a pārājika offense and is not accepted [into the Saṃgha].
Within the mother’s womb, two faculties are obtained:

the body faculty and the life faculty. If a bhikṣu, harboring an intent to kill, uses incantations to cause an abortion, he who commits such a killing incurs a pārājika offense and is no longer accepted [in the Sangha].
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Bakula was staying in a workshop within a smithy; because the smiths established this park, it was named after them. While residing in his dwelling there, he fell ill and suffered from disease.
The Venerable Bhaddā assisted [the Buddha] by attending to him and providing him with water and food.
At that time, Bakkula said to Bhaddā, "Go to the place where the Buddha is;
carrying my name, prostrate yourself before the World-Honored One and ask whether his holy body is healthy, strong, and at ease."
"Are you physically strong enough to practice the Path?
Go and say these words:
'Recently, the bhikṣu Bhakara has fallen ill and is suffering in his dwelling within the workshop garden.'"
This bhikṣu bows from afar to the World-Honored One: Is your holy body healthy, strong, and agile?
Are you vigorous in your daily activities and able to practice the Path?
The bhikṣu Bakula wishes to come and visit the World-Honored One, but he suffers from illness and lacks the physical strength to reach the World-Honored One’s presence to pay his respects.
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will deign to come to the Forge Garden for the sake of the bhikṣu Bakula.

At that time, the bhikṣu Panthaka very quickly accepted the words of the bhikṣu Bakula and went to where the World-Honored One was. Prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed him thus:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you would deign to go to the blacksmith’s park to visit the bhikṣu Bakula, for the sake of the bhikṣu Bakula.
The World-Honored One remained silent and did not reply.

At that time, seeing that the World-Honored One had consented by remaining silent, Piṇḍola-vatsa rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and departed.
Not long after Piṇḍola-vatsa had left, the World-Honored One arose from meditation following his meal and went to the Sūkarakhata Park where the bhikṣu Bakula was staying.
When the bhikṣu Bakula saw the Buddha coming from afar, he wished to rise from his seat, but he lacked the physical strength to do so.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the bhikṣu Bakula:
"There is no need to rise; simply remain lying down."
"There is another seat; I shall ascend it.
Once he was seated, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣu Bakula:
"Are you able to endure this gruel? Has it been digested?"
“Is the pain and suffering within your body subsiding?
Is there an increase in what is felt to be subsiding, or a decrease in what is felt to be increasing?
The bhikṣu Bakula replied to the Buddha:
“Yes, World-Honored One!
I am unable to endure the gruel; it has no digestive power. There is painful distress, which only increases and does not diminish. I perceive its increase, but do not perceive its diminution.”
It is just as if, World-Honored One, a strong man were to wrap a rope around his head; this person would experience such pain and agony in his head.
So it is, World-Honored One!
My headache is no different from that person's.
For this reason, I cannot endure gruel or porridge; there is no digestion, only an increase and no decrease. I perceive the increase but do not perceive the decrease.
"It is as if, World-Honored One, a strong man were to take a sharp blade and drill it into the crown of one's head; such would be the suffering and pain at the crown of the head.
Now, World-Honored One, I have a headache."
It is likewise; there is only an increase in awakening, with no diminution.
World-Honored One, it is like a strong man who seizes a knife and pierces the belly of an ox; the ox suffers from this abdominal pain beyond description.
I am now just like this; my abdominal pain is exactly as his was.

World-Honored One, it is as if two strong men were to seize a weak person and, each grasping his hands and feet, turn him around over a pit of fire; the pain of that person would be beyond description.
"World-Honored One, my body is now like this.
For this reason, I cannot endure even thin gruel; I only perceive an increase [in suffering] and do not perceive any decrease."
“World-Honored One, I now wish to take up a blade to stab myself to death; I cannot endure this life.
The Buddha said:
“I ask you further, Bhaggava, and you should answer me:
Regarding what is called ‘form,’ is it permanent or impermanent?”
He replied, “It is impermanent. [The Buddha asked,] “Regarding that which is suffering and impermanent, is it suffering or is it pleasure?”
He replied: "It is suffering,
World-Honored One!"

"If something is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would there be anyone who, upon hearing that various paths have been realized therein, would say with faith: 'This is mine' or 'This is not mine'?"
"No, World-Honored One! Why is that, Bhāradvāja?"
“Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness permanent or impermanent? “They are impermanent,
World-Honored One.”
“If it is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?
He replied, “It is suffering.”
“World-Honored One!

If things are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would there be anyone who, upon hearing of the realization of the various paths regarding these, would say, ‘This is mine’ or ‘This is not mine,’ and yet possess faith?”
"No, World-Honored One! For this reason, Bhārgava!"

Whatever form there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; great or small; good or bad; far or near—all of this is neither "mine" nor "not mine," being entirely non-existent; one contemplates all phenomena as equal.
For this reason, Bhakhula!
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—whether past, future, or present—even up to the contemplation of all phenomena as equal. Bhakhula!

Having heard the teaching on the realization of the various paths, one awakens to the fact that form is empty and non-existent, thereby attaining liberation. Once liberation is attained, wisdom arises: "My birth and death are now exhausted; I have reached pure conduct; what was to be done has been accomplished; I shall no longer dwell in a womb."
In this way, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness will no longer undergo renewed existence, nor will they even dwell within a womb.
For this reason, Bhakhula! Do not fear, do not be terrified;
you shall no longer enter the evil realms, you shall not be born within the evil realms, and wherever you go, you shall encounter no evil.
When the World-Honored One had finished speaking, he returned directly to the vihāra.
That very night at midnight, two celestial beings of peerless appearance came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and stood to one side.
One celestial being came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Venerable Bakula has attained the third degree of liberation with dull faculties.
Next, a second celestial being came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The Venerable Bakula has attained liberation within liberation; there are two types of liberation: first, liberation by occasion (*samaya-vimukti*); second, liberation without doubt (*akopya-vimukti*).

'Occasion' refers to the dharma of faith and absence of doubt. Regarding the dull-facultied and sharp-facultied dharmas across the three times, that person spoke of six Arhats as having liberation without doubt, while four and below have liberation by occasion. The fifth is able to penetrate the six fire-gases, whereas those four and below cannot."
The person said, "This is indeed the case for those with three [defilements] or fewer; it is merely a teaching concerning those with four or more at this time.
Since this person has three or fewer, they are called 'protected'.
Having spoken these words, the devas paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
*Pinaiye*, Scroll One; *Pinaiye*, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
At that time, during that very night, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Just now, two devas came and inquired about this matter; the Venerable Bhāradvāja has attained liberation through protection."
On the following day, when questioned, he attained liberation from liberation and departed after receiving his instructions.
The Buddha addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"Go to the smithy at the park where the bhikṣu Bhakhula resides. Within the walls of the Jetavana there are six monasteries; this is the first. He spoke these words:"

"Listen, sir, to the teaching of the World-Honored One and the inquiry of the deva: do not fear, do not be terrified; you shall not be born in an evil realm, nor shall you arise from an evil realm, and there shall be no evil in the place where you are born."
"This is the teaching of the Blessed One.
Last night, two devas came to my place; one of them asked:
'Venerable Bhāradvāja, have you attained the liberation of protection?'"
On the second day, he asked:
"Venerable Bakula, have you attained liberation through liberation?
"This, Bakula! [he replied].
"This is the language of the devas.
Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣu went to the smithy.
At that time, Bakula said to the bhikṣu who was attending to his illness:
"Venerable friends, lift me up onto a bed and carry me out;
I am unable to live, so I now wish to take a knife and commit suicide.
The bhikṣus immediately placed him on a bed and carried him out. At that time, a great assembly of bhikṣus was walking back and forth outside the gate.
A bhikṣu sent by that Buddha went to where the walking-bhikṣu was and spoke these words:
"Where does the bhikṣu Bakula reside?
I wish to go and pay my respects to him."
The bhikṣus replied:
"The bhikṣu Bakula is now being carried out of the door; he is holding a knife and intends to stab himself to death.
If you wish to pay him your respects, you may go."
Then that bhikṣu went straight to where Bakula was.
Seeing a bhikṣu approaching from afar, Bakula said to the attendant who was nursing him:
"Stop for a moment at the bedside and wait for this bhikṣu to come."
He then stopped the bed.
When that bhikṣu arrived, he spoke to Bakula exactly as the Buddha had instructed, saying all of it up to: "This is the Buddha’s teaching; this is the word of the devas."

Bakkula replied: “What I have attained, the World-Honored One also knows; what I have seen, the World-Honored One also knows. Therefore, I have no doubt regarding whether form is permanent or impermanent, and so on, up to volitional formations and consciousness. Furthermore, as for that which is impermanent, suffering, empty, and subject to change, and regarding all phenomena, having heard the realization of the śramaṇa, there is neither ‘mine’ nor ‘not mine’ in them at all; I see them as they truly are, with equal vision.”
What I know, the devas also know; what I see, the devas also see. Therefore, I have no doubt regarding permanence or impermanence, and so forth, up to having equal vision and being free from doubt.
"Driven by the pressure of past karmic retribution, I shall take my own life with this blade.
Having spoken these words, he raised his sword and cut his own throat.
All the attendant monks who were tending to him were filled with doubt.
"We have not committed a *pārājika* offense, have we?
Let us carry him out together and go to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha replied:

"If one, out of a sense of revulsion, hands over a knife with the intent to kill, or instructs another to cause death, or carries [the victim] away with the intent to kill, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense that is not to be accepted."
"If one possesses loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; if one complies with the wishes of the sick person and does not oppose them;

and if one does not commit a *pārājika* offense, one shall not be expelled. There were bhikṣus residing within the realm of Kosala who repeatedly incited two kings to fight. If a bhikṣu acted as a messenger to deliver letters, or led an army into battle, or killed people himself, or incited others to kill, he was to be expelled for a *pārājika* offense.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Bamboo Grove, Kalandaka, in the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, Devadatta had been reciting the sūtras and studying the Way for twelve years; he received instruction without ever flagging or becoming weary. During this period, he heard all the sūtras spoken by the Buddha and committed them entirely to memory. He frequented mountain caves, secluded trees, open spaces, and cemeteries as companions to Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Nandi, Kapphiṇa, and other bhikṣus.
While Devadatta harbored no ill will toward the World-Honored One, he did not transgress even a hair’s breadth of the precepts.
Later, when he actually gave rise to an evil mind toward the World-Honored One, he then committed a breach of the precepts.

The floors of all those halls and rooms were completely covered with sitting mats; previously, the World-Honored One had established a precept that one must not enter without having washed one's feet, yet at that time, Devadatta entered without having washed his feet.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā said to Devadatta:
"How can this be, Devadatta!
The World-Honored One has established a precept stating that one must not enter without having washed one's feet."
Devadatta replied, "What a wretched and evil bhikṣuṇī! Do you think your knowledge of the precepts can surpass mine?
He then struck the bhikṣuṇī on the head with a fist as powerful as that of a strongman, and the bhikṣuṇī immediately passed away.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the World-Honored One as it had occurred.
The World-Honored One told them:
"Have pity on this evil man who has incurred limitless transgression."
"This bhikṣuṇī has attained the path of arhatship.
Then, on account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and established a precept:
"If a bhikṣu, or a man, or a woman, should take life with their own hands, the offender commits a pārājika offense and is not to be received back into the order."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana was struck by a staff held in the hand of the brahmin Daṇḍapāṇi; the blow was like crushing a bamboo tube, and his life came to an end.
The people of that country immediately learned that the Venerable Maudgalyāyana had been killed by the brahmin Daṇḍapāṇi, his body crushed and mangled like a flattened bamboo tube.

When Aśvajit and Punarvasu heard that their teacher had been killed by a man, their fury blazed forth and the hair on their bodies stood on end; with the strength of great athletes, they seized and slaughtered every last one of the brahmins from the Daṇḍa clan.
The Buddha, observing this matter, knowing it, addressed the bhikṣus Aśvajit and Pūrṇa:
“I shall now explain to you the fourfold dharma-meaning, the four noble truths.”

At that time, the horse trainer Punnavaṭa was filled with shame and embarrassment; he knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Our transgressions are heavy, and we do not dare to hear this profound meaning of the Dharma."
The World-Honored One questioned him earnestly, even up to three times.
Out of compassion for this evil man—who was far removed from me and far removed from the profound Dharma—the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, established this precept for the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu kills a person with his own hand or instructs another to kill, he commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion."

"These two individuals have fallen among the nāgas, dwelling in the waters of Mount Shilihutou in the kingdom of Gandhāra to the west. Because they were angry that the Buddha did not previously preach the Dharma to them, they intend to emerge from the water and destroy the Buddha-dharma."
Suddenly, a transformation Buddha appeared before him and stood there, saying:
"You! You wish to hear the four profound meanings of the Dharma, do you not?"
His anger then ceased.
Such instances occurred more than once.
These two individuals were the younger half-brothers of the Buddha; at that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Bhikṣu Yaśas was accompanied by two hundred and fifty disciples;
the Venerable Bhadrika Bālaputra was likewise accompanied by two hundred and fifty disciples.
Coming from the kingdom of Kosala to the city of Śrāvastī, he wished to visit the World-Honored One and pay his respects.
At that time, various bhikṣus were conversing outside the gate of the Jetavana Monastery, and the sound reached within the gate.
The World-Honored One heard the loud sound; knowing its cause, he asked Ānanda, "Who is outside the gate whose voices are so loud that they reach all the way here?"
Then Ānanda reported in full to the World-Honored One:
"While these bhikṣus were engaged in debate, a great crowd of people gathered and their voices became increasingly loud.
He then dispatched Ānanda.
He said to the group of Yaśas and the group of Bhadrika,
"The World-Honored One has informed you that you must not observe the summer retreat here in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, immediately went to where the group of Yaśas and the group of Bhadrika were.
“The World-Honored One has commanded you all that you must not observe the rains retreat within Śrāvastī.
Thereupon, the Venerable Yaśas and the group led by Bhadrika went to the banks of the Bahuka River and constructed huts to observe the rains retreat.
During that year of famine for the people, when frost, hail, and locusts devoured the grain and alms were difficult to obtain,
the bhikṣus thought to themselves: "Do you all know?"
"Now that grain is expensive, and with frost, hail, and locusts devouring the crops, it is difficult to obtain food through begging.
Let us go together to the houses of the elders in the kingdom of Vaiśālī and each praise one another, saying:
'Do you know, elders?'"
