This bhikṣu, named so-and-so and of such-and-such a clan, has attained the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna; he has also reached the [four immeasurables of] loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; he has attained the four formless attainments, śamatha and vipaśyanā, and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti); and he has realized the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship.
Having spoken these words together and praised one another, they shall thereafter receive offerings in this land.
Kings, ministers, elders, brahmins, those who practice the Way, and commoners shall provide them with robes, alms-food, bedding, and medicine for their ailments.
At that time, when the bhikṣus entered the country of Vaiśālī, the elders there praised one another, saying:
"Elders, you should know that this certain bhikṣu is named so-and-so and belongs to such-and-such a clan; he has attained the fruit of srotāpanna, up to and including the fruit of arhatship."
At that time, all the elders believed him and, thinking he had attained the Way, provided the assembly of monks with seasonal offerings of robes, food, and drink.
It is the constant rule of the Buddhas that there are two occasions for the gathering of the Saṃgha:

during the third month of spring—according to the foreign system of dividing the year into three seasons—and during the month following the summer retreat. On these two occasions, they go to the Buddha and their teachers; likewise, on these two occasions, they go to the Buddha’s presence to pay homage, behold him, and receive the Dharma teachings he has spoken, thinking, "We shall study and recite them during the summer retreat."

After the year has passed and the summer retreat is concluded, during the three months of the rainy season, he mends his robes; when the work on the robes is finished in a single day, he takes up his bowl and proceeds to where the Buddha is.
These two periods are times of great assemblies for the Sangha.

At that time, the bhikṣus who were observing the summer retreat on the banks of the Bahukamata River finished mending their robes after three months and completed them in one day. They then proceeded to Śrāvastī, to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, and approached the Buddha.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when a bhikṣu arrives from afar, they first ask: "During your summer retreat, were you able to recite the sūtras and practice the Path without weariness?
Then, with these words and this meaning, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"O bhikṣus, in your recitation of the sūtras and practice of the Path, have you been free from weariness?"
The bhikṣus replied: “We are not exhausted, World-Honored One!”
“The śramaṇas who observed the summer retreat at the Bahukā River were plump and robust, with their veins full and swelling;
whereas the śramaṇas who observed the summer retreat in Śrāvastī were emaciated, their complexions lacked luster, and their physical strength was meager.”
The śramaṇas by the banks of the Ganges said to the bhikṣus from Śrāvastī,
"Why are you so emaciated and why do your faces lack luster? They replied:
"Do you not know? In this country, grain is expensive and it is difficult to obtain through begging.
For this reason, my body is emaciated and dark, and my face lacks luster."
“Why is it that you alone are so plump and flourishing, with such radiant and glowing countenances?
These bhikṣus explained the situation to him in detail.
Upon hearing these words, the emaciated bhikṣu was greatly astonished by the reason.
“How is it that you, sirs, on account of some trifling, putrid food, claim this to be a state of superior manhood?
These monks then severely rebuked those monks:
“How can a monk do this, when the World-Honored One has, by countless skillful means, spoken of the fault of false speech and praised the virtue of one who does not speak falsely?”
The bhikṣus each went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
Knowing [the situation], the World-Honored One asked:
"Bhikṣus, is it true that you have done this?"
The bhikṣus felt ashamed and, placing both knees on the ground with palms joined toward the Buddha,
said: “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One said:
"How is it, bhikṣu? Was it not previously for the sake of foolish people that I, through countless skillful means, spoke of the fault of false speech and praised the virtue of not speaking falsely?"
"How have you, sirs, planted this root of evil?

With countless skillful means, the Buddha, on account of these circumstances, assembled the Saṃgha; having fulfilled ten merits, he established the precepts for the śramaṇas so that all śramaṇas might understand this meaning:
"If a bhikṣu, without knowing or seeing the qualities of a superior person (uttarimanussa-dhamma)..."
"I have attained various virtues; I know and I see them.
I am well-established in the unconditioned; I know this and I see this.
If, at another time, someone were to ask that bhikṣu:
"Are you an Arhat? He replied, "No; I am without such status."
Having previously spoken these words, one should purify that transgression.
One must recall the actions performed—having known while claiming not to know, or having seen while claiming not to see—which were empty, false, and deceptive speech.
"If one does not purify their transgression and intentionally commits it again, that bhikṣu is defeated and no longer receives [the precepts].
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a young bhikṣu who had been practicing the Way for but a short time; he did not fully understand the Dharma or its departure from the mundane, his faculty of mindfulness was not yet settled, and his conduct lacked discipline. When he visited the homes of others, he claimed to possess the qualities of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*).

At that time, a great assembly of bhikṣus took up their alms bowls, donned their robes, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. There they heard that a young bhikṣu had claimed for himself, "I possess the qualities of a superior person."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they obtained food and left the city, going to where the young bhikṣu was and saying to him:
"Do not go frequently to the homes of others, and do not claim for yourself the state of a superior person."
The young bhikṣu replied,
"If the elder bhikṣus frequently visit the homes of others, why should I not be permitted to do so?
Thus he was admonished, yet he did not comply.
The elder bhikṣus spoke to the other elder bhikṣus, and they went to the place where the Buddha was and reported this matter in detail.
The World-Honored One said:
"It is just as if, bhikṣus!"

In a vast, desolate deep mountain where there is a spring, there are dragon-elephants who descend into the spring to select lotus roots; they wash away the mud until they are perfectly clean and then take them to eat.
These dragon-elephants each eat their fill, possessing great strength and vigor; they are joyful and not violent, do not harm one another, and are free from the suffering of death.
Among the great elephant herds, the smaller dragon-elephants, when descending into deep springs or marshes to gather lotus roots, do not wash them clean but eat them together with the mud.
Having eaten, his physical strength grew even more feeble and he no longer experienced joy; for this reason, they began to kill one another, resulting in the suffering of death.
Thus, the elder bhikṣu became free from lust, anger, and delusion, long cultivated pure conduct, and no longer frequented the homes of donors.
Because he does not frequently visit the households of donors, those who do not yet believe in the Dharma come to seek faith, while those who already believe are led to deepen their faith.
If he receives items for which he has offered prayers of blessing, his mind remains unstained by attachment and free from envy.
If one receives offerings from the faithful and digests them without fault, without slandering others regarding their suffering, and without deceitful intent—

yet among this assembly of elder bhikṣus there are young bhikṣus who have studied the Path for but a short time, who do not yet understand the Dharma and have not departed from the truth, and who praise themselves, claiming to possess the qualities of a superior person (uttara-manuṣya-dharma).
Wherever they go, those who do not believe in the Dharma increase their lack of faith, while those who already believe see their original resolve diminished.
Regarding the offerings of faith they receive, they harbor thoughts of attachment, form friendships out of jealousy, and consume the food without understanding impermanence.
"Once he has eaten it, his countenance lacks luster and he is devoid of physical strength; for this reason, there is the suffering of death.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and established a precept for the śramaṇas:

"If a bhikṣu goes to the house of a householder and constantly praises himself by claiming to possess the qualities of a superior person (uttaramanuṣyadharma), that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, in Rājagṛha.

At that time, Devadatta first sought ordination as a śramaṇa; he brought three hundred thousand taels of gold, and the elephant upon which he rode was also worth one hundred thousand taels of gold, as were the trappings for the elephant, all of which were worth one hundred thousand taels of gold each. Furthermore, the robes and ornaments worn by Devadatta were also worth one hundred thousand taels of gold.

Having left the household life, he shaved off his hair and beard and donned the kāṣāya; abandoning his kingdom, he entered the mountains to practice the Way. There he recited the sūtras and received instructions, until he had memorized all the discourses on the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One during that interval.

There are also bhikṣus there who possess great supernormal powers; because of the name of the Jambu tree, this land is called Jambudvīpa. Those bhikṣus with supernormal powers go to gather jambu fruits and bring them back to eat.

Not far from the Jambū tree, there were a great grove of harītakī trees and a great grove of āmalaka trees, each fifty yojanas apart; they would go to the Udañcanī mountain to gather wild non-glutinous rice, which they brought back to eat.
Sometimes he goes to the Tuṣita Heaven, taking celestial ambrosia and bringing it back to eat;
sometimes he goes to the east, south, west, or north, manifesting various transformations as he flies through the void.
Upon seeing this, Devadatta gave rise to thoughts of hatred and envy, thinking:
"When shall I possess such great supernormal powers that I may go beneath the Jambu tree, take its sweet fruit, and eat it; and even fly through the void without any obstruction?"
He then thought to himself:
"I should now first go to the Buddha's dwelling to inquire about the path of supernormal powers (ṛddhi).
He then went to the Buddha's dwelling and inquired about the path of supernormal powers.
The World-Honored One knew that this Devadatta was destined for a crime from which there would be no salvation, and that he would perform useless deeds within this Buddha-dharma.
For this reason, the Buddha said to Devadatta:
"Go; you need not inquire about the path of supernatural powers (ṛddhi). You should simply contemplate impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; reflect upon these matters."
When Devadatta heard this, it did not enter his mind; he still set his thoughts on the supernormal powers (ṛddhi) and again thought to himself:
"Śāriputra is a man of great wisdom; I shall go and ask him about the way of supernormal powers, and he will surely not oppose me."
He immediately went to ask Śāriputra about the way of supernatural powers (ṛddhi).
Seeing that the Buddha did not do so, he did not speak of it to him.
He then thought again:
"This Maudgalyāyana is foremost among the śrāvakas in great supernormal power (ṛddhi); we should go and ask him about the way of supernormal power.
They then went and asked him about the way of supernormal power.
Maudgalyāyana did not speak with him either.
He then thought to himself:

"This Ānanda is my younger brother, and the World-Honored One has also declared him the foremost among the śrāvakas in learning. I shall go and ask him about the way of supernormal powers; he will surely explain the way of supernormal powers to me."
He went to where Ānanda was and asked about the path of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).

At that time, Ānanda had not yet attained supernatural powers and did not consider this matter; furthermore, because his own defilements were not yet exhausted, he explained the supernormal powers exactly as he had heard them.

At that time, Devadatta received the instructions on the path to supernormal powers from Ānanda and did not forget them. He then went to a secluded place—a tree beneath which there was a mountain grove with fruit—and practiced this method day and night without slackening. He soon attained the four mundane dhyānas, and by relying on these dhyānas, he attained supernormal powers.

As previously stated, I vowed to go beneath the Jambu tree to fetch its fruit to eat, and even to take the celestial nectar from the Tuṣita Heaven; through countless skillful means, my manifestations were not of one kind alone.
At that time, Devadatta gave rise to feelings of envy and jealousy, and toward the Tathāgata he further thought:
"As for this śramaṇa Gautama’s birthplace and clan, they cannot surpass mine; he too is of the Śākya clan and I too am of the Śākya clan—what difference is there between us?"
"The reason people come to make offerings is because of his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
I too should now teach and transform others by means of supernormal powers; thus, those who receive my transformation will be many.
He then thought further:
"Now that King Bimbisāra has entered the path of the śramaṇa Gautama as an avaivartika śrāvaka,
I am unable to transform him through my supernormal powers."

Devadatta was exceptionally intelligent and quick-witted; he possessed thorough mastery of astronomy, geography, and the movements of the stars and constellations in the heavens. Observing all the people present, he saw that only Prince Ajātaśatru possessed the complete marks of a sovereign:
"This prince will certainly become king, without a doubt."
"I shall now go and transform the Prince with my supernormal powers, so that this gatekeeper shall receive my instruction.

At that time, Devadatta transformed his body into an elephant and went to the place where Prince Ajātaśatru was; he entered through the wall and emerged from the gate, performing various transformations, desiring to make Prince Ajātaśatru recognize him as Devadatta.
He further manifested as a horse, moving in and out without obstruction; sometimes he would enter through a gate and exit through a non-gate.
Or he transformed various precious jewels into a jeweled crown and placed it upon the knees of Prince Ajātaśatru, whereupon the prince took it and donned it.
Nevertheless, he knew this was a transformation created by Devadatta.
Devadatta further manifested himself as a small child, his body adorned with necklaces of gold and silver, and sat upon the Prince’s lap.
When the Crown Prince took him in his arms to play with him, feeding him with saliva and kissing his mouth, he likewise recognized that this was a transformation created by Devadatta.

At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru gave rise to feelings of jealousy and malice, thinking, "Devadatta’s supernormal powers are now surpassing those of the Buddha. He then provided offerings of clothing, food, drink, bedding, and medicines for the sick; every day he sent five hundred cauldrons of rice to Devadatta’s residence. He also prepared five hundred chariots and, taking his retinue with him, went in person to Devadatta’s residence.
There were also five hundred bhikṣus who were sitting and eating at Devadatta’s place.
At that time, the great assembly of bhikṣus, when the hour arrived, put on their robes, took up their alms bowls, and entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms.
At that time, the bhikṣus heard that Prince Ajātaśatru’s offerings to Devadatta were unsurpassed; consequently, he prepared five hundred chariots and proceeded to Devadatta’s location.
The five hundred bhikṣus who had been led by Devadatta were sitting and eating.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they went to where the Buddha was and reported the matter in detail.
The World-Honored One told them:
"Do not go to where Devadatta receives offerings, and do not give rise to envy.
Why is this? Is there anyone who would not die if they drank a poisonous drug?"
Having already drunk the poison oneself, one further causes others to drink it as well.
For example, bhikṣus!
When the fruit of the *khaṇḍalī* tree grows, the branch breaks; when the seed of bamboo or reed grows, it dies; and as a mule conceives, both its own life and that of the fetus perish together.
Thus it is, bhikṣu!
Devadatta’s offerings have caused him to drink poison himself and to cause others to drink it as well.
It is just like this, bhikṣu!
"If a person of great strength were to seize a staff and strike an evil dog, perhaps breaking its head or nose, would the dog then become less evil?
The bhikṣu replied,
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
As Devadatta thus received such offerings, his mind became increasingly inflamed with desire.
He thought, "This fool shall suffer the retribution of Mount Tai for a long night.
At that time, Devadatta gave rise to this thought:
"I am now making offerings that surpass those for the Tathāgata; why does the Tathāgata restrict the Saṃgha and not allow them to come and receive these offerings?
As soon as Devadatta finished forming this thought, he lost his supernormal powers.
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana was at the Kalinga Valley in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a fellow disciple of Maudgalyāyana named Śarabha, the son of the householder Koṭikarna, who had cultivated the four immeasurable minds and been reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
The Brahmā Śaphaṭa immediately perceived with his divine eye that Devadatta had lost his supernormal power of flight.

Then, in the time it takes a person to bend or extend their arm, the Brahmā Śaphaṭa descended from the Brahma realm to the presence of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana before Mount Kālaṅgara and addressed the Venerable Maudgalyāyana:
"Does the Venerable One know?"
“Devadatta has already lost his supernormal powers.
Maudgalyāyana, you should go and inform the World-Honored One that Devadatta has lost his supernormal powers.
Maudgalyāyana then gave rise to this thought, sat down and entered *samādhi* to observe Devadatta’s mind.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana entered into samādhi and knew that Devadatta had already lost his supernormal powers.
Maudgalyāyana then silently assented to what the deva had said, and the deva returned to the heavens.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana saw that the deva had departed not long before; he immediately sat in samādhi and traveled to the Bamboo Grove.

Not far from the Buddha, he arose from samādhi, adjusted his robes, and approached the Buddha. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“As Śarabha the brahmin said, Devadatta has lost his supernormal powers.”
While these words were being spoken, Devadatta was accompanied by five followers: Gavāmpati, Khaṇḍadravya, Kālodāyin, Samudradatta, and Revata.
The World-Honored One saw from afar that Devadatta was approaching with his five followers. He turned to address Maudgalyāyana:
"Stop, stop! Guard your speech; you need not speak such words."
"When this foolish man arrives, he shall surely speak for himself.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"I shall now enter the samādhi of right reception and remain seated here, so that Devadatta may not see me."
At that time, Devadatta came to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Now the World-Honored One is aged and your physical strength is weak; your years have already reached their end.”
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
Please command the assembly of monks to accept my offerings.
The World-Honored One replied:
"If even when people of great supernormal powers such as Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana came to request the community of monks, I would still not give them to you;
how much less so now that you are in my lap, receiving the spittle and food from others—how could I give you to the community of monks?"
At that time, Devadatta gave rise to this thought:
"Why does the World-Honored One alone praise Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, while cutting off my own merit?"
At that time, Devadatta gave rise to an evil intention; without taking leave of the Buddha, Śāriputra, and Maudgalyāyana, he immediately rose from his seat and departed.
The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Faithful offerings are exceedingly weighty."
A bhikṣu who has fallen into the darkness of human delusion must not claim what he has not attained.
If he is now negligent and fails to recite what he previously memorized, he must not falsely testify that he has attained what he has not realized.
It is like a strong man who cuts his own tendons to make a rope with which to bind his legs and arms, pulling both ends against one another.
This rope wounds the skin and the flesh; when the flesh is exhausted, it wounds the sinews; the sinews are severed and reach the bone, penetrating through the bone to the marrow.
Thus, bhikṣus, you should know that the gift of faith is also like this.

Having fallen into the darkness of human existence, one must not claim attainment when one has not attained it; that which was previously recited, one now neglects and fails to chant. One must not claim realization when one has not realized it.
If there are bhikṣus who accept offerings of faith yet become attached to them as their own property, they wound themselves from the skin all the way through to the marrow of their bones.

"Excellent, bhikṣu! From this day forward you should train yourself thus: regarding the offerings of faith you receive, do not savor them as your own possession; you should accept them exactly as they were given, with a mind free from doubt."
"A bhikṣu should train himself in this way.
Then, for this reason and on this occasion, and so forth, until he was fully endowed with the ten merits, the World-Honored One established a precept for the śramaṇas:

"If a bhikṣu, relying upon worldly dhyāna, gives rise to supernormal powers (ṛddhi) and falsely claims for himself the qualities of a superior person (uttara-manuṣya-dharma), this bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and is no longer accepted [in the Saṃgha]."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know that there are bhikṣus who, for the sake of robes, food and drink, bedding, and medical requisites for the sick and infirm, claim to be arhats when they are not."

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu acts as a leader of bandits, taking along a hundred, two hundred, three hundred, or even a thousand followers—what difference is there between these two types of great thieves?
The bhikṣu replied:
"Those who lead a following of a hundred or a thousand are merely petty thieves.

This second kind of thief—among the devas, humans, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—is one who, for the sake of robes, food, bedding, and medical requisites, claims to be an arhat when he is not; this is the greatest thief among thieves."
Then the Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One:
"Bhagavān, what is the meaning of 'pārājika'?
The Blessed One replied:

"All the faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment—having ascended beneath the tree of enlightenment and attained the fruit, all fetters are exhausted and completely abandoned; therefore, it is called 'abandoning.
For example, O Bhikṣu!"
Suppose there were a person who, having committed an offense against the King, had all their means of livelihood seized and their house cast away;
in this same way, by successively committing offenses against the four pārājikas, one casts away all roots of merit.
What is meant by "not receiving"?

If one does not receive the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the observance of the *varṣā* retreat, or the secret matters of the Saṃgha, that bhikṣu is one who has not received [these duties]; he is not a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya.
The Piniye, Scroll Second; The Piniye, Scroll Third.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharma 1: One of the Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Kālodāyin—Kālodāyin means "Black Light," and he was the younger cousin of Ānanda—was observing the rains retreat at the Jetavana. He swept and sprinkled the rooms, spread mats within them, placed a water jar in front, and set another water jar outside.
When the time came, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. Having received food, he returned, entered his cell, and set aside his robe and bowl to rest.

Kāḷudāyin, however, was excessively prone to lustful thoughts; he recalled the women from the families where he had received food, and his passion flared so intensely that he manipulated his organ with his hand until his semen was emitted.
Even though he washed his hands, bathed, and swept the rooms three times like this, it continued until the end of the summer retreat.
At that time, there were bhikṣus who were acquaintances of Kālodāyin staying in the Kosalas for the summer retreat.
Having sat down, he completed his *pāṃsukūla* robe in a single day; having donned the robe and taken up his bowl, he arrived at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to the place where the bhikṣu Kālodāyin was, and after each had paid homage to one another and exchanged greetings, they sat down to one side.
"How is it, Udāyin? Are you physically well and strong?
During the summer retreat, have you had no suffering and no need to beg for alms?"
Udāyin replied, “I swept and cleaned the rooms here, even up to engaging in masturbation,” and he related all this in detail to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus replied:

"In how many ways, Udāyin, has the Blessed One through countless skillful means spoken of sexual intercourse as impure, directed his thoughts toward sexual intercourse and sexual desire, and described the foulness of sexual intercourse?"
"How could you give rise to lustful thoughts toward her?
Thus did those bhikṣus reprimand and admonish him most severely.
Having finished their reprimands and admonitions, he rose and departed, went to the World-Honored One, and reported the matter to the World-Honored One in full detail.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, questioned Udāyin himself:
"Is it true that you have done this?

At that time, Udāyin felt inward shame and outward embarrassment before the assembly; he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"It is so, World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One said:

"How can such a deluded person fail to understand? By means of countless skillful methods, I have taught that sexual desire is impure; I have directed [the mind] toward sexual desire, contemplated sexual desire, and shown the foulness of sexual desire when it is rampant."
"How can a foolish person receive the faithful offerings of a householder with this hand, and yet use that same hand to grasp and toy with such a form?

Thus, through countless skillful means, the Blessed One rebuked him. On account of this matter, he assembled the Saṃgha and, endowed with the ten merits, the World-Honored One established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"All śramaṇas must together guard against this."
"If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen by masturbating, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa; 'saṃghāvaśeṣa' in the language of Qin means 'that which is to be decided by the Saṃgha.
The World-Honored One was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu staying for the summer retreat at Jetavana.
During a dream, this bhikṣu emitted semen; upon waking, he became filled with doubt:
"Have I not committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?"
He then questioned the bhikṣus. Not knowing how they should respond,
the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"There is no offense for emitting semen in a dream.
However, if a bhikṣu intentionally manipulates his organ and emits semen—excluding cases occurring in a dream—he commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
Then the Venerable Upāli asked the Blessed One:
"In how many instances does the emission of semen constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
The Blessed One replied:
If one plays with his own hands, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; the same applies if he causes another’s hand to play with him.

If another bends both elbows to play with him, or if [he plays] between the knees, between the two armpits, on both sides of the navel, between the thighs, in the cleft of the buttocks, on both shoulders, or on the back of the neck—playing with the exposed parts of the body where they bend or stretch, or within clothing, or while lying upon a bed or mattress—if he emits semen through such acts, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. This also applies if he plays with a painted image of a woman, a wooden image of a woman, or at the place where such images are made, and thereby emits semen. It is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda, whose sensual desires were particularly strong, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for alms.
There was a householder’s wife who received Nanda’s foot with her hand to pay him homage; as the woman’s hand was moist, Nanda immediately emitted semen, which fell upon the person’s hand.
The woman then raised her hand and touched the crown of his head, saying:

"I have now attained a great benefit, for I have caused the Venerable Nanda’s lustful mind to blaze so intensely that his holy life remains entirely intact and his mind has not transgressed the precepts."
Nanda then became filled with doubt, thinking,
"Have I not committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense?
and he questioned the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not know how to respond and went at once to inform the Blessed One in detail.
Then, on account of this matter, the Blessed One assembled the Saṃgha.
Knowing [the situation], the Blessed One questioned Nanda:
“Is it truly as you say, Nanda? At that time, the Venerable Nanda,

feeling inward shame and outward embarrassment before the assembly, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"It is so, World-Honored One! At that time,
in the presence of the great assembly, the World-Honored One praised Nanda, saying:
“Excellent, excellent,
Nanda! You are indeed capable of performing this entire holy life in such a manner.”
"One who practices the holy life attains great rewards and great merit.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"As for those sons of good family who have seen Nanda, who could possibly disparage him by saying he is not upright?"
His body was supple and his physical strength surpassed that of others; yet, as his lustful intent was particularly excessive, who could surpass Nanda? Thus, O Bhikṣu!

The son of noble family Nanda closed the gates of the sense-faculties, was moderate in eating and drinking, did not lose the proper time at night, and maintained mindfulness and concentration without distraction—these four preceding phrases constitute what is called a *sūtra*, which is fundamental illumination. Thus, Nanda was able to purely cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*) for as long as he lived.
How does that son of good family, Nanda, close the doors of the sense faculties?

In this regard, Nanda, when the eye sees forms, the mind is without attachment; even if the eye faculty is not fully controlled upon seeing forms, he should reflect on ignorance, sorrow, and unwholesome states, and by not directing the mind toward them, he guards the eye faculty.

Having thus understood the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind with respect to mental objects (*dharma*), one does not give rise to defiled attachment. Even if the faculty of the mind (*manendriya*) is incomplete, one should reflect upon ignorance, sorrow, evil, and unwholesome states; by ensuring that the mind does not incline toward them, one guards the faculty of the mind.
This is how the noble son Nanda guards the doors of the sense faculties.
How does the noble son Nanda practice contentment regarding food and drink?

In this regard, the noble son Nanda is content with the morsels of food he eats; he is free from greed and gluttony, seeking neither beauty nor strength, and harboring no desire for softness or smoothness.
The reason for eating is to desire that the body endure for a long time, so that old ailments may be extinguished and new ones do not arise, thereby delighting in the practice of the Path.
It is like a person who has a wound or an ulcer and applies medicinal ointment to it.
Why is it smeared? It is because one wishes to heal the wound.
In this same way, Nanda, the son of noble family, is moderate in eating and drinking, free from gluttony, and even delights in practicing the Path.
It is, for example, like a person who greases a cart with oil. Why does he grease it?
Because it is carrying a heavy load.
In this way, the noble son Nanda is moderate in eating and drinking, free from greed and gluttony, and even delights in practicing the Path.
This is the noble son Nanda’s moderation in food and drink.
In what way does that son of good family, Nanda, not lose his time during the night?
In this case, Nanda, the son of good family practices walking meditation and sits in dhyāna during the day, and likewise practices walking meditation and sits in dhyāna at night.

During the first watch of the night, he practiced walking meditation and seated dhyāna, subduing his mind and not allowing himself to sleep. During the middle watch, he folded his *uttarāsaṅga* into four layers and spread it upon his seat; he placed his *saṃghāṭī* at the head of the bed, lay on his right side with one foot resting upon the other, and fixed his attention on the light, wondering, "When will dawn break?"
During the latter part of the night, he immediately rises to practice walking meditation and seated dhyāna, subduing the mind and its phenomena.
This is how the noble son Nanda does not lose his time during the first and last watches of the night.
How does that noble son Nanda maintain mindfulness and concentration without distraction?
In this regard, Nanda, if this son of good family wishes to look toward the east, he straightens his body and contemplates as he looks toward the east, without any distracted mind.
If he wishes to look toward the south, west, or north, he straightens his body and contemplates as he looks, without any distracted mind.

Thereupon, the noble son Nanda, when experiencing sensations or perceptions, never loses his wisdom; it is the same for his formations and consciousness. He does not allow sensations or perceptions that have not yet arisen to arise, and if sensations or perceptions do arise, he extinguishes them in their proper sequence.
This was the son of good family Nanda’s concentration through mindfulness, undisturbed by distraction.
Therefore, Nanda’s emission of semen was without fault.
Furthermore, should anyone else experience such an emission, it likewise would be without fault.
"O Bhikṣus! From this day forward, you shall wear the *saṃkakṣikā* and the *antarvāsaka*.
What is the meaning of 'caressing the private parts'?"
"To dwell alone and give rise to thoughts and mental imaginings—whether regarding oneself or another—of physical proximity and the fondling of the private parts;
this is the meaning of 'fondling. The Buddha was traveling among the Śākyas at Anupiya in Kapilavastu.
At that time, the Venerable Kālodāyin was on five-day duty. Several women from prominent families came to the various rooms within the garden to look around.
Then, the Venerable Kālodāyin stood outside the gate holding the key and bolt, calling out:
"Sisters, come forward; enter this garden to stroll and observe, for within it there are bathing pools and springs."
Then the women entered the garden for recreation; he opened the doors of the various rooms to allow them to enter and look about.
He passed through the inner chambers, seizing the women, embracing and kissing them, and fondling their bodies.
Among the women, some wished to follow [the monks] while others did not.
Those who did not follow went out and said to the bhikṣus:
"In this place which is always fearless and secure, there has now arisen a great terror."
The bhikṣus asked, "What fear do you have?
He then reported in detail to the bhikṣus everything he had seen.
The bhikṣus, not knowing how they should respond, went to the World-Honored One and reported this matter in detail.
The World-Honored One, knowing [the situation], asked the Venerable Udāyin:

"How shall I repay that enemy?

At that very time, that bhikṣu had a sister who was a bhikṣuṇī named Mithilā by clan.

What equality is there?

The assembly of bhikṣus said:

In this manner, he rebuked and censured the sympathetic bhikṣu a second and a third time, speaking these words.
Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Kalandaka Feeding Ground.

At that time, the Venerable Daṇḍa Bhikṣu distributed the rice and assigned the seats for the bhikṣus; he did so without personal bias, without anger, and without delusion, proceeding from top to bottom and from bottom to top, never violating the rules of decorum.
At that time, encountering an invitation at a poor and destitute household, he received coarse food and drink, whereupon this thought arose:

"This bhikkhu, Dhoṇa, has placed us in a position where we may be found at fault; we shall bring charges against him so that he falls into the offense of groundless censure.

"I spoke those words out of anger, hatred, and delusion.

At that time, the bhikṣus joined their palms toward the Buddha and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

Did I not originally state this principle?
When the bhikṣu Dharmadinna reported what the bhikṣuṇī Madhuvāsinī had said, and she herself admitted it was true, she immediately fell into the offense of *pārājika*.
At that time, for this reason and endowed with ten merits, the Blessed One established a precept for the śramaṇas:

"If a bhikṣu, out of hatred, jealousy, or envy, slanders another pure bhikṣu by falsely accusing him of an ungrounded offense involving expulsion, saying, 'I shall fall into this loss of the holy life,' [he commits an offense]."
"If, at a later time, he is questioned and accused, yet speaks groundlessly of abandonment and slander,

Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One, while traveling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Dharmadinnā was residing in a stone cave.
Those bhikṣus were instructing the bhikṣuṇīs in succession, and it was now Dharmadinnā’s turn to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.

Then the bhikṣuṇīs went to where the bhikṣu Dharmadinnā was; at that time, the bhikṣus who were sympathetic to Mṛgāraputra, on account of their prior resentment over food and drink, were constantly seeking out her faults.
As they watched the bhikṣuṇīs entering and leaving the stone chamber, some bhikṣus observed them from afar within a stone niche and thought to themselves:
"These bhikṣuṇīs are now coming out and now going in; this bhikṣu Dharmadinnā must surely be grabbing hold of them and engaging in private conversation with them."
They said to one another, "This is certainly so; there is no doubt.
They then informed the bhikṣus, and that dull-witted bhikṣu believed their words.

At that time, for this reason, the Blessed One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and, being endowed with the ten merits, the Buddha established a precept for the śramaṇas:

"If a bhikṣu, out of hatred, envy, or jealousy, slanders a pure bhikṣu by falsely accusing him of unchaste conduct, or observes a minor transgression that does not constitute a *pārājika* offense and yet claims he has committed a *pārājika* offense."
If, at a later time, he is reproached and subsequently repents, it is permissible;
if he does not repent, but instead seeks out minor faults and magnifies them into major offenses, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having dressed in their robes and taken up their alms bowls early in the morning, entered the city of Rājagṛha from Vulture Peak Mountain to beg for food.
Encountering a torrential rain on the road, he entered a stone grotto to take shelter from the rain.
A cowherd woman had already entered the grotto earlier to seek refuge; she lay down and dreamed that her vital essence was lost.
When Śāriputra and the others saw this, they immediately sought out and left.
At that time, the bhikṣu Gopālī, a disciple of Devadatta, saw Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana emerge and immediately entered the stone cave. Seeing this woman there, he thought to himself:
"Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana must have engaged in impure conduct with this woman."
Then Gopāli entered the city and said to the bhikṣus, "Gentlemen, you have often said that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana defile pure conduct; I have just now witnessed this matter with my own eyes."
The bhikṣus did not know how they should answer, so they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"This foolish person has committed a grave and heavy offense."
“A pure bhikṣu who practices pure conduct casts out baseless slander; this deluded person will suffer for a long night and fall into hell.
At that time, the bhikṣu Gopāli went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
The World-Honored One addressed Gopāli: "Gopāli Bhikṣu!
You should, in a timely manner, repent and turn your mind toward Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana."
"Why is that? Because these constitute the complete holy life.
Gopāli said to the Buddha:
“The Tathāgata knows that those people’s intentions are pure; he does so only because he sees with his own eyes that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have been harmed.
The World-Honored One spoke again to Gavāmpati: “Gavāmpati!...”
You should take this opportunity to repent and turn your mind toward Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. Why is this?
Because their holy life remains complete.
Gopāli said to the Buddha, “I know that the Tathāgata trusts Śāriputra and the others; it is only because he saw with his own eyes that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have become evil.”
The Buddha addressed Gopālī thus three times:
“Gopālī! You should, in a timely manner, repent and turn your mind toward Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.”
"And why? Because these constitute the complete holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Gopāli said to the Buddha:
"The Tathāgata knows that those people have pure intentions; he does so only because he sees with his own eyes that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana are wicked.
At that time, the bhikṣu Gavāmpati, having not accepted the Buddha's words after they were spoken three times, rose from his seat and departed.
Not long after he had departed, sores broke out on his body, resembling mustard seeds.

They gradually grew larger, becoming like *bīja* beans, then like *māṣa* beans, then like *caṇaka* beans or jujube pits; they grew as large as *āmalaka* fruits and then like *karkandhu* fruits or hundred-seeded gourds, until the entire body became festering and putrid, with pus and blood flowing forth.
At that time, the bhikṣu Gopāli passed away during the night and fell into the Pātāvana hell.
That very night, a certain deva came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The cowherd bhikṣu Gopāli gave rise to evil intentions; he slandered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, claiming they had violated the holy life, and has fallen into the Mahāpātāvana hell.”
Having addressed the World-Honored One in this way, he prostrated at his feet and vanished, returning to the heavens.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Last night, a deva came to where I was; having bowed his head at my feet, he stood to one side and said to me:"
"The bhikṣu Gopāli gave rise to an evil intention and slandered Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, falsely accusing them of violating the holy life (brahmacarya).
Upon death, he fell into the Mahāvīci Great Hell."
If this bhikṣu, on account of a minor matter, brings a great calumny against the pure conduct (brahmacarya) of a pure bhikṣu,
and if a bhikṣu makes such a calumny, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Then the World-Honored One said, "O bhikṣus!
Do you wish to hear about the length of the life-span of sentient beings in the great hell of Pātāla?
Now is precisely the right time."
“May the World-Honored One explain the great hell of Pātāla; having heard it, the bhikṣus shall receive and practice it accordingly.
“Bhikṣus, it is like this:”

A large Magadhan bushel holds twelve hu; a basket is filled to the brim with sesame seeds, and a sharp blade is placed upon them. If someone were to remove a single sesame seed every hundred years, [the basket would eventually be emptied].

"O Bhikṣus! It may still be possible to count the number of sesame seeds; however, it is impossible to know the lifespan of those in the Arbuda hell, for twenty lifespans in the Avīci hell do not equal even one single lifespan in the Avīci hell."
Twenty empty, unreal hells are not equal to one Crying-out Hell;
twenty Crying-out Hells are not equal to one River-of-Slaves Hell.
Twenty *vīci* hells are not equal to one *sugandha* hell;
twenty *sugandha* hells are not equal to one *mṛdvīkā-gandha* (grape-liquor-scented) *mādhuka* hell.
Twenty *mādhuka* hells are not equal to one *utpala* hell;
twenty *utpala* hells are not equal to one *kumuda* hell.
Twenty times the duration in the Kūṭaśālmalī hell is not equal to one part of the Pundarīka hell;
twenty times the duration in the Pundarīka hell is not equal to one part of the Padma hell.

The Third [Section] of the Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas: The Precept on Schism in the Sangha.
When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove of the Kalandakas.
That Devadatta received offerings of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the sick;

he was highly esteemed by Prince Ajātaśatru, who provided him with supplies according to his needs, sending five hundred cauldrons of rice daily and preparing five hundred chariots, with a retinue following him day after day to Devadatta’s residence.

While [the Buddha] sat and ate, Devadatta sought to cause dissension within the Saṃgha of bhikṣus; he enticed the bhikṣus by offering them robes, alms bowls, keys, needle cases, leather sandals, large and small keys, shallow iron bowls, and other various requisites.

"He was born into the Śākya clan; I too was born into the Śākya clan.

At that time, there was a famine within the kingdom and it was difficult to obtain alms. Then, many bhikṣus, having put on their robes and taken up their bowls, entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.

Having finished his almsround, he heard that Devadatta intended to cause dissension within the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, and was enticing the bhikṣus by offering them robes, bowls, keys, needle-cases, leather sandals, large locks, and small locks.

The World-Honored One said:

"O Bhikṣus! It would be better to drink poison and kill oneself than to accept the offerings of Devadatta, thereby drinking poison oneself and causing others to drink it as well.
It is like a bhikṣu who strikes a vicious dog on the nose with a staff until its nose is broken."
"How is it, bhikṣu!
Has this dog become even more wicked? "Indeed, he has."
"World-Honored One!
"The Buddha replied, "It is so, bhikṣu!
This deluded person shall suffer for a long night without end."
I also know that Devadatta shall indeed destroy the Saṃgha of bhikṣus; at the very time of this meal, he shall cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, that if the harmonious Saṃgha is divided during the time of a meal, it must be reunited by evening. During that interval, one cannot be a practitioner of the Way, nor a bhikṣu, nor a bhikṣuṇī, nor a śikṣamāṇā, nor a śrāmaṇera, nor a śrāmaṇerī; one cannot observe the eightfold precepts of the fast, nor be an upāsaka, nor an upāsikā. One cannot attain the realization of the fruits of the Way, nor can one give rise to the aspiration for the three types of Buddhahood.
At that time, heaven and earth were shrouded in darkness, and the devas and humans lost their sight.
When the Dharma of the Tathāgata approaches its end, the Saṃgha must inevitably be reunited; if it is not reunited, heaven and earth will overturn.

At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana heard that Devadatta had brought about a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha. Having heard this, they went to the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I now wish to go to where Devadatta is, in order to reconcile the Sangha.

"Now is precisely the right time.

"Just as the World-Honored One, seeing Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, called out, 'Welcome,

As the Blessed One had folded his *uttarāsaṅga* in four layers and spread it upon the bed, placed his *saṃghāṭī* at the head of the bed, and lay down on his right side upon the lion-seat with one leg slightly bent and the other extended, he fixed his mindfulness on the light, thinking: "When will it be dawn?"
Devadatta was likewise in this state.
At that time, while Devadatta was asleep, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven descended and pressed down upon his body.

He desired intensely to wake up, yet though he exerted all his strength, he could not awaken; his breathing became labored and harsh, and at times he uttered incoherent words, his hands and feet flailing about, groping against the four walls and performing various contortions, yet still unable to wake.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra praised the Buddha’s Dharma and the Saṃgha of bhikṣus.

Then Maudgalyāyana performed various supernatural transformations: he vanished in the east and reappeared in the west, vanished in the south and reappeared in the north, and sat and lay down in mid-air.
Or they sit in samādhi, emitting various kinds of light within that samādhi—whether blue, yellow, red, black, or the color of lapis lazuli.
Fire issued from the lower part of his body while water issued from the upper part; fire issued from the upper part of his body while water issued from the lower part.
In the southwest, he performed various transformations above and below without any obstruction, emitting rays of light that illuminated everywhere.
At that time, when the five hundred bhikṣus saw Maudgalyāyana manifesting various supernatural transformations, they said to one another:
"Have we not fallen into perverted views?
How is it that we have abandoned the Tathāgata to rely upon Devadatta?"
He further thought to himself:
"This is certainly so, without a doubt.

At that time, as the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana spoke the Dharma to him, his mind was opened and his understanding attained; he gave rise to a heart of loving-kindness toward the Tathāgata and repented for his former deeds.

At that time, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and five hundred bhikṣus came to where the World-Honored One was; the seat of Devadatta was entirely empty and unoccupied, with only Devadatta and his four disciples remaining.
At that time, the bhikṣu Khaṇḍadravya kicked Devadatta with his left foot to wake him and seized him, saying:
"Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have led away five hundred people; the seats are now entirely empty."
At that time, Devadatta realized that the seat was empty and no longer occupied by anyone; he then threw himself from the seat onto the ground.
His disciples sprinkled water on his face, and he returned to sit upon the couch.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from his quiet chamber and went out to the outer hall, where he spread a *niṣīdana* upon a seat and sat cross-legged.

Then, seeing the Tathāgata sitting cross-legged in the hall from afar, five hundred bhikṣus felt inward shame and outward embarrassment before the assembly; they stepped forward and approached the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata also saw five hundred bhikṣus approaching, and looking back, he said to Ānanda:
"If I do not speak with them, boiling blood shall gush from my facial orifices."
At that time, the Tathāgata, wishing with great compassion to deliver that person, spoke to him:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu! A Tathāgata is difficult to encounter; he appears only once in a long while."

Even though a Tathāgata has appeared in the world, it is difficult to hear the Dharma. To seek parinirvāṇa is likewise difficult to attain. One who wishes to enter nirvāṇa should practice this Dharma:

conditioned by ignorance, volitional formations arise; conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness arises; conditioned by consciousness, name-and-form arises; conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases arise; conditioned by the six sense bases, contact arises; conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, clinging arises; conditioned by clinging, existence arises; conditioned by existence, birth arises; conditioned by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair arise. In this way, the suffering of the five aggregates is formed.

Ignorance is unaware of volitional formations; volitional formations are unaware of consciousness; consciousness is unaware of name-and-form; name-and-form is unaware of the six sense bases; the six sense bases are unaware of contact; contact is unaware of feeling; feeling is unaware of craving; craving is unaware of clinging; clinging is unaware of becoming; becoming is unaware of birth; birth is unaware of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair; thus the disease of the five aggregates is formed.
When this teaching on the twelve links of dependent origination was spoken, five hundred bhikṣus attained the path of arhatship, and eighty hundred thousand goddesses attained the pure Dharma-eye.
At that time, the World-Honored One, endowed with the ten merits, established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu causes dissension within a harmonious Saṃgha, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"Devadatta has committed this; there is no rescue for him as he enters hell.
While the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain at the dwelling place of the Kumbhīra yakṣa, there was a great stone cave.

At that time, Devadatta, wishing to harm the World-Honored One, hired four strong men for four thousand taels of gold. Together with these four men, he ascended Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, where he took up a great rock, stood above the stone chamber, and waited for the Tathāgata to emerge.

At that time, the Buddha emerged from the stone cave and was about to perform a walking meditation (caṅkrama). Devadatta, together with these four men, rolled down stones from the mountain to strike the Tathāgata.
At that moment, the yakṣa Kumbhīra was behind the World-Honored One; looking up as the great rock came hurtling down, he caught it with both hands and hurled it toward the Southern Mountain.
At that time, this rock shattered and broke apart; a small fragment, seventy paces in length and breadth, flew toward the World-Honored One.

Then, for the sake of sentient beings, the Tathāgata manifested his past karmic conditions and their retributions; he immediately sat in samādhi and ascended into the void, and the rock followed after him, seen by all sentient beings;
in the south, west, and north, the rock likewise followed after him from every direction.
When the Tathāgata entered the waters of the great ocean, the rock followed behind him.
When the Tathāgata ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru, the rock likewise followed him.
When the Tathāgata went up to the celestial palaces on Mount Cāturmahārājika, the rock also followed him.

At that time, as the Tathāgata ascended to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, Yama, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha heavens, the stone followed after him as well.
At that time, the World-Honored One returned to the door of the stone chamber by means of his supernormal power.
This rock struck the right foot of the World-Honored One, breaking his foot and causing blood to flow.
Thus, Devadatta and the four strongmen incurred a crime for which there is no refuge.
At that time, the World-Honored One suffered from pain in his foot and, with his own strength, spoke this verse: "Not in the sky,
nor in the midst of the sea, Nor by entering into mountain clefts or rocks—
There is no place on earth Where one can escape the retribution of past misdeeds."
At that time, many bhikṣus were on either side of the stone chamber, sometimes sitting and sometimes walking, fearing that Devadatta might harm the Tathāgata.
When the Tathāgata saw them from afar, knowing their thoughts, he asked Ānanda:
"What are those many bhikṣus doing outside the stone chamber, now walking and now sitting?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “Looking at the Tathāgata from afar, I feared that Devadatta might harm him; for this reason, he was here and there, now walking and now sitting.
The World-Honored One told Ānanda:
“Once a Tathāgata has appeared in the world, Devadatta can never harm him.
Have you ever heard of a Tathāgata being harmed by anyone? “No, sir.”
“World-Honored One!

At that time, the World-Honored One looked up. When the four strongmen saw the Tathāgata looking at them, fear arose in their hearts and the hair on their bodies stood on end; they wished to run, yet their feet would not move.
Then the śramaṇas each seized him and brought him to the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Tathāgata said to the four strong men, "Welcome, youths!"
"I shall preach the Dharma to you.
Then the four strongmen prostrated themselves at his feet and sat to one side.
Thereupon the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to them, explaining it so as to delight their minds and cause each of them to rejoice.
"Young man, return to your own home; do not go back to where you came from.
At that time, seeing that these four men were late and had not yet arrived, Devadatta further hired eight powerful wrestlers for eight thousand taels of gold, saying:
"Go and kill these four men so that their very roots are severed."
At that time, the World-Honored One saw the eight Mallas approaching from afar and said to them, "Welcome, youths!
I shall speak words of the Dharma for you."
Then the eight strongmen prostrated themselves at his feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to them, explaining and gladdening their minds, causing each of them to rejoice.
"Young man, return to your own home; do not go back to where you came from.
At that time, seeing that these eight men were still delayed and had not yet arrived, Devadatta again hired sixteen strongmen for sixteen thousand ounces of gold, saying:
"Go and kill those eight men and cut off their very roots."
The World-Honored One saw the sixteen youths approaching from afar and said to them:
"Welcome, youths! I shall preach the Dharma for you."
Then the sixteen men prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
Thereupon the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to them, explaining and gladdening their minds so that each was filled with joy.
He told the youth:
"Return to your own home; do not go back to where you came from.
At that time, seeing that the sixteen men had not yet arrived, Devadatta hired another thirty-two men.
“Go and kill sixteen men; cut off their very roots.
The World-Honored One saw the thirty-two men approaching from afar and addressed them, saying:
“Welcome, youths!”
"I shall preach the Dharma for you.
Then the thirty-two men prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
Thereupon the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for them, clarifying and gladdening their minds, so that each of them harbored great joy.
“O youth! Return to your own home and act as is appropriate.
Then the thirty-two individuals, having received the command of the World-Honored One, rose from their seats, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and departed.
At that time, not long after the thirty-two men had departed, the World-Honored One looked back and said to Ānanda:
"Go into the city of Rājagṛha and, at the head of the four streets in the great marketplace, proclaim these words:

'Whatever deeds Devadatta performs, whatever he does with body, speech, and mind, do not say it was done by the instruction of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; Devadatta has his own trusted disciples.'"
At that time, Ānanda said to the Buddha:
“Previously you praised Devadatta, and now you speak of his evil.
When people among the assembly mock this, how should one answer them?”
The World-Honored One told Ānanda:
"To one who speaks such words, answer with these words:
'Though one was formerly practiced in goodness, if they now practice evil again, what is there to be surprised at!'"
At that time, Ānanda took a bhikṣu and went immediately to the city of Rājagṛha. Standing at the head of a major street in the marketplace, he addressed the passersby:

"As for the deeds performed by Devadatta—whatever he has done with body, speech, and mind—do not call them the teachings of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; Devadatta has his own disciples who trust and follow him."
At that time, the attendants and ministers of Prince Ajātaśatru who served Devadatta heard these reports of Devadatta’s ill repute and said to one another:
“The śramaṇa Gautama is full of malice and jealousy; he slanders the worthy Devadatta.”
"Does Devadatta perhaps have some fault in his body or speech?
At that time, Devadatta also heard this voice: "The śramaṇa Gautama has sent a messenger into the city of Rājagṛha, who stands at the head of the great marketplace and proclaims:
'If Devadatta’s conduct, or whatever he does with his body, speech, and mind, do not call it the teaching of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.'"
“Devadatta has his own devoted disciples.
At that time, Devadatta’s anger intensified; he went to Prince Ajātaśatru and spoke these words:
“You shall kill your father, and I shall kill the śramaṇa Gautama.”
"You shall become the Great King of Magadha, and I shall become a Buddha.
Would it not be most delightful for there to be both a new king and a new Buddha within the realm of Magadha?
When the king heard these words, he was filled with joy.
At that time, King Bimbisāra mounted a carriage adorned with peacock feathers and went to the rear garden to observe it.
Meanwhile, Prince Ajātaśatru, with a sharp sword tucked at his waist, hid himself between the doorposts and waited for his father, the king.

The king spent the entire day sporting and returned to the palace in a carriage drawn by four horses. Just as he was entering the gate, the crown prince hurled a sword from afar; however, because the horse was moving so swiftly, the weapon failed to strike its mark.
At that time, the prince fled, and four men pursued and caught him.
They asked, "What do you intend to do, Prince? The prince replied:
"I wish to kill the king.
The four men asked again,
"Who are your accomplices?"
"It was this worthy Devadatta and his four disciples.
At that time, the four men deliberated, saying,
"If it is truly so, we must go and kill all those śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas."
Others again proposed:
"Let us set aside the śramaṇas, the sons of Śākya; we shall simply seize Devadatta and his followers and kill them.
Still others proposed:
"Furthermore, do not kill the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, nor kill Devadatta and his followers.

Why is this? This King Bimbisāra is auspicious, noble, and virtuous; he habitually grants pardon to those condemned to death and imprisoned—how much more so should he spare the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, and Devadatta and his followers?"
In the morning, they went to inform the king, saying, "The King himself shall adjudicate this; why should we bring this grievance upon ourselves here?
They immediately went to inform the king.
On the following day, the king came forth and sat upon the palace terrace, and sent a messenger to summon the crown prince Ajātaśatru.
When the prince arrived, he immediately asked:
"Young man! What do you intend to do?"
"I wish to kill the king.
"Why would you assassinate me?
the crown prince said.
"The King has sounding drums, but I have no sounding drums; the King has the curved parasol, but I have no curved parasol; the King has the ceremonial retinue, but I have no ceremonial retinue."
The King said to the Crown Prince, "You shall take my place;
let the sounding drums, the curved parasols, and the ceremonial procession all follow behind you.
At that moment, the sounding drums, the curved parasols, and the ceremonial procession immediately followed behind the Crown Prince.
At that time, a sycophantic and deceitful minister spoke these words to the crown prince:
"If this is indeed the case, let the Crown Prince take his place upon the throne.
Once you have ascended the throne, seize and slay the Father King so that you may possess absolute freedom."

At that time, the crown prince approved what had been reported to him; he immediately dispatched a caṇḍāla to seize his father, the king, and confine him in prison, and he went at once to arrest the king and bind him in the jail.
The King had always been benevolent toward his people, and several million people brought food as offerings to him.
Ajātaśatru asked his attendants:
"Is my father, the former king, still alive?"
He replied, "I am still alive. [The other asked,] "By what means do you survive?"
He replied,
"The people bring food as offerings, and thus I remain alive.
The king then commanded that no one be allowed to approach him.
At that time, the various ladies-in-waiting sent food as provisions. Ajātaśatru asked,
"Is my father, the King, still alive?"
He replied, "She is alive.
He then commanded the gatekeepers not to allow the lady to come forward.
At that time, the first lady smeared her body with food and drink; she put on outer garments so as not to reveal them and entered to see the king, causing him to eat from her body.
The king asked again,
"Is my father, the king, still alive? He replied:
"Go! he commanded, "and do not let the lady enter.

The prison gates were turned toward Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, from which she saw from afar the World-Honored One with the community of bhikṣus—Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Ānanda, Nandi, and Kapphiṇa—ascending and descending the mountain.
Having attained the stage of the Path, the king beheld the community of bhikṣus with joy, and he was free from any thought of hunger or thirst.
King Ajātaśatru asked his ministers,
"Is my father, the king, still alive?"
He replied, "The King is alive.
The King asked his attendants:
"For what reason do you live?
A jealous courtier replied, "I go to pay my respects to the Tathāgata every day; for this reason I live."
The king said, "Go quickly and build a high wall to block the front of the prison so that Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa cannot be seen.
They immediately went and built it so that it could not be seen.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present that when they wish to enter a city, various auspicious omens appear: elephants trumpet with their trunks raised and their faces uplifted; horses likewise neigh; oxen bellow; wild ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, parrots, white cranes, *qianqiu* cranes, and storks all sing in harmony; and lutes, zithers, drums, lutes, *zhu*, and flutes sound spontaneously without being struck.
The treasuries of the various elders—containing gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, musaragalva, and agate—resounded spontaneously without being touched.

The blind regained their sight, the deaf were able to hear, and those suffering from various ailments such as blindness, lameness, paralysis, or goiters all found relief; hidden treasures spontaneously emerged.
When the World-Honored One entered the city, there were these auspicious omens.
King Bimbisāra, knowing that the Buddha had entered the city, leaped for joy;
through a crack in his prison cell, he gazed upon the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus.
The King attained the stage of Stream-winner (srotāpanna) and beheld the World-Honored One’s removal of the perceptions of hunger and thirst.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru asked his ministers:
"Is my father, the King, still alive?"
He replied, “I am still alive. He asked:
"For what reason was he kept alive?
The ministers, out of jealousy, replied to the king:
"It was because your father, the King, looked through the cracks of the prison and saw the World-Honored One entering the city; for that reason, he was allowed to live."
"Go and shave his feet with a sharp blade so that he cannot walk, and further bind him with fetters.
He went at once and shaved his feet, then bound him tightly with shackles and chains.
The king grew increasingly emaciated day by day.
At that time, Ajātaśatru entered the palace to eat with his consort.
Ajātaśatru had a young son who was outside playing with fighting cocks.
King Ajātaśatru asked his queen,
"Where is our young son?
She replied:
"He is outside watching the fighting cocks.
The King said to his consort,
"Call him here to eat with us."
At that time, the young son immediately took the chicken inside with him and refused to eat it.
The king asked,
"For what reason do you not eat?"
"If this fowl does not eat, I shall never eat.
Then Ajātaśatru said to his wife,
"What will become of this young child?"
"I now wish, Great King, for you to eat together with the chicken!
The lady replied, "What is it that Your Majesty finds so distasteful?"
"Or there may be someone who eats chicken for the sake of their child.
The King listened to what the Queen had reported and recalled the hardships endured by his late father, the King.
The King then asked the Queen:
"What suffering do you have?
The lady replied to the king:
"When Your Majesty were young, you suffered from your left thumb; day and night it pained you so that you could not sleep."
Then the father king took the prince onto his lap, took the prince’s painful finger, and placed it in his own mouth; as the finger received warmth, the prince was able to sleep a little.
At that time, the pus from the finger burst into the king’s mouth, whereupon the king thought to himself:
"If I were to pull out my finger to remove the pus, it might cause me pain."
He then swallowed the pus and did not withdraw his finger.
"Your father endured such suffering and did not reveal it to the outside world.
I pray that Your Majesty will grant him clemency and spare the king's life."
Upon hearing these words, the king remained silent and said nothing.
Then the lady addressed him with the word "pardon," immediately leaving the hall and crying out:
"I grant the king his life!"

Word spread throughout the city until it reached tens of millions of people in the prisons; everyone rejoiced and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! and they all rushed toward the prison site, crying out, "The King has already been liberated!"
"The king has already been liberated.
Upon hearing these words, the king said:
"My son was cruel and lacked a heart of filial piety."
Realizing that he would only be subjected to further punishment and that his life was certainly not spared,
he threw himself from his bed onto the ground, whereupon King Ajātaśatru died instantly.
Thus, King Ajātaśatru committed the unpardonable crime of patricide.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I previously sent Ānanda to proclaim in the marketplace the deeds committed by Devadatta through body, speech, and mind; it was precisely for the sake of today's events."

One who has killed his father may not practice the Way or wear the dharma robes; he may not become a bhikṣu, nor a bhikṣuṇī, nor an upāsaka, nor an upāsikā, nor may he be permitted to enter the eightfold fast.
Why is this? Because this person possesses no traces of the Path nor has they attained the realization of its fruits.
Not only does he kill his father, but it is the same when he kills his mother as well.
"If a bhikṣu knowingly permits one who acts as a leader of a schism to do so, he is the same as those who have already caused a schism in the Saṃgha.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One, while traveling at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in Rājagṛha, accompanied by five hundred great bhikṣus.
At that time, Devadatta intended to cause dissension within the community of bhikṣus. Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others wished to go and admonish him, saying:
"Devadatta! Do not cause dissension within the community of bhikṣus."
"Why is this? Because the Saṃgha is in harmony, like water and milk mixed together, and they receive the teachings as one.
At that time, the disciples of Devadatta—Khaṇḍadravya, Kāṭhila, Tiṣya, Samudradatta, and Kokālika—spoke to Śāriputra and the others:
"Friends, do not speak thus regarding Devadatta. Why is this?
Devadatta proceeds toward the truth in accordance with the Dharma; whatever Devadatta speaks, we shall all follow and practice."
Śāriputra and the others said to Khaṇḍadravya and the rest:
"Do not speak such words, claiming that Devadatta acts in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
Gentlemen, do not follow Devadatta’s teachings to cause strife and division among the Saṃgha of bhikṣus; do not assist those who wish to cause such strife and division."
"Why is this? Because the Saṃgha is united as one, like water and milk, and receives its teachings as one; therefore, do not cause strife within the Saṃgha, and do not assist one another.
When that bhikṣu spoke these words to the other bhikṣus, they did not follow his advice and went instead to follow the instructions of Devadatta.
At that time, Śāriputra and the others did not know what to do, so they went to inform the World-Honored One.
On account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and, having fulfilled ten meritorious qualities, the World-Honored One established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu assists one who is causing dissension within the Saṃgha, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha together with five hundred great bhikṣus.

At that time, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and descended from Vulture Peak to enter the city of Rājagṛha for alms. Having finished his almsround, he returned to Vulture Peak, sat cross-legged in a stone cave, and remained there for seven days without rising, entering into various meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*).
After seven days had passed, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went from Vulture Peak Mountain into the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms.

At that time, Devadatta heard that the śramaṇa Gautama was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha, leading five hundred disciples; that at the proper time he had put on his robes, taken up his bowl, and gone from Vulture Peak into Rājagṛha to beg for alms; and that having finished his begging, he had returned to his stone cell and sat cross-legged, remaining there for seven days before rising.

King Ajātaśatru had an elephant named Vaṅgapa (pronounced *mù cáng fǎn*), who was fierce, cruel, and tyrannical; none of the kings of the bordering states possessed such a wicked elephant as King Ajātaśatru’s Vaṅgapa.
At that time, Devadatta, carrying five hundred ounces of gold, went to the elephant trainer Raṅgava and said to him:
"Do you know that King Ajātaśatru grants me great power and influence?"
He replied, “I know. [The King asked,] “If I were to employ you,
would you be able to make people wealthy and noble?”
He replied, "I possess such power.
At that time, Devadatta took five hundred taels of gold:
"I employ you for this; perform this task for me, and I shall also inform the King to grant you land and property.
"I do not understand what task this is."
Devadatta said:

"This śramaṇa Gautama is traveling on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha, accompanied by five hundred disciples; when the time comes, he will put on his robes, take up his bowl, and enter Rājagṛha for alms."
After he has finished his almsround, he will return to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and sit cross-legged for seven days without rising.
When he enters the city of Rājagṛha, you shall take this elephant Paṅgika and give him strong, clear liquor to drink; then, unfasten his iron chains and release him to kill the śramaṇa Gautama.
The elephant trainer replied,
"This is but a small matter and does not require such earnestness. However,
once my work is completed, I pray that you will not neglect me."
At that time, the elephant trainer counted the days on his fingers, waiting for the seventh day.

When the seven days had passed, he gave the elephant Vaṅgapa strong, clear liquor to drink, bound him with iron chains so that he could not move, and hid himself behind the city gate to await the Tathāgata.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they wish to enter a city, various auspicious omens appear: elephants trumpet with their trunks raised; horses neigh and oxen bellow; wild ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, parrots, white swans, *qianqiu* cranes, and herons all cry out in harmony; *konghou*, *zheng*, drums, *pipa*, *zhu*, flutes, and other instruments sound of themselves without being struck; and the treasuries of the elders—containing gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, *musāragalva*, and *aśmagarbha*—resound spontaneously without being touched.

The blind regained their sight, the deaf regained their hearing, and those suffering from blindness, lameness, paralysis, goiters, and all manner of pains found relief; hidden treasures spontaneously emerged.
Such were the auspicious signs that appeared when the World-Honored One entered the city.

At that time, the elephant trainer, knowing that the Buddha was about to reach the city gate, untied the iron and steel fetters and released the elephant.
