Tens of millions of people each fled in haste seeking a place of safety; the populace was terrified, some entering their houses while others climbed onto the roofs and upper stories to stand there.
The elephant rushed toward the place where the Tathāgata was; the people watched in astonishment, each shouting out.
Among them were those who did not believe in the Buddha, who cried: "Alas! Kill this śramaṇa!"
Those who had faith in the Buddha said, "This small elephant can do nothing to the Buddha.

A certain elder, seeing the elephant running from afar, mounted an elephant and arrived at the Buddha's location first. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I have caused the elephant Paṅkadhā to drink clear liquor until he is intoxicated, and I have unfastened his iron chains to let him come and harm the World-Honored One.
It would be well, World-Honored One,
if you would enter this house to take refuge, or else return out of the city.”
"This elephant is crazed with intoxication and will surely harm the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One replied,
"This elephant shall never harm me."
"The World-Honored One will never be killed by another.

Seeing the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus from afar, the elephant trampled the ground, bellowed in rage, gnashed its teeth, pricked up its ears, raised its trunk, and lashed its tail as it rushed swiftly toward the World-Honored One.

At that time, when the assembly of bhikṣus saw the elephant charging toward them, their body hair stood on end; they all abandoned the Tathāgata and fled to a distance, with the sole exception of Ānanda, who did not leave.

When the elephant reached the presence of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One directed his compassionate mind toward it; the elephant’s state of intoxication dissolved and its anger vanished, as it knelt on both knees and licked the Tathāgata’s feet with its tongue.
Then the World-Honored One extended his golden arm and stroked the elephant’s head, speaking these verses as a father might address his son:
"Do not give rise to anger, Nor harbor a harmful mind toward the Tathāgata.
Whoever directs anger toward the Buddha Shall never be born in a happy realm."
The elephant Airāvaṇa dwells in two celestial palaces,
like one among the various elephant kings situated at the side of Mount Sumeru;
likewise, atop that Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, there is the elephant king Anavatapta.
All bow their heads to the Perfectly Awakened One; you have sown the seeds of calamity that harm the Buddha.
While the elephants cultivate the roots of goodness and thus dwell in that place, you now harbor a drunken mind of malice—how could you possibly be born among them?

Then the elephant Vaṅgapa wept with sorrow and shed tears; bowing his head and face at [the Buddha’s] feet, he departed. For seven days he did not eat grass and passed away, immediately being reborn in the fourth heaven.
At that time, tens of millions of people, having witnessed this miraculous transformation of the Tathāgata, all came to where the Buddha was.
Then the World-Honored One looked toward Ānanda and said:
"Go and fetch a seat and water; I wish to wash my feet."
At that time, Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, immediately spread out a seat and prepared water.
Kneeling with his right knee on the ground, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The seat and water are ready; may the Tathāgata come to wash his feet."

Having washed his feet, the World-Honored One then sat in samādhi and manifested various transformations: he disappeared in the east and emerged in the west; he disappeared in the north and emerged in the south; he sat and lay upon the void; his body emitted light—blue, yellow, white, black, or the color of lapis lazuli; fire issued from the lower part of his body while water issued from the upper part, and water issued from the upper part of his body while fire issued from the lower part.
Having performed these various transformations, he returned to his original seat and sat cross-legged.
At that time, when the people saw the World-Honored One’s transformations, their minds were opened and their intentions were liberated.
At that time, the World-Honored One observed the inclinations of the assembly and preached the Dharma in various ways, so that each attained their aspiration.

Among the people there, some conceived the intent for supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), some developed the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), and some attained the patience regarding the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). Others attained the fruit of the Stream-enterer (*srotāpatti-phala*), the Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), or the Non-returner (*anāgāmi-phala*); some resolved upon the path of supreme, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), while others conceived the intent for the state of a Pratyekabuddha or a Śrāvaka. Thus, the people of the Kuru clan were delivered.
At that time, before the midday meal, the World-Honored One took Ānanda under his right arm and flew back to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
Meanwhile, five hundred bhikṣus fled into various valleys, begging for food among the Qiang tribes.

Having finished their almsround, they each returned to the vihāra; after putting away their robes, they went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side.
A great many bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How marvelous! How extraordinary!"
"Ānanda saw the great elephant approaching, yet he did not leave the World-Honored One's side.
The World-Honored One said, "Not only today."
Listen to me. Long ago, in a distant past, there was a king of deer named Śyāmaka who lived with five hundred deer in the Snowy Mountains.
At that time, a hunter scattered food among the grass and set out a large snare.
The deer king was at the front when his left hoof fell into a snare.
The deer king then thought to himself:
"If I were to tell the other deer that one has fallen into the snare, they would lose their desire for food."
When the deer had finished eating their fill, they said, "I have now fallen into a snare.
Upon hearing these words, all the deer fled in every direction; only one deer did not abandon Śrīmat and fled with him.
Then this deer said to the Deer King:
"Exert yourself to seek deliverance; the hunter has now arrived.
He replied:
"I now strive with all my might to escape, yet the rope is coarse and I have entered the net;
what shall I do? When the hunter approached, this deer said:
"It would be better for you to seize your blade and kill me first, rather than killing the King."
The hunter thought to himself:
"It is strange that this creature can speak; it is truly marvelous. Furthermore, it wishes to take another's place in death.
He then spoke to the deer, saying:
"I shall neither kill you nor kill your king.
I now release you from the snare and let your king go.
He then untied the snare and set him free.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The king of the deer at that time was none other than myself.
Those five hundred deer were these five hundred bhikṣus of today."
"At that time he abandoned me, and now he abandons me again.
That hunter of former times is this elephant, Raṅgapa;
formerly he did not touch me, and now he does not touch me again."
"The deer of that time is now Ānanda.
Just as he did not abandon me in the past, he does not abandon me now.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, recounted again the events of his former lives.
"Not far from Vārāṇasī, there is a pond named Kṣemavatī; its waters gush forth abundantly and abound with fish and turtles, as well as many geese and ruddy sheldrakes.
There dwells a king of geese named Tiṭṭibha, who, leading a retinue of five hundred geese, sports in that pond."
At that time, a hunter spread a net to capture wild geese.
When the goose king fell into the net, he thought to himself:
"If I cry out that I have fallen into the net, the other geese will be startled and unable to eat."
When the geese had finished eating their fill, they cried out,
"We have fallen into a net!
Hearing this, the other geese were terrified and each flew away in different directions.
There was a goose named Sumukha who lived alone and would not leave.
At that time, the Goose King said to Sumukha:
"I have now fallen into a net; you shall take my place as king."
The man should answer silently:
"I am not fit to take the King's place.
The King asks:
"Why are you unable?
He remained silent and replied with a verse:
"Better to die together with the king than to live alone without him."
"Life and death have bound us together for so long; I dare not seek liberation alone.
At that time, the king of geese sought a way to escape through skillful means, but he could not find a release.
When the hunter arrived, the goose remained silent for a moment and then addressed the hunter with these verses:
"The flesh and blood of the king of geese are no different from my own.
You have already killed me; I pray you, release the king from his snare.
At that time, the hunter thought to himself:
"This goose is truly extraordinary and remarkable; it even wishes to die in another's stead.
He then answered the goose with a verse:
"You possess the form of a bird and beast, yet out of loyalty to your lord, you have offered your own body as a substitute."
"I shall not kill you now, nor shall I harm your king;
I will now release you from the net, so that you may go wherever your heart desires.
Thereupon, the hunter untied the net and set him free.
Then the goose king drew back slightly and spoke again to his companion:
"This man is most compassionate; he has saved my life from death.
If he had killed me, who would have come to my rescue?"
The hunter came and asked,
"What were you saying?
Now that I have released you, why do you not fly away quickly?"
He replied:
"It is not that I am unable to fly.
The reason for my deliberation is that I wish to repay his kindness in small measure."
The hunter asked,
"Since you are a bird and a beast, how can you repay my kindness?
The king of the geese replied:
"Take these two geese to King Brahmadatta in the city of Vārāṇasī; once you have arrived there, we shall repay your kindness.
The hunter asked, "If they should harm you upon reaching that place, what plan would you make?"
The goose replied, "There is no need to worry about this; simply take me away.
Then the hunters, each carrying a goose, entered the city and went from the great marketplace to sit before the king's gate.
Seeing that the geese were lovely, various merchants gave five coins, ten coins, or twenty coins to this hunter; by the time they reached the king’s gate, he had obtained several thousand.
Then the hunter took the goose and released it at the king’s gate.
Thereupon, the Goose King spoke to the gatekeeper:
"The Goose King Titirilaṭṭha is at the gate seeking an audience."
Then the gatekeeper immediately reported this to the king, and the king commanded him to enter.
King Brahmadatta prepared a golden couch for him to be spread, and the Goose King took his seat, while Su-mo attended upon him.
Thereafter, at that time, the king of geese inquired with a verse:
"Is Your Majesty in peace?
Is Your Majesty in good health?"
"Is the realm secure and the troops and horses strong?
Are the people compliant with the transformation?
Then King Brahmadatta replied to the goose in verse:
"Your Majesty has come from afar, flying over mountains and seas; having traveled such a long distance, are you not weary?
At that time, the two kings conversed together in five hundred verses.
At that time, the goose remained silent and did not speak. King Brahmadatta asked, "Why are you silent?
The goose replied silently:
"One is a king of men, and the other is a king of geese.
These two kings engage in lofty discourse, and we dare not interject.
Then King Brahmadatta spoke to the king of the geese, saying:
"You may accept my invitation; you may dwell here in this garden with its ponds and trees, and I shall provide you with whatever food and drink you require.
The Goose King replied, "I dare not accept your invitation."
Brahmadatta asked, "For what reason do you not accept?
The king of geese replied:
"The king has become intoxicated from drinking wine and has ordered the kitchen to cook the geese.
If there are no others, he will take us and kill us.
For this reason, we did not dare to linger."
At that time, the five hundred geese, hearing that the Goose King was with King Brahmadatta, led one another in flight and soared above the palace.
The king asked,
"What kind of geese are these?"
The goose king replied,
"I am leading them. The king asked:
"Do you truly wish to depart? He replied, "I do."
"What do you require? the king of geese replied,
"I have no need for anything."
"Only this man carried me here; I pray that Your Majesty grant him gold, silver, precious jewels, food, drink, and all his necessities.
Having spoken these words, he immediately soared high into the air.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the king of geese, Tiṭṭhirattha, was none other than myself.
Those five hundred geese who abandoned me and fled were these five hundred bhikṣus who have run away."
The King Brahmadatta of that time was none other than Śuddhodana the Śākya of today.
He who instructed me to depart at that time has now again permitted me to leave the household life.
The hunter of that time was none other than the elephant Raṅgaka of today.
"At that time he did not harm me, and now he does not touch me.
He who was the goose named *Mūka* attending behind me at that time is now Ānanda.
Because he did not abandon me when I flew away in the past, he likewise does not abandon me now."
"Listen carefully, monks!
Far away from here there was a lion king who roamed the Snowy Mountains, leading five hundred lions.
This lion king was advanced in years and his faculties had matured; both his eyes were blind."
At that time, the lion king was walking at the head of his five hundred lion followers when he fell into an empty well;
all five hundred lions abandoned him and departed. Not far from the well, a wild fox saw the lion king fall and thought to himself:
"When this king was present, I was always satiated with food and drink."
"I must now devise a strategy to enable him to escape from the well.
Not far from the well was a large river; he immediately dug a tunnel to connect it with the water, causing the current to flow into the well.
As the water gradually rose, the lion climbed higher until he finally emerged from the well.
The mountain deity praised him with a verse:
"A person who has friends need not choose between the weak and the fierce; [The wise rely on them to cross over all difficulties. "
"Just as that small fox-like beast, the lion emerged from the deep well.
Having spoken this verse, he vanished from sight.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Lion King of that time was my own self in this present life.
Those five hundred lions who abandoned him at that time were these five hundred bhikṣus."
The wild fox of that time was none other than Ānanda now.

Because he practiced giving and diligence and refrained from committing evil deeds, those who direct their intentions toward the Path will not encounter adverse conditions in whatever place they are born.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the bhikṣus Aśvalāyana and Punarvasu were traveling in the kingdom of Naḍika at the Karanda Park; they frequented the homes of laypeople and engaged in evil deeds, such that there was no one in the neighboring villages who did not hear of it.
At that time, the Buddha dispatched the Venerable Ānanda to the kingdom of Kaśi to beg for alms for sixty days.
After Ānanda had departed, the Buddha ascended to the heavens and taught the Dharma to his mother for four months.
At that time, after the Venerable Ānanda had been on alms-round for ten days, he gradually made his way back through the kingdom of Nādikā.
At dawn, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city for alms; however, having received nothing, he came out with an empty bowl.

At that time, an upāsaka named Kāśyapa entered the city and saw from afar the Venerable Ānanda coming out of the city. He went forward, bowed his head to the Venerable’s feet in salutation, joined his palms, and said to Ānanda:
“It has been a long time since we last beheld your countenance. You have labored greatly in wandering for alms and teaching; when will you come here?”
Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the upāsaka Kappa:
"Venerable sir, do you know?
This morning, having dressed and taken my bowl, I entered for alms; however, my begging was in vain, as I obtained nothing."
"There are no sons of the Śākya lineage here who ruin lay devotees, act like those who are not śramaṇas, and commit offenses of body, speech, and mind.

The worthy one replied, "In this Kāla Grove there are two bhikṣus, Aśvajit and Punarvasu, who frequently go to the homes of laypeople to stay overnight and perform various evil deeds; there is no one in the neighboring villages who has not heard of or seen them."

Or they sit on the same bed or mat with women, eat from the same vessel, or drink from the same vessel; they fold their *saṃghāṭī* robes and place them upon a rack; they dance, sing, play the lute, strike the rhythm, or play the *pípá*; they clap their cheeks, make lewd gestures, or wear flower garlands—either tucking them into their hair or wearing fragrant necklaces and colorful garments while joining arms; they go to the houses of those of the lustful class to arrange marriages between men and women; or they wear secular clothing and practice with the five weapons, or engage in archery games, or practice throwing, dragging, leaping over high barriers, jumping down, or wrestling; or they race against one another, or ride elephants and horses to enter and leave gardens and pavilions.
In a short while, the time for the meal had arrived. "Excellent!
We pray that the Venerable Ānanda will come to our home for a light meal.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Upon arriving at the house, he took his seat; water was served, and with his own hands he portioned out and presented pure food and drink.
When Ānanda had finished eating, he provided water for washing. Then, having taught the Dharma to the Kātyāyanas, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat and departed.
Gradually, while wandering for alms, he arrived at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in Śrāvastī, and reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and, having established the ten merits, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, formulated a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu, while staying in the home of a layperson, commits a grave evil deed, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Cchanna (pronounced Chánzhī), who was stubborn, possessed a rigid mind, and was extremely difficult to transform.
He said to the bhikṣus:
"Gentlemen, do not speak words, whether good or bad, concerning me;
nor shall I speak words, whether good or bad, concerning you. Then the bhikṣus spoke to Caṇḍa.
"Since you do not speak to me of my good or bad qualities, I likewise shall not speak to you of your good or bad qualities.
Whatever wholesome Dharma and Vinaya you know, speak it to the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus' wholesome Dharma and Vinaya shall likewise be spoken to you."
If it be so, you shall long cause the lineage of the Buddha to flourish; let the bhikṣus transmit this to one another and instruct one another in turn.
Do not follow that which is evil, and do not harbor such a mind of stubbornness and rigidity.
At that time, the bhikṣu Cchannaka did not follow the words of the bhikṣus.
This Cchannaka was extremely difficult to convert, and the bhikṣus, not knowing what they should do, went to inform the World-Honored One.
On account of this matter, the Blessed One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha, prepared the ten merits, and for the sake of the śramaṇas, he established the precept:
"If a bhikṣu, such as Upāli, is stubborn in his own mind and does not accept admonition or instruction, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Set aside Cāṇūra; as for the bhikṣu Chanda, he shall naturally receive transformation after my parinirvāṇa."
Upāli asked the World-Honored One: “What is *saṃghāvaśeṣa*?

“The *saṃghāvaśeṣa* involves having fear toward the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*), having fear toward the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), having hope for the realization of the fruits (*phalasākṣātkriyā*), and having fear regarding the confession of transgressions.”
If one repents at the time of confession, twenty monks must be assembled;
one should repent for six nights, prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground, and must not conceal the transgression committed.
Since the Sangha’s adjudication and absolution are thus, it is called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
*Pinaiye*, Scroll Five; *Pinaiye*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
The Two Indeterminate Rules and the Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas.
While the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Kālodāyin frequently went to the house of the female lay follower Bhaddā, where they sat together in a secluded and private place.
Then, the female lay follower Bhaddā, desiring to engage in unchaste conduct, sat together with him in one place.
At that time, Kālodayin approved of his intention, yet fearing he might violate the precepts, he did not comply with him.
Then, the householder Viśākha saw this and returned home to speak privately among themselves:
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, has praised me, claiming my diligence is peerless."
"He is now sitting in a secluded and private place with a woman; there must certainly be a reason for this.
The dhūta bhikṣus went and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One, knowing the situation, questioned Udāyin:
“Is this truly so? Udāyin replied to the Buddha,
“It is indeed so.”
“World-Honored One!
On account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and, having fulfilled the ten merits, the Buddha established a precept for the bhikṣus:

“If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded and private place with a woman and receives her words—whether speaking of abandonment, speaking of formal monastic adjudication, or speaking of a pāyattika offense—he commits an offense.”
A bhikṣu who sits to listen to these three matters—
abandonment, formal settlement by the Saṃgha, and relinquishment—
is one who has fallen; he is an āniñja.
Then Kāḷodāyin went again to the house of the upāsikā Puṇḍravatī and sat down together with her on a seat spread in the open air.
At that time, the upāsikā wished to take hold of Kāḷodāyin’s body and sit together with him in that same place.
At that time, Kālodāyin felt a desire to follow them, yet he feared he might violate the precepts.
When the elders saw this, they whispered among themselves:
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, always praises himself as being peerless in his diligence."
"He is now sitting and conversing with women in the open air; there must certainly be a reason for this.
When the dhūta bhikṣus heard this, they went and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu sits with a woman on bare ground and listens to her speech, he commits two offenses:
saṃghāvaśeṣa and pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣu listens to these two dharmas, he is an Anirjita.
While the World-Honored One was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the Śākya son Upananda kept clothing in storage;
after a long time they became moldy and decayed, infested with insects and gnawed by rats.
When the various householders saw this, they each harbored resentment and said to one another:

"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are frugal in their clothing; yet now they store away garments that have been kept for so long that they are decayed and ruined, infested by woodworms and gnawed by rats."
When the elders saw this, they informed the dhūta bhikṣus.
Not knowing how they should respond, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One in detail.
On account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and, having fulfilled ten merits, established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu possesses three robes and a robe completed in a single day, he may keep them for the duration of his life."
"If one exceeds this limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
While the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Bamboo Grove,
the Kalandaka Feeding Ground in Rājagṛha, Mahākāśyapa was residing on Vulture Peak Mountain.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa had some minor business with the Saṃgha; he went to the Bamboo Grove without wearing his saṃghāṭī robe. As it was raining heavily, he was unable to return to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain.
The next day, upon returning to the stone cave, he immediately felt a doubt,
wondering, "Have I not lost my saṃghāṭī robe?
He went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:

"If a bhikṣu, not having put on his three robes or his one-day robe, goes to another's house for one night, and departs without carrying his saṃghāṭī, uttarāsaṅga, and antaravāsaka—except when sent by the Saṃgha—he commits a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Dāmatī who was observing the summer retreat together with other bhikṣuṇīs in Śrāvastī.
At that time, King Prasenajit’s soldiers were stationed near this bhikṣuṇī park.

These soldiers received their rations from King Prasenajit, but they squandered them daily on gambling and failed to provide for their own needs; the clothing of the women was insufficient even to cover their bodies.
This bhikṣuṇī heard the sound of laughter every day, and on the following day she went to the house of a woman from a family of strongmen and said to the women:
"How coarse and poor are these garments, insufficient even to cover your bodies?"
The woman replied, "The grain granted by the authorities is only sufficient for our food; it is not enough even for clothing and belts. The bhikṣuṇī said:
"Of the gift you have received, use half for food and clothing, and use half for giving as alms.
The women replied, "So be it."
"This is the teaching of the Tathāgata.
At that time, whenever he received a gift from the authorities, he would invariably set aside half for his own food and clothing, and use the other half for almsgiving.
Consequently, the household gradually became very wealthy; their food and clothing were abundant, and the garments they wore were superior to those of others.
The women said to one another:
"All our wealth is due to the power and grace of the bhikṣuṇī Dāmatī; we should join together to repay her kindness."
Then the woman said to her husband:
"We have become wealthy because of the bhikṣuṇī Dāmatīnā.
I wish to invite her to stay in one place for the four months of the summer retreat and provide her with offerings, preparing fine and pure food."
The husband replied to his wife,
"Very well. Then those strong men went to where the bhikṣuṇī Dāmatī was, prostrated themselves at her feet with their heads, and sat to one side.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī preached the Dharma to him; having finished preaching, she remained silent and said nothing more.
Then the strongman rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. I pray that you will accept me as an upāsaka, who shall refrain from taking life for as long as I live."
"I wish for all the elder nuns (āryikās) to accept my invitation for the four months of the summer retreat.
The bhikṣuṇīs replied, "The Buddha is currently nearby at Jetavana; those who have previously invited the Buddha should go to accept his invitation."
The strongman replied,
"I shall go and invite him.
The strongman then went to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, where he prostrated himself at [the Buddha's] feet and sat to one side.
The World-Honored One preached various teachings for him.
Having finished preaching the Dharma, he withdrew to sit for a moment and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One, together with the community of bhikṣus, will accept my humble invitation to spend the four months of the summer retreat in this garden."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Seeing that the World-Honored One had granted his permission through silence, the Mallas rose from their seats, bowed their heads at his feet in salutation, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then withdrew to return home.
He prepared food and drink for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to provide for their needs during the four-month period of the rains retreat.
Knowing that the date for the summer retreat was approaching, the World-Honored One, accompanied by the community of bhikṣus, went there to observe the four-month rains retreat.
At that time, the Mallas provided robes, food and drink, and medicinal requisites for the sick for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for the duration of the four-month rains retreat.
Having gained faith in the Buddha, the Mallas would not drink water that had not been strained; they constantly carried water-strainers, fastened to the side of their quivers.
At that time, King Prasenajit faced rebellion on his borders and summoned his warriors, saying:
"There is rebellion in such-and-such a place; you shall go there to attack and subdue it.
The warriors bowed in response.
"Only as Your Majesty commands.
Then the ministers said to the king:
"The soldiers sent by Your Majesty to attack and conquer that place have been unable to achieve victory."
The king asked,
"For what reason have you not prepared it?
The minister replied:
"The men of great strength do not drink water that has not been strained;
they do not even kill tiny insects, much less wage war.
Then the king questioned those men of great strength:
"Do you not intend to cause me to fail in my task?
The strongman replied,
"I do not understand what task."
The king said,
"I have heard that you do not drink water unless it has been filtered.
If you are thus toward even small insects, how much more so could you not attack and wage war against those who are great?"
The strongman replied, "This small insect has done no wrong to Your Majesty; even if it were to violate the king's law, it would still be put to death without hesitation.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"There are some people who are so pure that they will not drink water unless it has been filtered.
At that time, the strongmen said to one another,
"We have already completed our offerings to the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus, yet we have not yet bestowed robes upon them."
"If we were to set out on a military expedition, we might perish and never return.
Now is the proper time for us to jointly bestow robes upon the community of bhikṣus.
He then struck the *gandī* bell, and the bhikṣus gathered like clouds; only the Buddha did not come.
At that time, the Mallas offered robes to the community of bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus did not accept them, fearing they would incur the offense of possessing extra robes (*atirekacīvara*).
The Mallas insisted on making the offering, and the bhikṣus, not knowing how to respond, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"You may accept the robe, but do so with compassion.
Then, on account of this matter, the World-Honored One established a precept for the śramaṇas:

"If a bhikṣu possesses the three robes and the robe completed in a single day, and he obtains an extra robe, this bhikṣu may accept it with his own hands and wear it for one month; after one month, he must give it to another."
"If one keeps [the robe] for more than one month, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
At that time, when the soldiers were about to set out on a campaign, they entered the *maitrī-samādhi* as soon as they faced their enemies; consequently, the enemy forces retreated.
As for those who enter the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), fire cannot burn them, blades cannot pierce them, they do not die from drinking poison, and they cannot be killed by others.
King Prasenajit, hearing that this man of great strength had achieved merit in his military campaigns, further increased his landholdings and doubled his grain stipend and rewards.
The Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Ālavikā dressed in the morning, took her bowl, and entered Śrāvastī to beg for alms.

Having finished his almsround, he returned out of the city, took up his robe and bowl, washed his feet, placed his sitting mat (niṣīdana) upon his shoulder, and went to Mount Andhava; there, he spread the sitting mat beneath a tree and sat down cross-legged.
At that time, there were bandits who, having robbed people and obtained their wealth, fled into this mountain.

Among them was a bandit leader who had faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; from afar he saw a bhikṣuṇī sitting beneath a tree in meditation, her countenance upright and her faculties serene.
When the leader of the bandits saw the bhikṣuṇī, he was filled with redoubled joy and leaped for gladness; he took a piece of meat and offered it as a gift to the bhikṣuṇī.
The bhikṣuṇī replied, "I have already taken my single meal for today; once the time has passed, I do not eat."
The bandit leader was even more delighted; he wrapped a single piece of extremely fine white cotton cloth around the flesh and hung it upon a tree, saying:
"If any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa takes this, I shall give it to them forever."
Having spoken these words, he then departed from the mountain.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī reflected:
"That the bandit leader spoke those words to leave behind the cotton cloth and the meat was for my sake."

The next morning at dawn, the bhikṣuṇī took this meat and entered the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park; she delivered the meat to the kitchen to provide a meal for the assembly of bhikṣus, and then returned carrying the white cotton cloth over her shoulder as she came out.
When the Śākya son Upananda saw her, he asked:
"Auntie, where did you obtain this white cotton cloth, so bright, pure, and fine?
From whom did you get it? You may grant me a portion of it."
The bhikṣuṇī did not refuse him and immediately gave him the cotton cloth.
The Śākya son Upananda said to the bhikṣus:
"A bhikṣuṇī has given this cotton cloth to me."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"It would not be proper for me to return to the city without having seen the World-Honored One.
She then went to where the World-Honored One was, her robes being worn and tattered.
The World-Honored One saw the bhikṣuṇī approaching from afar and, turning to address Ānanda, said:
"Take one of your discarded robes and give it to this bhikṣuṇī.
Thereupon, Ānanda immediately gave a discarded robe to the bhikṣuṇī.
The bhikṣuṇī took it and went before the Buddha, prostrated with her head at his feet, and stood to one side.
The World-Honored One preached the Dharma for her.
Having finished preaching the Dharma, the World-Honored One addressed her, saying:
“Return to your place; now is the very time.
He then prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and departed.
Not long after the bhikṣuṇī had left, the Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Why is this bhikṣuṇī’s robe so tattered?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"This bhikṣuṇī previously possessed one end of white cotton cloth, which Upananda seized and took away."
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and addressed the bhikṣus:
"How can it be, bhikṣus!
That this bhikṣuṇī’s robes were worn out and ruined, yet you seized her cotton cloth?"
After the Blessed One had admonished him with countless skillful means, he established a precept for the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, or takes it from a beggar—except in exchange—it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Kālodāyin went to visit his acquaintance, the bhikṣuṇī Guptā, and traveled separately for two months on his almsround.
After completing his almsround in the second month, Kālodāyin gradually returned to Śrāvastī.

When the bhikṣuṇī Guptā heard that Kālodāyin had finished his almsround and was returning to Śrāvastī, she bathed her body, anointed her head with fragrant oil, applied powdered cosmetics to her face, whitened her teeth, and put on new garments. She then went to where Kālodāyin was, prostrated herself at his feet, sat before him, and gazed intently at him.
Kāḷodāyin likewise gazed intently at the bhikṣuṇī.
Kāḷodāyin rose from his seat, put on only his undergarment (nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī), and walked ahead.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī also wore only a single robe and followed behind Kāḷodāyin, not wishing for their bodies to touch one another.
Why was this? Because he feared violating the precepts.
Kāḷodāyin’s lustful mind was so intense that he sat upon the ground and emitted semen, thereby defiling the saṃghāṭī robe.
When the bhikṣuṇī realized that the semen had been discharged, she took another *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) in exchange for the first and took it away to wash it.
After Kālodāyin had put on his other garment, he gave it to her to wash.
The bhikṣuṇī took this garment and washed it in a secluded place; she drank half of the wash-water and poured the other half down below her body, whereupon she immediately realized she was pregnant.
She returned to her residence, and her body gradually grew larger.
The bhikṣuṇīs reviled her, saying:
"Shame on you, wicked bhikṣuṇī!
You did not become a bhikṣuṇī late."
"Entering the Path at such a young age—by what means was this achieved?
The bhikṣuṇīs questioned her thoroughly, and at that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gopā recounted the entire matter from beginning to end.
The bhikṣuṇīs, not knowing what they should do, went and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"You must not say that this bhikṣuṇī Gopā has violated the precepts."
For what reason?
This is the pure holy life (brahmacarya).
Do not harbor ill will toward the bhikṣuṇī Guptā.
In the eighth month, during the ninth month, she gave birth to a son whose countenance was upright and handsome.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard that a son had been born, they went and reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs:
"A single bhikṣuṇī must not sleep alone; two bhikṣuṇīs may sleep together.
She must not sleep with a man, but she may sleep together with the bhikṣuṇī Kūṭadantā."
The bhikṣuṇīs said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Previously, you taught that one must not sleep in the same room as a man."
“World-Honored One, this man now has a son; how should he sleep?
The World-Honored One replied:
"A child who has not yet been weaned may stay overnight with [a nun], but after being weaned, he may not.
Having received these instructions, the bhikṣuṇīs withdrew.
Then, on account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the Saṃgha and the Buddha established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash an old robe for him, or dye it, or press it to make it shine, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus frequently went to the houses of householders to beg for clothing.
The householders grew weary of their frequency and said to one another,
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim to be diligent.
Although we previously stated that we would not grant them garments, they come here repeatedly to beg for clothes."
When the Bhikkhus who observed the twelve rules heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One declared:
"If a bhikkhu, by force, compels a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative to give him a robe, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."

Whether he has been robbed of his robes by thieves, lost them, had them consumed by fire, seen them decay, or had them seized by a king, he goes to the house of a householder or a householder’s wife to beg for robes, taking what he has lost.
"If a bhikṣu takes [cloth] in excess of the [allowed] length, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
While the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
there was a householder’s wife who was making a robe for the Śākya son Upananda.
At that time, having heard that the wife of a certain householder was making a robe for him, Upāli (Bhadanta) went immediately to her home and spoke these words:
"If you are making a robe for me, make it as excellent as possible and give it to me as a gift."
At that time, the householder immediately had a fine one made and gave it to him.
Upon returning to his room, he praised himself and said to the bhikṣus,
"A certain householder had this fine robe made for me."
The bhikṣus remained silent, not knowing how they should respond, and went to inform the World-Honored One in detail.
The World-Honored One told them:

"If a bhikṣu hears that someone is making a robe for him, yet he has not previously given permission, and he goes there to manage the work, instructing them to make it exceptionally well so that he may take it when it is finished, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, two householders were making robes for Baddhālī.
When Baddhālī heard that the two householders were making robes for him, he went to their house and spoke as follows:
"Excellent, householder!
If you are to provide me with robes, it will not suffice to make two separate ones; you may join them together to make one fine garment.
Then the householder tore the two pieces into one, completed it, and gave it to him.
Returning to the midst of the Saṃgha, he became conceited and said to the bhikṣus:
"Two certain elders tore two robes into one robe and offered it to me."
The bhikṣus did not know how they should respond and went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu takes two robes that were previously promised by a householder’s wife who is not a relative, and causes them to be torn into one, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, King Udayana heard that the robes of the monks at Śrāvastī were poor and coarse. He immediately dispatched a Brahmin messenger carrying robes to Śrāvastī to present them to the monks.
The bhikṣus did not accept it, [thinking]:
"The World-Honored One does not permit the acceptance of the price for robes; one may only accept robes that have already been made.
The messenger asked the bhikṣus:
"Venerable friends, is there anyone who can buy these robes?
The bhikṣus replied, "No one."
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do and reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One.
On account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha; having prepared the ten merits, the World-Honored One established the precepts for the śramaṇas.
The World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu wishes to purchase robes, he should borrow from a nearby acquaintance, a park-keeper, or a virtuous person who observes the five precepts.
This bhikṣu should say:"
"This person is a buyer of clothes; this person is not a buyer of clothes.
Having said this, he went directly to the market to buy clothes.
Whether this person reached the market, or a money shop, a gold and silver shop, a copper and iron shop, or a shop for cotton, silk, and thread.
If a person is seated inside, the bhikṣu should go back and forth four, five, or six times, standing silently before them; if he succeeds, it is well.
If he goes beyond six times to seek [the item], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If he does not obtain the robe-cloth, he should go there in person or send a messenger to the house where the goods were kept, saying:
"The price for the robe-cloth previously offered was sent on account of my faith, but the bhikṣu so-and-so did not ultimately receive it."
"Go back yourself to seek it; do not say that the bhikṣu has obtained it, and do not waste or scatter the goods.
Thus spoke the Buddha while he was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took *kośika* grass to make new bedding.
When the householders saw this, they said:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not refrain from desiring what is fine; by taking *kośika* grass to make such bedding, how are they any different from kings or householders?"
When the twelve-group of bhikṣus heard this, they went and informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One declared:
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding using *kośika* wool, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."
Kosiya, these six groups of bhikṣus were using pure black sheep’s wool to make new bedding.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not use pure black sheep’s wool to make bedding."
"To make bedding [from such materials] constitutes an offense of expiation with forfeiture.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus again made bedding from pure white sheep’s wool.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not make bedding out of pure white sheep's wool.
If one makes bedding, it shall consist of two parts black sheep's wool, three parts white sheep's wool, and four parts variegated wool."
"If one makes [a new bedding] in violation of the time limit,

it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. When the monks of the twelve dharmas heard that the group of six bhikṣus had discarded their old bedding to make new bedding, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu makes bedding, it must be kept for a full six years.
If, before the six years have passed, he discards it and makes another, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."
"If a large robe is ruined or destroyed, one should inform the community; if the community permits it, one may make [a new one].
If one makes one without permission, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Śākya son Upāli (Baddhalita) made a new *niṣīdana* and discarded the old one.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, he must take the border from an old one and apply it to the four edges to preserve its appearance.
If he does not take the border from an old one to apply to the four edges, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Udāyin and a large number of bhikṣus traveled from Kośala to Śrāvastī.
On the road, they encountered merchants driving their chariots and urging on their horses, carrying a great load of wool as they traveled toward the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were many bandits along the way, so the bhikṣus said to the merchants,
"We wish to accompany you as companions to Śrāvastī."
The merchants replied,
"We also desire you as our companions.
The bhikṣus, fearing that dust and dirt would soil their bodies, always walked behind them.
There was a merchant whose cart axle broke;
he said to his companions, "All of you, give me a small amount of wool. His companions replied:
"I cannot even obtain my own allotted share, much less your goods," he said,
and then he left and moved forward.
At that time, the merchant sat there in dejection and distress facing the wool.
In a short while, the bhikṣus arrived; at that time, the merchant offered the wool to the community of bhikṣus, and each of the bhikṣus took his portion and departed.
At that time, this road passed through the interior of a city, and the people by the roadside said to the bhikṣu,
"How much is this wool worth? Is it expensive or cheap?"
"What goods do you trade?
What profit do you gain from the toil of carrying these burdens?
When the twelve Dharma-following bhikṣus heard these words, they did not know how they should answer.
He proceeded to Śrāvastī and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told him:
"If a bhikṣu is traveling on a road and someone offers him sheep’s wool, he may accept it and carry it for a distance of three yojanas."
"If one exceeds this limit, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
Kālodāyin received a portion of wool and gave it to some bhikṣuṇīs, saying, "Wash, sort, and dye this for me."

Kālodāyin was a close friend of King Prasenajit and the preceptor of Queen Mallikā; because the bhikṣuṇīs did not disregard his words, they accepted the wool, washed, sorted, and dyed it, thereby obstructing their recitation and reception of the teachings.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went and reported this in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, sort, or dye wool for him, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Stone Terrace by the Monkey River in Vaiśālī.
At dawn, the Śākya son Upananda dressed, took up his bowl, and entered Vaiśālī to beg for alms.
At that time, there were some youths within the city of Vaiśālī who, standing at the head of the streets and alleys, saw the Śākya son Upananda coming from afar and said to one another:
"This Upananda is a fierce and wicked bhikṣu; let us take some gold and silver and place them by the side of the road."
"If anyone takes it, we shall seize them and lead them before the elders.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda arrived at that place and immediately took the gold and silver.
The youths came forward and seized him, saying:
"You have become a bhikṣu; why did you take gold and silver without it being given? Baddhananda replied:
“I have not stolen it either; this [fruit] fell to the ground, and I took it.
He then went to where the elders were.
The youth said to the elders:
"This bhikṣu has stolen my gold and silver.
All the elders, who placed full trust in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, said to the youth:
"This śramaṇa son of the Śākyas truly would not steal your gold and silver."
He spoke again to Bāḍhananda:
"Venerable, return to your quarters; do not act like this again.
Bāḍhananda immediately returned and told the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus, not knowing how they should respond, went and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu takes gold or silver in his own hand, or instructs another to take it, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya)."
The Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda sat in a marketplace selling gold and silver to seek profit.
The elders were displeased and said to one another:
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, sits at his own stall selling gold and silver to seek profit; how is he any different from those merchants?
When the bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu sits at a marketplace to trade gold and silver for profit, no different from a worldly person, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Śākya son Baddhālita again took various goods and divided them into two parts to trade and sell.
When the elders saw this, they said to one another:
"This śramaṇa, the son of the Śākyas, claims to be diligent, yet he carries miscellaneous goods and trades them for profit; whose life does he intend to sustain?"
The Bhikṣus who observed the twelve dharmas went and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this incident, the World-Honored One assembled the Saṃgha of harmonious monks, prepared the ten merits, and established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu goes about the market carrying various goods to trade and sell them, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda was acquainted with a young perfume seller who worked at a shop.
On the sacrificial altar there was a maṇi bowl; seeing it, the Śākya son Upananda said to the boy, "This bowl is excellent.
You should give it to me."
He immediately filled the bowl with rice and gave it as an offering.
Carrying this bowl, he went to the Jetavana and said to the bhikṣus,
"Whenever I go out on a journey, all is auspicious and nothing is unfavorable."
"Before passing a perfume shop, a young boy gave me this bowl as an offering.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they said,
"How can a bhikṣu keep an extra bowl?"
He immediately went and reported this in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told him:
"If a bhikṣu obtains an extra bowl, he must not keep it for more than ten nights."
"If one does not relinquish [the item] after ten nights have passed, it constitutes an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
At that time, the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Bamboo Grove, the Kalandaka Feeding Ground, in Rājagṛha.
Then, the elder Jyotiṣka dispatched his son and younger brothers to sea to gather treasures; they obtained a single piece of ox-head sandalwood and returned home with it.
The young disciples then thought to themselves,
"We shall take this and present it to the elder Jyotiṣka.
They immediately offered it to him.

The elder possessed a great deal of sandalwood in his storehouse; although he had obtained this sandalwood, he did not set his mind upon it for personal use. Instead, he commanded a skilled artisan to carve it into a bowl. He erected a tall, long wooden pole ten *zhang* high from the ground and placed the bowl upon its top.
He made a vow, saying:
"Should there be any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who can take it without the aid of a ladder or a platform, I shall give it to him.
At that time, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa heard that the householder Jyotiṣka had fashioned a fine sandalwood bowl for him; he immediately went to his residence and said to the householder Jyotiṣka:
“Have you carefully crafted this sandalwood bowl specifically to offer it to me?
The householder replied,
“I did not make it for one person alone.”
"Now I have erected a tall, long pole ten *ren* above the ground, with an alms bowl placed upon it.
Should there be any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who can take it without using a ladder or a platform, I shall bestow it as a gift upon them."
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa then thought to himself,
"Does he lack such supernormal power that he cannot obtain that bowl?
He immediately rose from his seat, shook his head, and departed.
Shortly thereafter, Mahāli, Gayākāśyapa, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Katyayana, Vairatīputra, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra came to the house of the householder Jyotiṣka and said to him:
"Are you truly making a sandalwood bowl for us?"
The householder replied,
“I am not doing this for the sake of a single person.
Now, a tall wooden pole has been erected ten *zhang* above the ground, and a bowl rests upon it.”
"If there be any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who can reach and take it without the aid of a ladder or a platform, I shall bestow it upon him.
The six teachers then thought again:
"Without such supernormal powers (ṛddhi), one cannot reach and take that bowl."
He immediately rose from his seat and shook his head to depart.
At that time, the Venerable Piṇḍola heard that the householder Jyotiṣka had prepared a sandalwood bowl and erected a tall wooden pole ten fathoms high above the ground.
"If there be any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who can reach and take [it] without being provided a ladder or a platform, I shall give it to them.
At that time, the Venerable Piṇḍola went to the place where the Venerable Maudgalyāyana was, prostrated himself at his feet with his head, and sat to one side.
Piṇḍola said, "Maudgalyāyana,
you should know that the householder Jyotiṣka fashioned a sandalwood bowl and erected a tall, large wooden pole ten fathoms high from the ground, placing the bowl upon it."
"If there are any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who can reach it without using a ladder or a platform, give it to them.
The World-Honored One has always praised Maudgalyāyana as the foremost among his disciples in supernormal powers; he may go and retrieve it."
Then Maudgalyāyana replied:
"Is it because of a wooden bowl that you manifest such supernatural power?
For this reason, I have not gone to fetch it."

Then the Venerable Piṇḍola returned to his cell. At dawn the following day, he dressed and took up his bowl; with his robes properly adjusted, neither looking left nor right, and holding himself as if carrying a bowl of oil, his mindfulness undistracted and his five faculties restrained, like an ox harnessed to a yoke, he went to the house of the householder Jyotiṣka.

Seeing from afar the Venerable Piṇḍola approaching with a steady and composed gait, wearing his saṃghāṭī robe, holding his alms bowl, and carrying his staff, the elder rose to meet him, joined his palms, and said: "Welcome, Piṇḍola!"
"It has been a long time since you last came here.
Is your holy body light and robust? You may sit here."
Then the Venerable Piṇḍola sat down. The householder Jyotiṣka prostrated himself at his feet and sat to one side.
Piṇḍola asked the householder:
"I have heard that you had a sandalwood bowl made, set up a tall wooden post, and placed the bowl upon it."
"If there were any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who could reach it without being provided with a ladder or a platform, you would give it to them;
is this truly so? The householder replied: "It is indeed so."
"It is indeed so. At that time, Piṇḍola did not rise from his seat, but reached out his hand from afar to take the bowl.
When the elder witnessed this supernatural transformation, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
The elder said, "I pray that you will use this bowl to enter my house and receive some rice.
He then went inside, filled the bowl with rice and soup, and presented it to Piṇḍola.
Pindola immediately rose and went to the Bamboo Grove at Kalandaka, where he said to the bhikṣus:
"Just now I went to the house of the householder Jyotiṣka and took this bowl from a large wooden beam."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they did not know how to respond and went to inform the World-Honored One in detail.
The World-Honored One, knowing the situation, asked Piṇḍola:
"Is it true that you have done this?"
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One said to him:
“How is it that a bhikṣu sits upon a small wooden bowl and displays his supernormal powers?
Piṇḍola! I now expel you;
for the rest of your life you shall not enter parinirvāṇa, nor shall you dwell in Jambudvīpa.”
Then the Venerable Piṇḍola, having received the Buddha’s dismissal, rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Not long after Piṇḍola had left, the World-Honored One assembled the Saṃgha and established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu’s alms bowl is constantly broken into five pieces while he eats, and he continues to use it by mending it..."
If he seeks another that is better, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
When a bhikṣu obtains a new bowl, he must return his old one to the community of bhikṣus (*bhikṣusaṃgha*).
The community of bhikṣus shall then give the new one to this bhikṣu; he must hold it for as long as he lives, ceasing its use only when it is broken.

Then Piṇḍola returned to his cell and gathered his belongings; he immediately entered samādhi, vanished from Jambudvīpa, and appeared in Aparagoyānī. There, during that summer retreat, he conferred the precepts upon five hundred upāsakas, five hundred upāsikās, and granted full ordination to five hundred disciples.
Five hundred stūpas were erected, along with five hundred rooms furnished with mats, couches, and five hundred each of *ku-yao* pillows;
Piṇḍola performed the work of a Buddha in Aparagoyānī.
The Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Kapilavastu, Śākya-śrī.
At that time, the Śākyas had a separate workshop for weaving robes.
Then the group of six bhikṣus requested thread from various elders and went to their kinsmen, the Śākyas, saying:
"You may issue an order to the weaving workshop to weave and produce a robe for me.
At that time, the weavers, having received neither payment nor food, each spoke with resentment, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have forcibly coerced us by their power to make us weave this robe."

The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu goes to a householder's home to beg for thread and compels a weaver who is not a relative to weave a robe for him, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."
The Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Kapilavastu, Śākya-śrī.
At that time, the Śākyas of Kapilavastu were weaving a robe for the Śākya son Upananda.
When Bāṇaṃdā heard that the Śākya clan was making him a robe, he went immediately to the weaving workshop and said to the weavers: "Do you know?

"If a bhikṣu, having previously given no consent, goes secretly to a weaver's workshop and says to the weaver:

"If one obtains such a robe, it constitutes an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Upananda had a disciple whose observance of the precepts was perfectly complete.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had completed the summer retreat, he took his bhikṣus, donned their robes, and held their alms bowls to go on a general tour for alms.
Upananda’s disciple requested leave to follow the Buddha, but Upananda was unwilling to let him go.
The disciple replied,
"This is not something that should be left behind.
Then Upananda said to the disciple:
"The reason I gave you this robe was because of the need for manual labor.
If you wish to leave, leave this robe behind," he said,
and immediately stepped forward to seize it by force.
The disciples wept and went to where the Tathāgata was; prostrating themselves at his feet, they reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to another bhikṣu, and later, out of anger, forcibly takes it back, or instructs another to take it back:..."
If [a monk] says, "Monk, bring this robe here;
I will not give it to you," and that monk returns the robe, then the monk who took the robe commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus were observing the summer retreat at Śrāvastī.
During that year, people offered robes to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus did not accept them; they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu receives a robe offered by someone during the rainy season retreat, he should accept it with a wholesome mind and not oppose the intention of the donor.
On account of this matter, the World-Honored One established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If ten days have not yet passed until the end of the year, a bhikṣu who obtains a robe should accept it immediately.
If he obtains a new robe, he should keep it until the end of the year.
Once the ten days have passed, he must give it away to others."
"If one leaves it behind, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Pāvāriya, who was constantly dwelling in forest retreats, left his saṃghāṭī robe in an empty place and entered Śrāvastī.

The World-Honored One said:
"Three months hence, at the end of the month, when forest-dwelling bhikṣus staying in secluded places wish to go somewhere and encounter tigers, wolves, or bandits ahead of them."
If this bhikṣu sends his three robes from a secluded place to be kept within a city, he may be separated from those three robes for six nights at most.
If it exceeds six nights, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, and that very night she prepared the offerings of food.
On the following day, having prepared the seats, he dispatched a messenger to Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, to inform the Buddha and the Sangha:
“The meal is ready; the time has now arrived.”
At that time, the messenger arrived at Jetavana and encountered the bhikṣus bathing in the open air like the Nirgranthas. The messenger then thought to himself:
"There are no śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas here; the Jetavana is filled entirely with Nirgranthas."
She immediately returned and reported:
"There are no śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas; the entire Jeta Grove is filled with Nirgranthas.
Viśākhā, a person of keen intelligence who had attained the fruit of the path, then thought to herself:
"The community of bhikṣus must certainly bathe in the open air.
He again sent [messengers] to inform the Buddha and the Saṃgha:
"The meal is prepared; now is the proper time."
The messenger went and informed [Vaiśākhā].
The Buddha, accompanied by the community of bhikṣus, went to Vaiśākhā’s residence, where they each sat down in order.

When the community of bhikṣus had finished eating and the water for washing hands had been distributed, he sat to one side and reported the previous matter in detail to the World-Honored One, saying:
“I pray that the World-Honored One will permit the gift of a dwelling for the bhikṣus.”
The World-Honored One granted his permission.
After the Buddha had given the blessing and departed, he arrived at the Jetavana. On account of this matter, he established a precept for the bhikṣus:
"When one month of spring has passed, a bhikṣu must prepare a rain-shelter (*varṣa-śālā*).
It may be kept for half a month or one month; if it exceeds that period, it is an offense of relinquishment and forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
When less than one month remained until the end of the year, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

After the monk Daqin had taken the goods obtained as offerings and entered the lay residence with them, the other bhikṣus saw him and said to one another,
"How can this bhikṣu take property belonging to the Saṃgha?"
He immediately went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that it is the property of the Saṃgha of bhikṣus, takes it for himself;..."
"If a donor intends to give property to the community of bhikṣus, but seeks to have it enter into one's own possession, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
While the Buddha was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Pilindavatsa suffered from pain in both eyes; various householders and brahmins sent him offerings of food and requisites, as well as the four kinds of medicinal substances—clarified butter, sesame oil, honey, and black rock sugar—which he accumulated and consumed daily.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they went and reported it in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and, having established the ten merits, the Buddha formulated a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu stores the four kinds of medicine, he must not exceed seven days."
"If one exceeds [the limit], it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
Upāli addressed the Buddha: "What is meant by 'niḥsargika'?"
"World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied:

Whether trading or begging from others, this is called *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
It is called "burning the roots of the Noble Path" and "a person who has become a mere island"; one cannot give rise to *samādhi*, and this is termed a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Lohitya spoke false words in jest among a crowd of people.

"Why do you joke and speak falsely?
He then admonished and rebuked Rāhula with these verses:
“The hell of lying is near; though one commits it, one says, ‘I did not.
One will suffer both sins hereafter, for such conduct drags one away.
Though the Dharma robes are upon his body, he does not restrain himself from evil.”
Those who persist in evil conduct, their lives will end in falling into hell.
Receiving offerings without precepts, they beg in the streets without shame;
upon death, they shall swallow glowing iron balls, amidst extreme heat more fierce than blazing fire.
After the World-Honored One had thus rebuked him, he established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu speaks falsely out of playful mirth, it is a pāyattika.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus reviled other bhikṣus in various ways.
The bhikṣus went and reported this in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu insults another bhikṣu by means of their lineage or appearance, it is a pāyattika.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were constantly disputing with the group of seventeen bhikṣus.
Having heard these words here, they went and informed those people;
having heard these words there, they came and informed those here.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went and reported it to the World-Honored One.
The Blessed One said:
"If a bhikṣu engages in frivolous speech, double-tongued talk, or incites strife between this party and that party, it is a pāyattika.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling at Kuśāmbī in the Ghoṣitārāma.
Those monks of Kauśāmbī were fond of quarreling and engaging in disputes; they had been confined and sat among the assembly of elders until the matter was resolved.
The group of six monks returned and raised the original case again, saying:

When the bhikṣus heard that the group of six bhikṣus had resolved their dispute but were subsequently raising it again, they went to inform the World-Honored One in detail.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu raises again a matter of dispute that has been settled in accordance with the Dharma, he commits a pāyattika offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Kālodāyin entered the palace alone and preached the Dharma to Queen Mallikā.
The king’s various ministers said to one another,
"How can a bhikṣu enter the palace alone to preach the Dharma?
The bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma alone to a woman, he must not exceed five or six words, unless another person is present; [if he does so], it is a pāyattika."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were reciting the Vinaya to śrāmaṇeras.
When the other bhikṣus saw this, they asked, “How can you recite the precepts to those who have not yet received full ordination?”
He went and reported this in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu explains even a single sentence of the precepts to one who has not yet received full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu entered among a group of śrāmaṇeras and proclaimed his own praises, saying:

They then went and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu, toward one who has not yet received full ordination, speaks in self-praise, saying:

"Truthful one, this is a pāyattika. While the Buddha,

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The bhikṣu said to the group of six bhikṣus:

The group of six bhikṣus replied,
"Very well. Subsequently,
the latter bhikṣu purchased large quantities of grain and rice to await his guests.
The group of six bhikṣus said to the other bhikṣus,
"Who has instructed you all to disperse the Sangha's property to purchase grain and rice in order to wait upon guests?
The bhikṣus replied:
"You previously made a promise before me.
He replied again,
"I did not grant you permission."
The bhikṣus did not know how they should answer, so they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu has previously made an agreement with another, yet later speaks these words:..."
"If you diminish the property of the Saṃgha of bhikṣus by using it in contravention of previous agreements, it constitutes a pāyattika. While the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, on the fifteenth day, the *gandī* was struck and the community of monks gathered for the recitation of the precepts.
The Venerable Channa said to the monks,
"What is the use of reciting these minor rules every half-month?"
"This will cause the bhikṣus to be distressed and unable to practice the Path.

"If a bhikṣu, on the day of the recitation of the precepts, speaks thus:
'What is the use of reciting these trivial precepts every half-month?
and thereby rejects the precepts, it is a pāyattika."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The group of six bhikṣus cut down trees to make beds; the tree deity became enraged and went to speak to the twelve-group bhikṣus, saying:

The World-Honored One told them: "There is a deity who dwells at the root of a tree; there is a deity who dwells at the fork of a tree; there is a deity who dwells within the branches; there is a deity who dwells within the bark; there is a deity who dwells within the fissures of the bark; there is a deity who dwells in the buds; there is a deity who dwells in the leaves; there is a deity who dwells in the flowers; there is a deity who dwells in the fruits. "The reason deities dwell there is that they consume its fragrance.
If a bhikṣu cuts down a tree himself or instructs another to cut it down, he commits an offense.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One, while traveling in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The group of six bhikṣus were constantly quarreling with the group of seventeen bhikṣus; the group of seventeen bhikṣus could not endure it and suddenly became angry.

The World-Honored One said:
"One who gives way to sudden anger falls.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus disturbed and agitated the forest-dwellers, saying:
"Gentlemen, you have already attained the first, second, third, and fourth dhyānas; you have brought an end to birth and death and practiced the holy life."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu provokes someone to anger, he commits a pācittiya offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus spread out couches, mats, and grass seats in an open space and sat there discussing matters all day long, then rose and departed.

"This bhikṣu is shameless; he accepts the faithful offerings of others and causes them to rot from being drenched by rain.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu spreads out the sitting mat of the bhikṣu-saṃgha within a room and sits or lies down upon it..."
"If one leaves [a seat] after rising and neither puts it away oneself nor instructs another to put it away, one commits an offense of transgression.

While the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the Venerable Yaśas arrived in Śrāvastī from Kośala leading a group of five hundred followers. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus said to one another:
"Let us step aside for a moment until this bhikṣu has swept and sprinkled the room and spread out the sitting mats; then we shall go and ask him:
'How many years have you been ordained?'"
He himself shall state how many years it has been.
They replied,
"We are your great lord."
"If they do not leave, you must forcibly drive them out.
After the bhikṣus had swept and sprinkled the rooms and spread out their sitting mats, he went immediately to ask them:
"How many years of seniority do you have?"
He replied, "I am so many years old.
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"O Great Lord, depart quickly; you need not remain here.
The bhikṣus, not knowing what they should do, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu goes to a bhikṣu’s dwelling and, feigning anger, drives him out himself or causes another to drive him out, he commits an offense of falling (pārājika)."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
A large number of bhikṣus had spread out their sitting mats in front of the lecture hall during the night, some for meditation and others for sleep.
Kālodāyin arrived from behind and likewise spread out his sitting mat and lay down.
At that time, Kālodāyin feigned labored breathing; his breaths were coarse and harsh, as if he were gasping in distress, while his hands and feet were restless and agitated.
