The bhikṣus practicing meditation did not remain, but immediately gathered up their sitting mats and withdrew.
When the bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas heard of this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:

"If a bhikṣu has already spread bedding in a room, and another later comes and forcibly spreads a sitting mat there, [the first one should think]: 'If you do not like me, you should leave of your own accord.'"
"And those who are agitated fall.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha.
There was a newly constructed multi-storied pavilion; upon the upper floor of the pavilion was spread a couch with legs, while below the pavilion was a certain bhikṣu.

The bhikṣu Śreṇika Bāṣpa, son of a Śākya, threw himself down from the upper story onto a bed; the leg of the bed sank down and struck the head of another bhikṣu, breaking it, whereupon the first bhikṣu cried out in pain.
The assembly of bhikṣus gathered and asked,
"Why is your head broken?
He related the circumstances in full detail.
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do and went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu ascends an upper story of a multi-storied building and sits or lies down upon a corded bed with pointed legs using force, he commits an offense of defeat."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
The Venerable Cunda was sprinkling water containing living beings upon the ground to mix with the mud.
The bhikṣus said to Cunda:
"Do not sprinkle water containing insects upon the ground to mix the mud.
Channa was stubborn and perverse, refusing to follow this admonition.
The bhikṣus, not knowing what to do, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living beings, sprinkles it on the ground, or instructs another to sprinkle it; or if he himself mixes mud, or instructs another to mix it, he commits a pācittiya offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

There was a certain mahallaka bhikṣu who, having taken one hundred thousand taels of gold from a donor, constructed a great lecture hall. He applied layers of plaster over it in a single day, and that very night it collapsed.
When the elder heard this, he was struck with wonder and anxiety, thinking:
"Having spent such a vast amount of money, the lecture hall has still not been completed.
He immediately went to inform the World-Honored One in detail.
On account of this matter, the Blessed One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and, having fulfilled ten merits, the Buddha established a precept for the śramaṇas:

"When a bhikṣu constructs a large lecture hall, he should first install a threshold and windows so that sunlight may pass through; he should plaster the floor with fine mud, apply it two or three times, and cover it with layers of grass."
"If one exceeds three [times], it is a pāyattika.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
the group of six bhikṣus went in person to preach the Dharma to bhikṣuṇīs when it was not yet their turn to do so.
The Bhikkhus who observed the twelve dharmas heard of this and went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:

"If a bhikkhu, when the turn of the bhikkhu-saṃgha to teach the Dharma to bhikkhunīs has not yet been assigned, goes of his own accord to preach the Dharma to them, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya)."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The bhikṣus were, in turn, preaching the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs; it was the turn of the Venerable Nanda to go next, yet he was unwilling to do so.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, leading five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to where the Tathāgata was; she prostrated herself at his feet and stood to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to Mahāprajāpatī and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs.
Having finished preaching the Dharma, he said:
"Now is the right time; each of you return to your respective places.
Mahāprajāpatī and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs prostrated themselves at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and departed.
Not long after he had departed, the Buddha turned to Ānanda and asked:
"Who should be the next to preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"The assembly of bhikṣus has already completed its circuit; next it is Nanda’s turn.
Yet Nanda is unwilling to go.
At that time, Nanda was also seated there.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Nanda:
"You should go and preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs. Why is this?"
"What difference is there between my teaching of the Dharma and your teaching of the Dharma?
Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, Nanda accepted it in silence.

Then, at dawn, the Venerable Nanda put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī for alms. Having finished his almsround, he returned out of the city, set aside his robe and bowl, placed his sitting mat upon his shoulder, and entered his cell to practice meditation.
When the community of bhikṣuṇīs heard that Nanda was next to preach the Dharma, they said to one another:
"Nanda could not even master a single verse during the four months of the summer retreat; how does he intend to preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs?"
Nanda emerged from his private chamber and, having spread out his seat in front of the hall, sat down cross-legged.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī and five hundred bhikṣuṇīs approached Nanda, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side.

Then the Venerable Nanda entered into samādhi; by the power of that samādhi, he disappeared in the east and reappeared in the west, and disappeared in the west and reappeared in the east. He sat and lay down in mid-air, emitting various kinds of light—blue, yellow, red, white, or the color of lapis lazuli. From his lower body he emitted fire while his upper body emitted water, and from his upper body he emitted fire while his lower body emitted water. Having displayed such transformations beyond counting, he returned to his original seat and sat cross-legged.
Nanda addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"I shall teach the Dharma to you; listen well and reflect upon it.
What do you think, sisters?"
"Is the eye permanent or impermanent?
He replied, "It is impermanent."
"Nanda! If it is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering? He replied:
“It is suffering,
Nanda! If it is impermanent and suffering, it is subject to change.”
“Does that person who has seen the truths seek in this way, saying,
‘Is this mine, or is it not mine? “No, Nanda.”
“Sisters, how is it? Are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind permanent or impermanent? “They are impermanent.”
"Nanda! If something is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering? "It is suffering."
"Nanda! If it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,
would one who has seen the truth seek it, saying, 'This is mine' or 'This is not mine'?"
"No, Nanda! Why is that? Because—"
Now, through the wisdom and vision that accords with reality, one sees that the eye is impermanent; the eye-consciousness, as well as pleasure and pain, are likewise impermanent.

In this same way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent; the mental consciousness, the perceptions it gives rise to, and the feelings of pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain are likewise impermanent.
“Excellent, excellent, sisters! Just as you have said,
the eye is impermanent, and the pleasure and pain cognized by the eye are likewise impermanent.”
In this way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent; the perceptions of pleasure, pain, and neither-pleasure-nor-pain that arise in the mental consciousness are likewise impermanent.
What do you think, sisters?
“With the eye as a condition, consciousness arises. Is that eye-consciousness permanent or impermanent? “It is impermanent, Nanda.”
“If it is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering? “It is suffering, Nanda!”
“If it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,
would a person who has seen the truth seek it, saying, ‘This is mine’ or ‘This is not mine’? “No, sir.”
"Nanda! Thus, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: when consciousness arises conditioned by the mind, is that mental consciousness permanent or impermanent? "It is impermanent."
"Nanda! If something is impermanent, is it suffering or not? "It is suffering."
"Nanda! If it is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change,
would a person who has seen the Truths seek it, saying, 'This is mine' or 'This is not mine'?"
"No, Nanda! Why is that? Because..."

Just as through the knowledge and vision of the truths one perceives that the eye is impermanent, that the eye, forms, and visual consciousness are impermanent, and that the perceptions of pleasure and pain arising from visual consciousness are likewise impermanent;

so too are the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness impermanent, and the perceptions of pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure produced by the conditions of mental consciousness are likewise impermanent.
“Excellent, excellent, sisters! It is as you have said:

the eye is impermanent, and visual consciousness is impermanent; the perceptions of pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain that arise through the conditions of visual consciousness are likewise impermanent.”

In this way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, dharmas, and mental consciousness are impermanent; the perceptions of pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure that arise through the conditions of mental consciousness are likewise impermanent.
Sisters! With the eye as condition, there are forms; with forms as condition, there is consciousness. When these three things come together, there is contact.
What do you think, sisters?
"Is that which changes permanent or impermanent? "It is impermanent, Nanda!"
“If it is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering? “It is suffering, Nanda!”
“If that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change were to be sought by one who has seen the truth, saying, ‘This is mine’ or ‘This is not mine,’ would they do so? “No, sir.”

"Nanda! Regarding these—the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; the consciousness of phenomena (dharmas), the mental consciousness, and the contact-consciousness—is that which is contacted permanent or impermanent? "It is impermanent."
"Nanda! If it is impermanent, is it suffering or not suffering? "It is suffering."
"Nanda! If something is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, would a person who has seen the Truth seek it, saying, 'This is mine,' or 'This is not mine'?"
"No, Nanda. Why is that? Because..."

Just as one observes with wisdom corresponding to the truths that the eye is impermanent, so too are form, eye-consciousness, and eye-contact; and the perceptions of pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain arising from the conditions of eye-contact are likewise impermanent.

In this same way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mental objects—the consciousness of the mind, the contact of the mind, and the perceptions of pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from the conditions of that mental contact—are likewise impermanent.
“Excellent, excellent, sisters! It is as you have said:
the eye is impermanent; and the forms, the eye-consciousness, and the contact of the eye—which give rise to perceptions of pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain—are likewise impermanent.”

In this same way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mental phenomena—the consciousness of the mind, the contact of the mind, and the perceptions of pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising through the conditions of that mental contact—are likewise impermanent.
"What do you think, sisters?
With the eye as a condition for forms, and with forms as a condition for consciousness, the conjunction of these three things constitutes contact (*phassa*).
Contact is a condition for feeling (*vedanā*); is that contact and feeling permanent or impermanent?"
“‘It is impermanent, Nanda! If it is impermanent, is it suffering or not?’”
“It is suffering, Nanda! If it is impermanent, suffering,
and subject to change, would one who has seen the Truth seek it, saying, ‘This is mine’ or ‘This is not mine’?”

"No, Nanda! In the same way, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mental phenomena (dharma), as well as consciousness, mental contact, and the feeling produced by mental contact— would these be permanent or impermanent?"
“‘It is impermanent, Nanda! If it is impermanent, is it suffering or not?’”
“It is suffering, Nanda! If something is impermanent,
suffering, and subject to change, would one who has seen the Truth seek it, saying, ‘This is mine’ or ‘This is not mine’?”
"No, Nanda! Why is that? Because..."

Just as one observes with the wisdom of the truths that the eye is impermanent, so too are forms, eye-consciousness, and eye-contact impermanent; the sensations of suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure arising from the causal conditions of eye-contact are likewise impermanent.

In this way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and dharmas are likewise. Consciousness and mental contact are impermanent; because of the conditions of contact, there arise perceptions of pain, pleasure, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure, which are also impermanent.
“Excellent, excellent, sisters! It is as you have said:

the eye is impermanent; forms, eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the sensations of pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from the causal condition of eye-contact are likewise impermanent.”

In this same way, the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mental phenomena—the consciousness of the mind, the contact of the mind, and the sensations arising from the conditions of that contact, whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—are likewise impermanent.

"What do you think, sisters? With the eye as condition, there are forms; with forms as condition, there is consciousness; with consciousness as condition, there is contact; with contact as condition, there is feeling; with feeling as condition, there is craving. Is that craving for the eye permanent or impermanent?"
“‘It is impermanent, Nanda! ‘If it is impermanent, is it suffering or not?’”
"It is suffering, Nanda! If something is impermanent,
suffering, and subject to change, would one who has seen the truth seek it, saying, 'This is mine' or 'This is not mine'?"

"No, Nanda! In the same way, regarding the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, mental phenomena, consciousness, and mental contact—when there is mental contact, there is feeling and craving. Is that feeling and craving permanent or impermanent?"
“‘It is impermanent, Nanda! If it is impermanent, is it suffering or not?’”
“It is suffering, Nanda! If that which is impermanent, suffering,
and subject to change were to be seen by one who has realized the Truths as ‘this is mine’ or ‘this is not mine,’ would they do so?”
"No, Nanda! Why is that? Because..."
"Just as one observes them with the knowledge of the truths and so forth, phenomena arise by themselves and phenomena cease by themselves. "Excellent,
excellent, sisters!"
Those phenomena arise by themselves and those phenomena cease by themselves.
Thus, sisters, the perceptions of pleasure,
pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure that arise through the conditions of the six sense-faculties are likewise impermanent.

"Sisters! It is just as when a butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, wielding a sharp knife, slaughters an ox, flays its hide, extracts its flesh and sinews, places them in pieces in one spot, and then covers them again with that very hide."
"What do you think, sisters!
Would they be able to become cows again?
The bhikṣuṇīs replied:
"No, Nanda! Why is that? Because..."
"The cow, having been separated from its calf, is truly not as it was originally.
"The reason for citing this analogy is that you should understand this meaning.
Thus it is, sisters!"

The "ox" refers to the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) which, through mutual dependence, give rise to perceptions of pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure; it is eternally abiding and indestructible, a phenomenon free from change.
One who seeks in this manner shall be able to attain the Way.
Why is this? Because when one contemplates with the knowledge of the truths and so forth, one does not perceive the arising of those phenomena, nor does one perceive the cessation of those phenomena.
The reason for citing this analogy is that the contemplative mind does not aggregate.
The cow represents the six sense faculties, which are no different from it; its flesh and sinews represent the six sense objects; and that sharp knife represents equalizing wisdom (*samatājñāna*).
Why is this so? O sisters!
The sword of wisdom completely severs all fetters of birth and death; one is no longer reborn there, for in this realm, severance is equal to total cessation.
Excellent, sisters!

You should train yourselves thus: let the mind not be stained by phenomena that cause defilement and attachment; seeking to bring rest to the phenomena of entanglement, let the mind not follow after anger or delusion, but find rest.

Next, sisters, you should train in the four foundations of mindfulness, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and the eight doors of liberation; therefore, you should train in these.

Those who train in this manner are from whom all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas emerge; it is from within these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that countless wholesome dharmas arise. One should always maintain equanimity of mind and body, never allowing them to be interrupted.
When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs attained the path of arhatship.
Upon seeing the initial manifestation of the transformation, two hundred and fifty bhikṣuṇīs attained the path of arhatship.
As for those two hundred and fifty bhikṣuṇīs, because they had previously heard this Dharma during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, they now attained the fruits upon hearing the Dharma.
Nanda said: "Sisters!..."
"Now is precisely the time; each of you should return to your respective places.
Then Mahāprajāpatī and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs prostrated themselves at his feet and departed.

On the following day, at dawn, Mahāprajāpatī and the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to where the Tathāgata was. They prostrated themselves at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The World-Honored One observed that all the bhikṣuṇīs had attained the Way in an instant, and the Buddha addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Now is precisely the time; each of you return to your respective places."
After the bhikṣuṇīs had paid their respects and departed,
the World-Honored One said, "Nanda!"
"Tomorrow, furthermore, you shall preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, Nanda silently accepted the instruction.
The next day, Nanda put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī to beg for alms.
Having finished his almsround, he returned out of the city, set aside his robe and bowl, washed his hands and feet, placed his *niṣīdana* over his shoulder, and entered his room to sit in meditation.
Emerging from the room, he spread his sitting mat in front of the hall and sat down cross-legged.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, leading five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to the place where Nanda was, prostrated with her head at his feet, and sat to one side.
The Venerable Nanda preached various subtle and wondrous Dharmas to them.
Having finished preaching the Dharma, he said:
"Now is the right time; each of you return to your respective places.
The bhikṣuṇīs prostrated at his feet and departed.

When the sun set and the city gates were already closed, some stayed the night beneath trees, some stayed by the edge of mounds, some stayed by the waters of ponds, some stayed by flowing streams, and some stayed by the moats and ditches.
Tomorrow the gates will open, and the bhikṣuṇīs will enter the city.
The gatekeepers said to one another, “These bhikṣuṇīs are the wives of śramaṇas; they sleep together outside the city and come in at dawn.”
When the twelve Dharma-following bhikṣus heard these words, they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"The community of bhikṣus shall preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs in due order, but must not remain until evening before returning."
"Those who go until sunset fall [into an offense).
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus traveled along the same road as bhikṣuṇīs.
When the householders saw this, they said to one another, "This śramaṇa son of the Śākyas is traveling along the same road as the bhikṣuṇīs; he is the husband of these śramaṇas."
"If she is not his wife, by what means could they travel together?
When the twelve-group bhikṣus heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu travels along the same road with a bhikṣuṇī from one village to another within a village, he commits a pācittiya offense.
However, if they must travel together because there are merchants on the road, or if there are tigers, wolves, bandits, or robbers ahead, it is permissible for them to travel together."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus came from the kingdom of Kośala to Śrāvastī.
Then, they had to wait for a boat before they could cross the Āciravatī River.
The group of six bhikṣus traveled in the same boat as a bhikṣuṇī, either going upstream or following the current downstream.
After several days had passed and the sun had set, they crossed the water and dispersed in different directions.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī was robbed by bandits and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told her:
"If a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī travel on the same boat, whether going upstream or downstream, except for crossing directly across, it is an offense of falling (pārājika)."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Kālodāyin gave a robe to the bhikṣuṇī Guptā. The bhikṣuṇīs asked:
"By what means did you obtain this robe?
He replied, "Kālodayin gave it as a gift."
The bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One declared:
"If a bhikṣu accepts a robe offered by a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya)."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Kālodāyin had the bhikṣuṇī Guptā make a robe for him. The bhikṣuṇīs asked:
"With whom are you making the robe? He replied, "I am making it with Kāḷudāyin."
The bhikṣuṇīs, not knowing what they should do, went to inform the Blessed One.
The Blessed One told them:
"If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to make a robe for him, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya)."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Kālodāyin was sitting in a secluded place with the bhikṣuṇī Gopikā.
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One declared:
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a bhikṣuṇī in a secluded place, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya)."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Kālodāyin was sitting with the female lay disciple Buddhadevā in an open, unsheltered place.
When the householders saw this, they said to one another,
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, sit in an exposed place with women?
When the bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Blessed One said:
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in an exposed place, he commits an offense of falling.
At that time, the Bhikṣuṇī Upasamā was staying with the Buddha, the World-Honored One, at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Jeta’s Grove in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
There was a laywoman who invited Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Aniruddha.
At that time, the elder’s wife prepared various kinds of food and drink and spread out fine seats.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tuḷaṇanda, who was a close friend of the householder’s wife, dressed at dawn, took her bowl, and came to this house. Seeing various kinds of food and drink prepared and fine seats laid out, she asked the householder’s wife, “Whom do you intend to invite?”
"Prepare such excellent food and drink, and arrange fine seating.
The householder’s wife replied,
"I invite Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Aniruddha."
The bhikṣuṇī said, "You have abandoned the dragon-elephant to invite a mule and a donkey.
The householder’s wife asked:
"Who are the dragon-elephants?
The bhikṣuṇī replied,
"Venerable Devadatta, Khaṇḍadravya, Kāḷudāyin, Tiṣya, and Samudradatta— these superior men are they."
Kāśyapa, being the eldest, entered the house first; seeing him enter, the bhikṣuṇī Tuḷa said to the householder’s wife:
“Excellent, upāsikā!”
"This is what is meant by 'the dragon-elephants have arrived.
At that time, when the elder heard these words, he spoke thus: "Evil bhikṣuṇī!"
"Previously you spoke of mules and donkeys; now you speak of dragons and elephants?
Begone, wicked bhikṣuṇī!
Do not enter this dwelling again."
When the householder saw that Bhadrika was seated comfortably, he personally provided water for washing and laid out various kinds of food and drink.
When the meal was finished, he again provided water for washing and sat to one side to hear the words of thanksgiving.
Having finished reciting the *dakṣiṇā*, Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat and departed.
He went to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this matter, the Blessed One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and, having fulfilled ten meritorious qualities, the Buddha established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a bhikṣuṇī has praised one group of bhikṣus and disparaged another group of bhikṣus, goes there to eat—such as Devadatta’s son or Ānanda’s sister—it is a pāyattika."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a famine among the people, and it was difficult for them to obtain alms.
Some elders invited one bhikṣu, while others invited two; those who did not receive an invitation went in groups of four or five.
When the householders saw this, they said to one another:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know contentment and lack a sense of shame;
though only one was invited, five or three went themselves."
When the bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One declared:
"If a bhikṣu goes uninvited and by force, he commits an offense."
"Or when one ought to go [on a mission], or is ill, or is attending to monastic affairs, or making robes—in these cases, one may eat.
While the Buddha was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
In the realm of Kosala, there was a householder who built a monastery for the Saṃgha open to all visitors; any guest bhikṣu there could obtain a meal for one day.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra fell ill and traveled from Kosala to Śrāvastī, passing through this monastery where he stayed for three nights and took his meals.
Then Śāriputra set out and arrived at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
He then felt doubt, thinking:
"Have I not overstepped by partaking of the food belonging to the Saṃgha of the universal community?"
He went to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said to him:
"If a bhikṣu who is not ill receives food for one night’s stay and eats beyond that, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya)."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Many bhikṣus were traveling from Kośala to Śrāvastī when an elder invited them along the way to a meal abundant in ghee and curds.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were carrying two or three bowls filled with alms-food at once, which the other bhikṣus did not approve of.
When the laypeople saw this, they said to one another:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, carry two or three bowls stacked together filled with alms-food at once, which the bhikṣus do not approve of."
He went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu is invited into a house and a householder provides excellent food with an abundance of ghee and curd, he must not take more than two or three bowls."
One who commits this offense falls into a transgression.
If two or three bowls are taken out, they should be divided equally and given to monks who have not yet received any.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One, while he was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was an elder in the kingdom of Śrāvastī whose household was in a state of decline due to successive deaths and mourning, with only one young son remaining.
This boy heard that those who provide meals for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus would be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the second heaven:
"I shall go and perform labor, exerting my strength; with the money and goods I earn, I shall provide meals for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus."
He immediately went to the village and spoke to an elder, saying:
"I wish to work as a hired laborer; would this be acceptable?
The elder replied:
"How much do you require? the boy said,
"Give me five hundred taels of gold, and I shall serve you with all my strength."
The householder then reflected:
"At present, there is such a famine that it is difficult even to obtain alms; one cannot even find someone to give a single meal, let alone two pieces of gold such as those."
The elder asked,
"What skills does this young child possess?
The young child replied:
"He is able to sit at stalls of gold, silver, copper, iron, cotton, silk, and thread,
yet he refuses to take payment.
When the ten months had passed, the elder thought to himself:
“While some first demand payment and then perform the labor, this young boy first performed the service for others and now demands his wages.
He was then appointed as the manager of the gold and silver shop.
This young boy has accumulated merit and virtue from past lives; while ordinary people sitting at their stalls obtain a profit of double, this boy obtains eightfold or tenfold.
The elder then thought to himself:
"To have obtained this young boy is my good fortune."
"An ordinary person sitting at a stall gains a profit of double; this child sitting at a stall gains a profit eightfold or tenfold.
Next, he had him sit at stalls for copper, iron, cotton, silk, and thread, and he gained profits in exactly the same way.
Next, he was made to manage the fields and estates; while ordinary people who plow and sow obtain a profit of only one-to-two, this young boy obtained a profit eight or ten times that amount.
When the ten-month period expired, he immediately demanded payment from the elder.
At that time, the elder did not wish to give it, yet he feared that if he did give it, the young boy would leave.
He therefore asked again and again for a third time:
"Do you wish to give it to me?"
The elder asked, "What will you do with this gold once you have obtained it?
The young boy replied:

"I have heard that by offering food to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, one is reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; this is why I work as a laborer, desiring to provide a meal for the Buddha and the bhikṣu-saṃgha.
I pray you will grant me an audience."
The householder then thought to himself,
"It is strange that this young boy performs such diligent service for the Buddha and the community of monks.
He immediately asked the boy:
"Do you wish to feed the Buddha?
He replied, "I wish to feed the Buddha."
"How could I obtain firewood, grass, cauldrons, stoves, utensils, and laborers!
It would be better to provide a meal right here for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; both parties will simultaneously obtain merit."
The child replied, “It may be so. The elder said:
"You yourself go and invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
He immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
The World-Honored One preached the Dharma to him; having finished preaching, he remained silent.
Then the young boy rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I wish to provide a modest offering; I pray that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus will deign to visit me for a brief moment."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

Seeing that the Tathāgata had consented through his silence, the young boy rose, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and departed. That very night, he prepared various kinds of food and drink and arranged excellent seating.
They went and informed the World-Honored One:
"The food and drink are prepared; now is the proper time.
The community of bhikṣus departed, while the World-Honored One remained behind, and the food was sent separately to him.
The monks went to the house of the elder and each sat down in their respective order.
The young boy personally served water and laid out various kinds of food.
It was the eighth day of the month; according to the custom of the land, on this day one makes offerings to deceased ancestors and gives the remaining food to the community of bhikṣus.
When the community of bhikṣus had finished eating, they went to the house of the young boy and ate very little.
The bhikṣus spoke with one voice:
"The server of food should distribute it more sparingly."
When the young child saw that the food and drink had not diminished, he thought to himself:
"If the community of monks does not eat, I shall certainly not be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three."
Weeping, he went to the place where the Tathāgata was and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The bhikṣu-saṃgha has eaten little and not much.
If the bhikṣus do not eat, I shall certainly not be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
The World-Honored One said, "Go and give him a little more food; he will certainly be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, of this there is no doubt.
The young boy then thought to himself again:
"By the words of the Tathāgata’s broad and long tongue, you shall certainly be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Overjoyed and leaping for happiness beyond measure, he immediately prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed to go to where the community of bhikṣus was.
When the bhikṣu-saṃgha had finished eating and the water for washing hands had been distributed, [the merchant] knelt before them and received the benediction.
Once the presiding elder had finished the benediction, he departed.
On that very day, five hundred merchants who had entered the sea returned home.
The Great Teacher entered the city seeking alms and asked a traveler on the road:
"In whose house is food for sale?"
The traveler replied, “A certain elder’s house is providing a meal today for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus; there must certainly be food and drink.
The guide then went to that residence and said to the gatekeeper:
"Go and inform the elder that there is a sea-captain outside who wishes to see him.
The gatekeeper immediately reported this; the elder came out to welcome him, exchanged greetings, and invited him in with a bow to take his seat.
After a short while, he rose and said to the elder, "I have heard that you sell food and drink; I shall send the payment.
At that time, a young boy was sitting to one side.
The elder replied,
"This is not my food," pointing and saying:
"This is the food of this donor," he said.
He then asked the young boy, "If you see any food, give it to me; I shall pay for it."
He replied, "I do not sell my food.
If you have need of it, simply call me and enter to sit; I shall provide for you without requiring payment."
He immediately went to call his companions to enter and sit down.
The young boy personally served water and laid out various kinds of food.
When the merchants had finished eating, the boy returned to his seat upon the couch.
Not far from where the young boy was, there was a great city called Kosambī, so named because it lay on the outskirts of the kingdom of Kosala.
At that time, the Great Guide said to the merchants, "This young boy has provided us with food until we were fully satisfied; let us each together repay his kindness."
The merchants praised this as excellent.
Then the great guide said to the young boy,
"Come along past these *kṛtaka* huts."
He immediately went over and gave it to him.
The leader opened his turban and took out a bright pearl worth a hundred thousand taels of gold, placing it in the *kaṇḍaka* bowl.

The other merchants likewise offered pearls worth ninety thousand taels of gold, or eighty, seventy, sixty, fifty, forty, thirty, twenty, down to those worth ten thousand taels of gold; these overflowed the *kaṇḍaka*, which he then held and gave to the young boy.
The children did not take it, saying, "We do not sell this meager food; we are merely giving it to one another.
The guide spoke again:
"This pearl is worth hundreds of thousands of millions of times more than your food and drink.
I wish to give it to you; I hope you will not refuse me.
The young boy then thought to himself:
"If I take [this], I shall not be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
"Stay here for a short while; let me go to ask the World-Honored One and return.
He then went to the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"Go and receive them.
These are all the flowers of retribution; the fruits will follow later."
The children were filled with joy and leaped for gladness, unable to contain themselves; they prostrated at his feet and then withdrew.
Not long after they had gone, the Buddha established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu has already eaten and goes again to eat, he commits an offense."
Then the elder went to his wife’s quarters and spoke these words:

"This young man’s family lineage and social standing are no inferior to our own; the price of a single jewel is sufficient to purchase my entire estate. You may give this daughter to him in marriage to become his wife."
The wife said,
"Very well," and immediately gave her daughter in marriage to him.
Before long, the elder and his wife both passed away.
When King Prasenajit heard that the elder had died, he asked his ministers,
"Does he have any brothers or children?"
He replied, "No. There is only my daughter's husband at home."
The king issued an edict to summon him, and he immediately went to bring him back.

Upon seeing his countenance from afar, the king was greatly pleased and held him in high esteem; he then conferred upon him one thousand households and appointed him as the governor of a frontier city.
At sunrise he took his seat, and was thus named Sun-rise State-Counsellor (Sūryodaya-rāṣṭrapāla).
While the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
a great number of bhikṣus set out from Śrāvastī for the territory of Kośala.
At that time, a disciple of Baddhālī wished to accompany the bhikṣus to Kośala and came to take leave of Baddhālī, saying:
"The bhikṣus are now departing; I, your disciple, wish to travel with them."
Out of fear of what had occurred previously, Bāṇaṃdita said to him,
"Wait a moment and eat.
The disciple replied:
"First, eat. Baddhananda said, "I know you have already eaten;
my intention is to have you eat again before you leave."
While they were lingering in conversation, the bhikṣus had already departed.
A disciple of Upananda was left behind and could not catch up; he and his companions were plundered by bandits, whereupon he went at once to inform the World-Honored One in detail.
The Blessed One said:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has already eaten, forcibly urges him to eat, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya).
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the elder Śrīgupta served non-Buddhist teachers and was constantly filled with doubt:
"Is the World-Honored One a Buddha or not a Buddha?
Is this Dharma the true Dharma or not?"
"Is this assembly of monks truly an assembly of monks, or not?
I shall prepare a meal and go to invite the Buddha to test them.
He then went to where the World-Honored One was, joined his palms in greeting, and sat to one side.
Then the World-Honored One expounded various subtle and wondrous Dharmas to him; having finished preaching the Dharma, the Buddha remained silent.
The elder Pāṭali-ga addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to invite the Śramaṇa Gautama and the community of bhikṣus."
At that time, the World-Honored One gave his consent by remaining silent.
Ciñcā-māṇavikā rose from her seat, joined her palms in salutation, and withdrew.
She then dug a pit in the doorway, filled it with glowing charcoal that was free of smoke or flame, and covered the top lightly with sand.
He gave rise to this thought:
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses all-knowledge and knows all future events; he will surely know [the truth].
If he does not possess all-knowledge, he himself shall fall into the fire along with his assembly of śramaṇas."
"In the hall, he has set out a rope bed that is not woven, yet he falsely spreads out sitting mats. He further thought:
"If the śramaṇa Gautama possesses all-encompassing wisdom, he should know this for himself."
"If there is no one who possesses all-knowledge, he shall fall upon his bed along with the assembly of śramaṇas,
and be ridiculed by others.
He then prepared food mixed with various poisons and further thought to himself:
"If the śramaṇa Gautama possesses all-knowledge, he will know it himself.
If he does not possess all-knowledge, he shall die from eating this poisoned rice, as will his fellow śramaṇas."
He immediately went to inform the Buddha, saying, "The meal is prepared; now is the very time.
The World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and together with the community of bhikṣus, came to the house of Śūrpāraka.
The World-Honored One looked back and said to Ānanda,
"Go and tell the bhikṣus that none of them shall enter the house of Śūrpāraka before the Tathāgata.
Ānanda immediately went and informed the bhikṣus.
"You must not enter the house of Śūrpāraka before the Tathāgata.

Then, as the Tathāgata stepped upon the fire pit, it spontaneously became a bathing pool, in which grew *utpala*, *kumuda*, *padma*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers; ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks warbled their melodies together in harmony.

Then the World-Honored One stepped upon the flowers and entered the house of Śiṅgi; the flowers were the color of lapis lazuli and the color of deep azure, while the Tathāgata was the color of golden-yellow, their respective hues outshining one another.
At that moment, the deceptive bed made of rope spontaneously transformed into a precious bed.
When the elder saw these two miraculous transformations, his mind was opened and his understanding awakened; he joined his palms toward the Buddha and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"This food is mixed with poison; I pray that you will remain for a short while, so that I may prepare excellent food."
The World-Honored One said, "Simply proceed with this meal; there is no hardship.
Then Piṇḍola Bharadvāja personally served water and laid out various kinds of food.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, “None of these bhikṣus may eat here; you must go to the place of Anavatapta.

Then the World-Honored One taught the meaning of the gift of Dharma, the meaning of the precepts, the meaning of the ten wholesome actions, and the meaning of rebirth in heaven to Śreṇika’s sons and daughters, as well as the matter of falling into evil states through greed and lust, and attaining the Way by leaving the household life.
Then the World-Honored One further preached the Dharma to him regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
At once, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa attained the fruit of the Path, just as pure white woolen cloth is easily dyed with color.
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and paid homage.
"From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; please accept me as an upāsaka who shall refrain from taking life for as long as I live.

Then the World-Honored One and the five hundred arhats filled their bowls with rice, immediately entered samādhi, and flying through the air from the gate of Śreṇika, they proceeded to the palace of Anavatapta.
At that time, Anavatapta also knew that the Tathāgata was coming, so he manifested five hundred lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels.
He further created for the Tathāgata one flower of supreme excellence; the Tathāgata sat upon it, and the five hundred arhats each sat in succession.
After the Tathāgata and his community of five hundred arhat bhikṣus had finished their meal, he extensively expounded the Anavatapta Sūtra.
Then the Tathāgata and the bhikṣu-saṃgha entered into samādhi, vanished from the palace of Anavatapta, and returned to the Jetavana.

At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ heard that the Buddha and five hundred arhats had accepted the invitation of Śailagha to eat at Anavatapta, where they extensively preached the Anavatapta Sūtra, and were now coming to Śrāvastī.
"I shall separately invite the Buddha and five hundred arhats.
He then went to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and stood to one side.
The World-Honored One extensively preached the Dharma for Viśākhā.
Having finished preaching, Viśākhā knelt upright and invited the Buddha and five hundred arhats.
The World-Honored One silently consented.
Viśākhā prostrated herself at his feet and departed.
That very night, she prepared a meal of exquisite food, spread out fine seating mats, reopened the doors and windows, and holding a censer in her hand with palms joined in reverence, she said:
"The meal is ready; now is the proper time."

The bhikṣus went there, some leaping forth from the earth, some entering through the walls, and some descending from the sky; only the Tathāgata remained behind, setting aside his own meal for the Buddha.
When Viśākhā saw that the bhikṣus were seated, she personally served water and laid out various kinds of food.
When the meal was finished, she again served water for washing and knelt before them with palms joined to receive their blessing.
After the Elder had finished reciting the blessing, he departed.
Ānanda came to take the Buddha’s food.
Knowing this, the World-Honored One asked Ānanda:
“How many bhikṣus are eating at the house of Viśākhā?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“The five hundred arhats who previously ate at the palace of Anavatapta are all there eating.”
The World-Honored One said:
"What do you think, Ānanda!
Is there perhaps a single bhikṣu who proclaims and directs others within the community of bhikṣus?"
"No, World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said:
“Have pity on this Viśākhā, who has not obtained even a single merit; why does she not feed a single bhikṣu?
Ānanda, if Mother Viśākhā were to feed a single bhikṣu-saṃgha, she would obtain great merit and reap a great fruit.”
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu does not announce his departure within the assembly and goes to a gathering in private, he commits a *pācittiya* offense.
There are occasions when one ought to go: if traveling on the road, if traveling by boat, if there is a great festival, or if there is a general assembly of śramaṇas; in these cases, one should go."

At that time, when the people of the entire kingdom heard the Buddha’s words—that giving a meal to a single community of bhikṣus brings greater merit than giving a meal to five hundred arhats—the elders and brahmins all attained faith in the Buddha and the pure community of bhikṣus.
The Thirty-Sixth Section Concluded. *Pinaiye* (Vinaya of the Mūlasarvāstivādins), Scroll Seven. *Pinaiye*, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
The Second Pāyattika Dharma.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One had not yet established the precept against eating after midday.
In the late afternoon, the Venerable Kālodāyin dressed himself, took up his bowl, and entered the Bhaddavatikā cemetery at Śrāvastī.
It was a dark, overcast night with thick clouds; lightning flashed and thunder crashed, the light stretching across the sky with brilliant clarity.
There was a pregnant woman who had gone out to fetch water. When the Venerable Kāḷudāyin arrived at her door intending to enter for alms, she saw him in the flash of lightning;
seized with great terror, she cried out in a loud voice, "A piśāca! A piśāca ghost!"
Kāḷodāyin replied, "I am a śramaṇa, not a ghost. The woman replied:
"If he were a true śramaṇa, he would not have killed your father nor harmed your mother, yet he has caused me to fall from my pregnancy.
Thereupon, this woman went and spoke to the bhikṣus of the Twelve Dharmas, and the bhikṣus of the Twelve Dharmas went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Blessed One declared:
"If a bhikṣu eats past midday, he commits an offense.
When the Venerable Pāṭaliputra heard that the Blessed One had established the precept against eating after midday, he spoke these words:
"Of the two meals, there is none better or more excellent than the evening meal, yet the śramaṇa Gautama has forbidden this food for me.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"This attachment to flavors has lasted for a long time; it is not only from today.
Listen as I speak."
In the past, during incalculable kalpas, at the end of a kalpa, heaven and earth were melted and dissolved.
Subsequently, there was a "fatty substance" (meda) upon this earth that was exceedingly sweet and delicious, like soft rock honey.

A certain *apramāṇa* devaputra descended to this earth; tasting the fatty substance with his finger, he found it to be exceedingly sweet and delicious. Delighted and full of joy, he returned to the heavens and spoke to the other devaputras, leading them down to the earth and instructing them to taste this fatty substance.
By the third day, their bodies became heavy and they could no longer fly.
The earth-fat gradually subsided, and the ground produced salt-encrusted soil that was exposed to the sun.
Later, non-glutinous rice appeared naturally, which they then began to eat.
"At that time, this man was attached to flavors; now he is again attached to flavors.
The Buddha was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

The Venerable Pilindavatsa had formerly suffered from eye pain, so various elders and brahmins sent him ghee, oil, honey, black rock sugar, and various kinds of fresh food. His disciples would often set aside these foods overnight and eat them.
At that time, the twelve Dharma-following bhikṣus saw this and went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu who is not ill sets aside food for it to pass the night and then eats it, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya)."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus ate food without first receiving water and without first receiving the food itself.
The twelve-group of bhikṣus saw this and went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu eats food or water that has not been formally offered, and places it into his mouth—except for water and tooth-sticks—he commits an offense of falling."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, wherever the group of six bhikṣus went to the villages, whenever they saw curd, milk, butter, fish, meat, or dried meat, they would immediately beg for them and take them for themselves.
When the various householders saw this, they said to one another,
"Why does this śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, beg for dried fish?
They went and informed the bhikṣus of the twelve dharmas, and the bhikṣus of the twelve dharmas went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and, having fulfilled ten meritorious qualities, the Buddha established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu knows that in a certain village there is fine ghee, milk, curd, fish, meat, or dried meat, and if that bhikṣu, being without illness, goes there to beg for them, it is a pāyattika."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus dwelling in the deep mountains within the realm of Kośala; they had never before seen the Buddha and constantly harbored a longing desire to behold him.
The two deliberated together and set out on their journey to see the World-Honored One.

It was the month following spring, and the heat was extreme; mirages appeared like water as the sun reached its zenith. Encountering a vast wilderness, they found not a drop of water or drink, and their bodies were parched with thirst.
The two men searched for water everywhere until they came upon a small pond;
however, the water was scarce and teeming with insects. One bhikṣu said to the other:
"Drink this insect-infested water and cross this vast marsh so that we may behold the World-Honored One."
A certain bhikṣu replied,
"Having received the precepts of the World-Honored One, how could I ever violate them?
At that time, one man drank and the other did not drink.

Those who had not drunk the water passed away and were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; wearing crowns of a hundred jewels, they came to the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads and faces touching them, and stood to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for them, causing them to realize the Truth.
Those who had been drinking water arrived later; seeing the bhikṣus approaching from afar, the World-Honored One removed his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) to reveal his golden body, saying:
"You foolish men, why do you gaze upon this body composed of the four great elements?"
"It is a place of pure excrement and stench.
Those who see the Dharma see my body.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu knowingly takes and drinks water containing living creatures, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya).
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
A certain householder invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus arrived first and stayed in the kitchen where the food was being prepared.
When the householders saw this, they said to one another, "These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have come here first and are obstructing the preparation of the meal."
When the Bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu arrives first at a house where he has been invited for a meal, and sits or lies down there, or plays with small children, he commits a pācittiya offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
A certain householder invited the community of bhikṣus.
The householder had gone out and was not present; the householder’s wife remained alone behind, preparing the food.
At that time, the Venerable Kālodāyin arrived first at the house of the elder and sat down.
When the elders saw him, they said to one another,
"How can a bhikṣu, a son of the Śākya, sit alone in the same place as a woman?"
The Bhikṣus of the Twelve Dharmas went and informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"If a bhikṣu, having arrived first at a house where food is being offered, sits alone with a woman, he commits an offense of falling (pārājika)."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great community of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, in the village of Veḷukaṇṭaka, there was a brahmin named Ajātaśatru who was very wealthy and possessed abundant riches, money, fields, and estates.
At that time, he arrived at Śrāvastī and stayed in the house of a certain elder. He said to the elder:
"In this place of yours, are there any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are intelligent and wise, leading a multitude of disciples and serving as teachers among the people?"
"If there were such a person, I would wish to go at times to pay him homage and inquire after his well-being, so that my mind might be opened and my understanding clarified.
The elder replied:

"In this very place there is a śramaṇa named Gautama, a son of the Śākyas, who has left the household life to study the Way, having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the three dharma-robes; he has now attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"If you wish to go and see him, now is precisely the right time; you may go and pay your respects.
The brahmin asked, "Where is Gautama at present?"
"I wish to go and pay my respects.
The householder replied, "The World-Honored One is currently at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park; you may go whenever you wish."

Then, on the following day, the brahmin Ajātaśatru departed from Śrāvastī for the Jetavana. At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to countless hundreds of thousands of millions of people.

At that time, the brahmin Ajātaśatru saw from afar that the World-Honored One was peerlessly handsome, with all his faculties complete and his body golden-hued; he immediately approached the Buddha, joined his palms in reverence, and sat to one side.
The World-Honored One expounded various subtle and wondrous dharmas for him; having finished speaking the Dharma, he remained silent.
Then the brahmin addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that the Śramaṇa Gautama and the community of bhikṣus will accept my invitation for the ninety-day summer retreat."
At that time, the World-Honored One, mindful that he could not avoid facing this past karma, silently accepted the Brahmin’s invitation.
Thereupon, the Brahmin rose from his seat, joined his palms in salutation, and withdrew.
From Śrāvastī he went directly to Vaiśālī and prepared various kinds of food and drink for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for the four-month summer retreat.
At the beginning of the retreat, he instructed the gatekeeper:
"I shall remain inside for these four months and do not wish to go out; do not allow anyone to enter."
"If there be any matters of suffering or pleasure, or of good or ill fortune, do not report them to me either.
The gatekeeper immediately received these instructions.
At that time, when the summer retreat had arrived, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Sangha and addressed them, saying:
"You each should gather your robes and bowls and proceed to where Vairaṇyā is.
Then, five hundred bhikṣus followed the World-Honored One, donned their robes, took up their bowls, and went to Vairaṇyā.

At that time, there were no houses or dwellings in Vairambhya; to the north was the great Mount Silas, where the valleys and gorges were vast and the vegetation dense, filled with various flowering trees and many kinds of birds.
At that time, the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus stayed overnight on that mountain.
At that moment, the brahmin Vairaṇabhūti lived there; due to a famine among the people, it was difficult to obtain anything through begging.
That very night, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and addressed the bhikṣus:
“Bhikṣus, you should know that this village of Veḷukaṇḍa is of pure Brahmin descent; its people are suffering from famine, and it is difficult for them to obtain alms.”
"Those bhikṣus who wish to observe the summer retreat here may do so; those who do not may each go where they see fit.

At that time, Śāriputra withdrew to the summit of Mount Aṃśa, where he accepted the invitation of Śakra Devendra and the daughter of the asura Sūyā—the consort of Śakra—and for four months partook of celestial food.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Veḷuvana, where five hundred bhikṣus, minus one, were observing the rains retreat.

Among the brahmin householders who had faith in the Buddha, some would provide only four, five, or six meals before stopping; consequently, the bhikṣus were unable to obtain alms through their begging.
Then the Venerable Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The reason this land is named Jambudvīpa is because it is named after the jambu fruit.
Countless thousands of li to the east of here, one may take a jambu fruit and give it to a bhikṣu to eat. Not far from where the fruit grows, there is a country called Harītakī-āmala."
He went to Uttarakuru and took the naturally grown non-glutinous rice;
he went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and took the celestial ambrosia, giving it to the bhikṣus to eat.
He took the essence of this earth, overturning the ground with his left hand and taking the earth-essence with his right hand, giving it to the bhikṣus to eat.
The World-Honored One said to Maudgalyāyana:
"I know that you possess such supernormal power.
As for these bhikṣus, regarding the karmic conditions from their past lives, where do you wish to place them?"
The World-Honored One did not permit it.
In the realm of Vairañjā, where soft water and grass abounded, a horse trainer was driving his horses through it.
Seeing that the bhikṣus were begging but obtaining nothing, he said to the bhikṣus:
"In this place, grain is expensive and it is difficult to obtain alms.
I have no cooked food, flour, or dry rice; I have only horse fodder, which I must offer to you."
The bhikṣus replied,
"The World-Honored One has not permitted us to eat horse barley.
They went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"Although you know this is horse-barley, you may drink water at any time to satisfy yourself; you may also take fresh grass to eat.
At that time, there were five hundred horses, while the community of bhikṣus was one short of five hundred.
The horse consumed one *dō* of barley daily, and the groom consumed two *dō* of barley daily.
They divided the barley equally between the man and the horse, and offered it as alms to the Buddha and the community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*).
At that time, Ānanda took his own portion as well as the portion belonging to the World-Honored One and entered Vairañjā to seek someone to cook them.
He saw a woman praising the virtues of the Buddha:

"The World-Honored One possesses this morality, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. His body is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty secondary characteristics. A halo seven feet in radius surrounds him; the Buddha’s hands and feet extend beyond this, covering his four limbs by more than seven feet. His body is the color of gold, and one never tires of beholding it."
Having shaved off his hair and beard and donned the *kāṣāya* robes to leave the household life and study the Way, he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

He rescues sentient beings from calamity: those not yet crossed over, he causes to cross over; those not yet liberated, he causes to be liberated; those not yet in *parinirvāṇa*, he causes to enter *parinirvāṇa*, so that they are free from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, affliction, and suffering.
Had he not gone forth to study the Way, he would have become a Wheel-Turning King, preceded by the seven treasures:
the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder treasure, and the military commander treasure.
He shall have a thousand sons, heroic, powerful, and valiant.
He shall rule over the four continents without the use of weapons or staffs;
both I and you all shall become his subjects.
Having accepted the invitation, he came here to Vairañjā for the summer retreat. "Sister!
Could you grind this barley into flour for me? he asked.
The woman replied: "My home, Ānanda,
has many tasks and duties."
"If I do not even provide for myself, how much less could I provide for others?
Not far from there, a woman heard this praise of the Buddha’s merit; finding it most extraordinary and marvelous, she thought to herself:
"Is there truly such a person in the world?"
He immediately called Ānanda:
"Bring this barley; I shall grind it into flour for you.
From this day forward, whenever the Buddha, Ānanda, or other fellow practitioners of the holy life bring barley, I shall grind it into flour for them."
Then the woman ground the wheat and brought it to Ānanda.
Ānanda took the flour to the Buddha’s dwelling, provided water for washing, and presented the flour to the Buddha.
The Buddha then ate it.
When Ānanda saw the Buddha eating groats, he wept with sorrow and shed tears.
He further thought to himself:
"The World-Honored Buddha was once a prince; he always ate fine food and never ate coarse food."
"How can one derive strength from eating such barley flour today? At that time,
the World-Honored One, knowing what was in Ānanda’s mind, spoke to him, saying:
“Can you eat this flour? He replied, “I can eat it.”
The World-Honored One then gave him a morsel, causing him to partake of the flavor of celestial ambrosia.
Ānanda again had this thought:
"The World-Honored One must surely possess vigor and strength after eating this."
When the World-Honored One had finished eating, washed his bowl, and set out the water for rinsing, [the householder] addressed the Buddha:
"Just now, I requested a woman to prepare some parched grain flour, but she was unwilling to do so.
There was another woman who prepared it herself without being asked."
"I wish to hear its meaning.
The World-Honored One replied:
"As for that which was not done but ought to have been done, she would have become the chief consort of a Wheel-Turning Sage King."
Those who perform deeds without being prompted shall obtain great merit;
though they do not further cultivate other blessings, they plant the root of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Before his reply was finished, there was no one who heard that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus were eating horse barley.

The celestial Māra Pāpīyān transformed himself into a community of bhikṣus, carrying bags filled with dried cakes and rock honey, and holding nine hundred flat cakes in his hands as he walked through the streets and alleys.
The householders asked the bhikṣus,
"From where have you come?
The bhikṣus replied:
“I have come from Vairambhya.
“Does the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus lack for nothing?
The transformed bhikṣu replied:
"The food and drink were so abundant that they could not all be consumed; we now send the remainder to Śrāvastī.
Having gone there and settled their accounts, at that time the sixteen great kingdoms all heard that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus were at Veḷuvana, eating horse-barley for three months.

Various wealthy householders and brahmins, who had accumulated a hundred million in wealth, as well as sea-faring merchants, set out with chariots, horses, and camels laden with all kinds of offerings to welcome the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus.
With seven days remaining until the New Year, the Buddha, knowing this, asked Ānanda:
"How many days remain until the New Year?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"There are seven days remaining," the Buddha said to Ānanda,
"take two bhikṣus into the town of Vaiśālī and say to the brahmin Ajātaśatru:..."
"The Buddha has already accepted your invitation for ninety days; now that it has concluded, he wishes to go throughout the human world to beg for alms.
At that time, the bhikṣu said to the Buddha:
"Ajātaśatru did not offer the Buddha even a single meal; for what reason does he now take his leave?"
The World-Honored One said, "Although no meal has been prepared, you are nonetheless the host; according to the Dharma, you should be treated separately.
Then, the Venerable Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, led the two bhikṣus into Veḷukaṇṭaka and stood at the gate of Ajātaśatru, saying to the gatekeeper:
"Go and inform him: 'Ānanda is outside and wishes to see you.
At that time, Ajātaśatru was in the central courtyard, having washed his head and wearing a white cotton garment, sitting cross-legged upon a rope bed.
The gatekeeper immediately informed him, and he replied,
"Let him enter.
Ānanda then entered and sat down slowly.
After remaining silent for a moment, the brahmin asked,
"For what purpose have you come? Ānanda replied:
The World-Honored One said:
"Brahmin! I have already accepted your invitation for ninety days."
"Now I wish to enter among the people to go on alms-round everywhere.
The Brahmin asked: "How is this, Ānanda?"
“Does Gautama observe the summer retreat here? Ānanda replied,
“Did you previously invite him to the summer retreat and now forget?”
The brahmin asked, "How did you obtain food during these ninety days? Ānanda replied:
"Great distress and great misfortune! The World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus have been eating horse barley for three months.
At that time, the brahmin recalled his invitation to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to prepare for the summer retreat; he then commanded the gatekeeper not to let anyone enter.
The brahmin Ajātaśatru thought again: "People from near and far in all four directions will surely hear that I have committed this evil deed—
that I invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus but provided them with no offerings."
He spoke again to Ānanda:
"Could you ask the śramaṇa Gautama if he might accept my repentance? Ānanda replied:
"You must not remain here.
At that time, Ajātaśatru was filled with grief and distress, and he threw himself upon the ground.
Then his kinsmen sprinkled him with water and raised him up; the kinsmen spoke to Ajātaśatru, saying:
"Do not grieve. We shall go to the presence of the śramaṇa Gautama and confess our transgressions to him on your behalf.
If he does not remain [in his seat], we will have these various foods and drinks carried there by bearers and follow behind."
"If there is a lack of provisions at the residence, you should provide for them.
Then Ānanda, together with the brahmin and his kinsmen, went to where the World-Honored One was and confessed their transgressions.
The World-Honored One saw him approaching from afar and thought:
"If I do not remain here, boiling blood shall gush from my facial orifices.

Out of great compassion, he remained for another seven days. The food and drink prepared for the previous four-month summer retreat were all carried out and brought back; they were abundant and overflowing.
At that time, when the people of Vṛji heard that the Buddha would arrive in sixty days, they went everywhere to beg for alms and each prepared offerings to await the Tathāgata.
Then the World-Honored One, having completed his collection of patched robes at Veḷukaṇṭa, finished his robe in one day; he put on the robe, took up his bowl, and set out for the kingdom of Vṛji.
Ajātaśatru also carried food and drink following behind the Tathāgata, providing whatever was lacking.
Knowing where the Tathāgata intended to stay for the night, he would promptly prepare offerings ahead of time, saying each time:
"I invite the Buddha today; I invite the Buddha tomorrow."
At that time, when the people of Vatsa heard that Ajātaśatru was carrying food and drink following after the Tathāgata, they thought, "This will surely prevent us from offering a meal to the Buddha.
They immediately assembled and established a restriction among themselves:
"Whoever prepares food for the Buddha shall prepare only light refreshments and honey syrup; do not allow the Brahmins to prepare a formal meal."
"Whoever sees Ajita, they shall revile him, saying:
'Evil Brahmin! You have provided the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus with horse-gram for ninety days!'"
"Are you now carrying food again to hinder others?
At that time, the brahmin stood dejectedly to one side; whenever he saw that the people's provisions were insufficient, he would immediately provide enough for them.

Seeing only that there was no bean gruel, he immediately ground sesame seeds, linseed, beans, *āmalaka*, *vibhītaka*, long pepper, and ginger to make a gruel, which he then offered to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"Distribute it to the community of bhikṣus.
The community of bhikṣus did not accept it.
“The Blessed One has not permitted us to eat this gruel.
Then the brahmin came and said to the Blessed One,
“The bhikṣus will not accept this gruel.”
The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, whether you are ill or not, you shall always consume this gruel.
There are five matters [to be observed]:..."

"It is beneficial for the body; it removes hunger and thirst, prevents diseases of wind and cold, keeps the intestines and stomach functioning smoothly, and digests raw food. Ajita then thought again:
"I have prepared various kinds of food and drink during the four months of summer and brought them here, yet once more I am unable to provide a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus."

"I shall now distribute the food upon the ground according to the ritual for sacrificing to the gods, so that the bhikṣus may pass over it with their feet; thus it will be as if they have already eaten.
The World-Honored One told him:
"This is not something to be trodden upon by the feet; this is a substance to be consumed by the mouth."
The World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the brahmin; having finished teaching the Dharma, the brahmin immediately departed.
Then, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and returned to Śrāvastī.
There was a non-Buddhist brahmin of stout build following behind the World-Honored One.
A certain brahmin, traveling along the road, asked this brahmin:
"Can food and drink be obtained here?"
He replied, “It can be obtained.
He asked again:
"From whom did you obtain it? He replied,
"I obtained it from this bald householder."
The brāhmaṇa said: "Begone, begone! You speak evil words.
That you have become so stout and robust is entirely due to the śramaṇa Gautama, yet you instead revile him."
"If the śramaṇa Gautama hears of this, he will surely establish a precept for the śramaṇas so that they no longer provide food and drink to the non-Buddhists.
The bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:

"These heterodox teachers and followers of other paths have long practiced perversity; if they are beaten, poisoned, or caught in legal entanglements, they will falsely claim that the Śramaṇa Gautama did it."
At that time, the World-Honored One had not yet established the precepts for the śramaṇas.
He arrived first at Śrāvastī, where an elder of Śrāvastī prepared hundred-petaled butter cakes and crisp wafers for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, that they never rise from their seats until their food and drink are sufficient; they must eat their fill.
Should a donor’s offering be insufficient, it shall be made complete through the power of the Buddha.
Two Brahmin women came and said to the Venerable Ānanda,
"Please give us some alms of cake.
At that time, he gave two portions of cake to one woman and one portion of cake to the other.
When one person had won a round, he asked another person:
"How many rounds have you won?
The other replied:
“I have won two rounds.
He asked in return:
“How many rounds have you won?”
He replied,
"I have won one round.
Since you have long been victorious by one round, you should share it with me."
He replied: "Each shall receive their own share.
I will not give you a share."
One person said,
"Ānanda must surely be your husband!
The two of them began to pull each other's hair and tear one another's clothes, shouting loudly.
The World-Honored One, knowing [the situation], asked Ānanda:
"Why were these people fighting?
Ānanda reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu gives cakes with his own hand to a brāhmaṇa or a brāhmaṇī wife, he commits an offense.
There are five kinds of food: [listing follows]"
First, food consisting of roots.
Regarding food consisting of roots: lotus root, radish, and the small, sweet *kṣipada* root.
Second, food consisting of stalks.
Regarding stalk-foods (*kāṇḍa-bhakṣa*): these are the stalks of bamboo, *tu-si*, *ji-zu*, and various other edible vegetables.
Third are leaf-foods (*patra-bhakṣa*):
these are all the leaves that are eaten.
The fourth is flower-food:
*pāṭala*, *bimba*, *li*, *puṣpa*, *bhallātaka*, and *babbūla*.
The fifth is fruit-food.
The fruits they consume are grapes, sweet oranges, and so forth.
Furthermore, there are five types of grain:
millet, rice, barley, peas, and non-glutinous rice.
If, while eating this food, five brahmins should come to beg, you should say, "This is not my food.
If there should be one who asks for water, you should say, "This is not my water."
"Regarding those who seek fruit, one should say, 'This is not my fruit.
One must not give anything at all, except for one's parents or the sick.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One, while he was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
King Prasenajit and Ajātaśatru were constantly at war with one another, and at that time they raised armies to attack each other.
The group of six bhikṣus said to one another:
"Let us go together to see the troops and horses."
He immediately went to inspect the troops and horses.
When the elders saw him, they said to one another, "This śramaṇa,
a son of the Śākyas who has left the household life to practice the Way, is now inspecting the military forces."
He went and reported this matter to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told him:
"If a bhikṣu goes to see an army when it is about to set out, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya)."
*Pinaiye*, Scroll 8 [and] Scroll 9.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
