The minister of King Prasenajit, Iṣṭadatta Pūraṇa Kautumbī—a stream-enterer—went with several bhikṣus to inspect the cavalry.
Some bhikṣus also had relatives within the army, who asked them to stay for three days.
When the elders saw this, they said to one another, "These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have left the household life to pursue the Way; they will surely transmit messages back and forth."
When the Bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu is within an army, he must not stay for more than two nights; if he stays longer, he commits an offense."
When King Pasenadi of Kosala was practicing military exercises and reviewing his troops, the bhikṣus went to watch.
When the householders saw them, they said to one another,
“These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have come to watch something that is not their proper practice.”
When the bhikṣus who observed the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
“If a bhikṣu attends a military drill or reviews an army’s ceremonial procession, banners, or standards, he commits an offense of defeat.”
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were constantly quarreling with the group of seventeen bhikṣus.
The group of six bhikṣus, relying on their own noble lineage, struck the group of seventeen bhikṣus.
When the lay elders saw this, they said to one another,
"How can bhikṣus strike one another?"
When the twelve-group bhikṣus heard this, they went and reported it in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger toward another bhikṣu, strikes him, he commits a pāyattika offense."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus became angry; they raised their staves to threaten one another and struck each other with their hands.
When the bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas saw this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu raises a staff to intimidate another, or strikes him with his hand, he commits a pācittiya offense.
While the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Nanda, a disciple of Upananda, said to another disciple of Upananda, "I wish to go somewhere; you may follow me there.
They then went along together.
On the road, he encountered a woman, and Nanda immediately took her to a screened-off place to engage in unchaste conduct.
A disciple of Upananda saw this and returned to inform the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
On account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and, having established the ten merits, the Buddha formulated a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu sees one who has committed an offense and conceals it for even one night, it is a pāyattika."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda thought to himself:
"This disciple has insulted my younger brother; now I shall take my revenge upon him."
He then said to his disciple:
"I wish to go somewhere; put on your robes, take up your bowl, and follow me. I shall also inform the donors so that they may provide you with excellent offerings."
They immediately followed him.
He led them from house to house, visiting one dwelling after another.
When he saw that midday was approaching and the *gandi* was about to be struck, he said to his disciples as the time passed:
“Return to Śrāvastī; I do not wish to travel with you.
He immediately returned toward the Jeta Grove, by which time the sun had already passed midday and the bhikṣus had finished their meal.
He immediately went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told him:
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu: [as follows]"
"I wish to go somewhere; come with me there, and I shall tell the donor that they should provide you with excellent offerings.
After taking him along, he then says: "Go away."
“Monk! I do not delight in traveling with you; I prefer to travel alone.
One who makes such a deceptive statement falls [into an offense].

It was not the elder Nanda, but one who shared the same name. While the World-Honored Buddha was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he wished to proceed from Śrāvastī toward the kingdom of Kośala. Along the way, there were no villages, so he stayed overnight on a mountain.
There was an elder bhikṣu who, carrying a large piece of rotten wood, came intending to kindle a fire.
A black viper emerged from within the wood; the bhikṣu, seized with fear, let out a cry.
When the other bhikṣus heard this, they thought he had been robbed by bandits and immediately went forward to ask,
"Why did you cry out in alarm?
The bhikṣu answered them according to the facts.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"If a bhikṣu who is not ill kindles a fire on open ground using gathered wood, grass, cow dung, husks, or leaves."
"If one lights it oneself or causes another to light it, one falls [into an offense].
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra came to take leave of the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, wishing to go on a general alms-round for sixty days.

At that time, the bhikṣu Kālatanti, having heard that Śāriputra intended to go on a sixty-day almsround throughout the region, immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Kāraṇḍavī addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Venerable Śāriputra is negligent; without taking leave of the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus, he wishes to travel throughout the human realm to beg for alms."
Then the World-Honored One commanded a certain bhikṣu:
"Go to where Śāriputra is and say, 'The World-Honored One calls for you.
At that time, the bhikṣu rose from his seat, prostrated himself at [the Buddha's] feet, and departed, going to where Śāriputra was.
"The World-Honored One has sent me to summon Śāriputra.
Śāriputra and that bhikṣu then went to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side.
The World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"Not long after you had departed, this bhikṣu came and said:
'Śāriputra has not taken leave of the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, yet he wishes to travel throughout the human realm to practice alms-gathering.'"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In all places where he has traveled, he has never lost the essential meaning, nor has there ever been a case where he departed from the assembly without taking leave.
It is only that this bhikṣu’s report of the matter was mistaken.”
It is like a fine bull whose two horns have been cut off; when led through the marketplace, it no longer gored or butted people.
I am likewise: never indolent or arrogant, I do not decline to go among the multitude.
For example, this earth contains all manner of filth and impurities, yet the ground where one voids excrement and urine does not say:
"I shall carry this here" or "I shall place that there.
I am likewise no different from the earth; how could I ever be indolent or arrogant, refusing to go among the multitude?
Then the bhikṣu Kāla-danti rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of Śāriputra, and apologized: “Śāriputra!
I repent; I pray that you will forgive me.”
I am as ignorant as a fool; how could I now slander Śāriputra’s pure conduct?
I myself have previously committed this falsehood; I pray that Śāriputra will accept my confession of transgression.
Then the World-Honored One said to Śāriputra:
"Accept his confession immediately; do not allow this bhikṣu’s head to shatter into seven pieces upon this very seat."
Then Śāriputra, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, immediately accepted his confession of transgression.
The World-Honored One declared:
"If a bhikṣu, having formally requested leave from the community of bhikṣus according to the constant rule of the Saṃgha, is granted permission by the Saṃgha to depart."
"Later, if a bhikṣu gives testimony that does not accord with the Dharma to the Saṃgha of bhikṣus—
first agreeing and later contradicting— he falls into an offense.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One, while traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the novice Rāhula, a disciple of Śāriputra, was not permitted to stay overnight in his own room. He went to various other rooms, but was not permitted to stay in any of them.
There was only one guest monk’s room that was unoccupied, and Rāhula stayed there.
Not long after he had lain down, another visiting bhikṣu arrived and said, "You are a śrāmaṇera;
get out of the way of me, a great śramaṇa!
He then dragged him outside by force.
At that time, Rāhula shed tears and went to the Tathāgata’s latrine.
Entering the latrine building, he took one of the Tathāgata’s sandals and rested his head upon it as if sleeping.

A venomous snake, which habitually dwelt in this latrine, had previously gone out in search of food; then, during the middle watch of the night, amidst a violent wind and rain, the snake came running toward the latrine.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas to observe sentient beings during the three periods of the night to see who should be delivered.

Seeing that Rāhula was about to be harmed by a venomous snake at that very moment, the World-Honored One immediately went to the latrine by means of his power of samādhi. Then the Tathāgata snapped his fingers three times, and Rāhula immediately awoke.
The World-Honored One asked, "Who are you?
The śrāmaṇera replied:
"It is Rāhula," [he replied].
The World-Honored One asked,
"Why are you sleeping here?"
Rāhula reported this in full to the World-Honored One.
Then the Tathāgata took Rāhula by the head with his left elbow and led him to a stone cave.
At dawn, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This śrāmaṇera has neither father nor mother; he relies solely upon his upādhyāya and ācārya for care at all times.
If they do not look after him, who else will?
From this day forward, it is permitted for a śrāmaṇera to stay with a mahābhikṣu for two nights; should he exceed this limit, he commits an offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣu Caṇḍa conceived this evil thought while observing the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.
"I fully know that this evil dharma which he has committed is not sufficient to constitute an offense.
At that time, many bhikṣus heard that the bhikṣu Channa had conceived such an evil thought:
"Observing the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma, I fully understand that those who commit evil deeds do not deserve to be considered guilty.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the bhikṣu Cchanna was and said to him:
"Is it true that you have spoken these words?"
"Does it not say: 'I fully understand the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata; for one who commits evil deeds, there is no offense'?
The bhikṣu Channa replied:
"This is indeed true.
I understand all that the World-Honored One has taught regarding the Dharma; those who commit evil deeds do not deserve to be considered guilty. The bhikṣus said:
"Stop, stop, Candra! Do not speak such words, nor slander the Tathāgata."
"One who slanders the Tathāgata shall not obtain good fortune in the present life.
The World-Honored One has, through countless skillful means, taught that committing sinful offenses leads to evil retribution.
You, Caṇḍa, must now abandon this perverted view."
The bhikṣus admonished him but he was unwilling to comply; not knowing what to do, they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu gives rise to such an evil thought:..."
"I observe that when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, I understand it all; those who commit evil deeds do not deserve to be considered guilty.
When a virtuous bhikṣu admonishes him thus a second and a third time, if he follows the admonition, it is well; if he does not follow the admonition, he falls into transgression.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the bhikṣu Cchanna persisted in his evil views; he did not associate with the community of bhikṣus, but instead kept company with the group of six bhikṣus and accepted their instructions.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu associates with one who has cultivated wrong views and has already been expelled—whether by sitting or lying down with him, or by conversing with him—he commits a pāyattika offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana had two śrāmaṇeras who did not maintain the precepts and practiced unwholesome dharmas; outside of the Jetavana, each of them committed evil deeds.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they said to the śrāmaṇera:

"The World-Honored One has, through countless skillful means, taught that sexual desire is impure; one turns toward sexual desire, dwells on sexual desire, and the mind’s passion for sexual desire is a foul discharge."
"How can you practice such impurity?
The śrāmaṇeras replied,
"We have also heard the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma, wherein he said that those who practice sexual desire commit no offense."
The bhikṣus spoke to him again:
"You are a śrāmaṇera; do not speak such words, saying:
'The World-Honored One has taught that there is no offense in committing sexual misconduct.'"
"Do not slander the Tathāgata; those who slander the Tathāgata shall not obtain good fortune even in their present life.
You, śrāmaṇera, must now abandon this evil view.
At that time, the śrāmaṇera did not follow the bhikṣu’s admonition.
The bhikṣus, not knowing what to do, went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a śrāmaṇera speaks these words:..."
"The Tathāgata taught that there is no offense in committing sexual misconduct.
At that time, a bhikṣu came and admonished him, saying:
"You śrāmaṇera, do not speak such words!"
"The World-Honored One has taught that there is no offense in committing sexual misconduct.
Do not slander the Tathāgata; he who slanders the Tathāgata will experience misfortune in this very life.
"If the śrāmaṇera follows this advice, it is well; if he does not follow it, the bhikṣu shall speak to the śrāmaṇera as follows:"
"From this day forward, you shall not pay homage to the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, nor shall you follow behind the bhikṣus.
Just as other śrāmaṇeras are permitted to stay with the great bhikṣus for two nights, you now have no such privilege."
"You must leave at once; you may no longer remain here.
If a bhikṣu, knowing that this śrāmaṇera has been expelled, employs him as a servant or stays with him for even one night, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya).
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ, adorned with a hundred kinds of golden necklaces, went to where the World-Honored One was.
On the way, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ thought to herself:
"It is not my proper etiquette to go to see the World-Honored One while wearing ornaments.
She immediately removed her jewelry, wrapped it in fine white cotton cloth, and entrusted it to a maidservant.
Then Mṛgāramātṛ approached, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Thereupon the World-Honored One expounded various subtle and wondrous dharmas to her.
Having finished preaching the Dharma, she rose from her seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
At that time, this maidservant forgot her golden necklace.
When Ānanda saw it, he immediately picked it up.
Thereupon, she became filled with suspicion:
"I have not committed a *pācittiya* offense?
He then addressed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told him:
"If a bhikṣu takes gold, jewels, or necklaces in his own hand, or instructs another to take them, he commits an offense of falling (pārājika).
This excludes cases where gold or jewels are found within the precincts of the saṃghārāma.
In such a case, one should ensure that no one takes them and leave them for ninety days."
If after ninety days no one comes to claim it, let it remain for three years.
If after three years no one comes to claim it, it shall be used for the affairs of the Saṃgha.
If after three years a rightful owner comes to reclaim it, the property of the Saṃgha shall be used to compensate them.
"This is what should be taken.
While the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
the group of six bhikṣus wore new robes without dyeing them.
When the various householders saw this, they said to one another:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have left the household life to study the Way, yet they wear clothes that are not dyed; how are they any different from worldly people?"
When the bhikṣus who followed the twelve dharmas heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu obtains new robes, he must dye them three colors: blue, black, or madder."
"If a bhikṣu dyes [his robes] with three colors—blue, black, or madder—and does not apply them [to the cloth], he commits an offense of falling.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One, while traveling in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
King Prasenajit had constructed a separate bathhouse and asked the various Ajitas,
"Should we bathe today? The bhikṣus replied:
"It is time for my bath today," the king said to the bhikṣu,
"bathe in my bathhouse."
The bhikṣus would bathe either before the morning meal, after the meal, or at night.
King Prasenajit came one night wishing to bathe; however, as the bhikṣus were already washing, the king was unable to bathe.
When night had ended and dawn was breaking, he was finally able to bathe.
The king then thought to himself:
"It would not be fitting for me to return to the city without having seen the Tathāgata."
At that time, King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
Knowing [the situation], the Buddha asked the king:
"The night has not yet dawned; from where have you come?"
The king reported all this in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Buddha taught various dharmas to the king and then remained silent.
Having heard the teaching of the Dharma, the king rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet with his head and face, and departed.
Not long after the King had departed, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and, having fulfilled the ten merits, established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu bathes once every half-month, and exceeds this limit, it is a pāyattika offense."
This [period] is the month following the end of spring and the month preceding the middle of the year; during these times, one may take a bath.
Except for when there is hot wind or rain, or when the Sangha is performing work, or when traveling on a road, one may always bathe.
[The sixty [sections] are concluded. The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the stone cave by the Monkey River in Vaiśālī.
At that time, various youths of Vaiśālī were practicing archery inside the city gate, with the butt of one arrow meeting the tip of the next.

At that time, the Venerable Kālodāyin, having dressed in the early morning and taken up his bowl, entered Vaiśālī for alms. Seeing from afar several boys shooting arrows in rapid succession, one after another, he went to the place where they were shooting and said to the boys:
"Though your collective shooting is indeed remarkable, it is not as skillful as mine."
The youths immediately handed him the bow and arrows. Kāḷodāyin asked,
"What object do you wish for me to shoot?"
At that time, a hawk was flying above, and the boys said, "Shoot that bird from below.
Kāḷodāyin immediately shot four forked arrows at the hawk; the forked arrows pinned the hawk so that it remained suspended in the air, unable to fly away.
The youth spoke again:
"If you do not kill this bird, how can you be considered skilled in craftsmanship? Kāḷodāyin asked:
"Where do you wish to shoot? The youth replied, "The right eye."
He immediately shot at the right eye, and the bird fell to the ground dead.
The youths went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu takes the life of a living being, he falls [into an offense].
Regarding the Buddha, King Bimbisāra, and Kālodāyin—these three were peerless in archery. At that time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The group of six bhikṣus were constantly at variance with the group of seventeen bhikṣus; the two groups were traveling together on the road.
The group of six bhikṣus said to the group of seventeen bhikṣus:
"You went ahead and trampled and killed insects; you have committed a pāyattika offense."
"You should come at once and confess your transgression to me.
Thereupon, these seventeen groups of bhikṣus immediately confessed their transgressions.
When the bhikṣus who uphold the twelve dharmas heard of this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Blessed One said:
"If a bhikṣu has not killed an insect, yet testifies that he has killed an insect, he commits a pācittiya offense.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
While the bhikṣus were sitting in meditation in a quiet room, it was extremely hot, and each of them felt sleepy.
To rouse the meditating bhikṣus, they poked one another with their fingers; when a bhikṣu woke up and yawned, they again poked him in the mouth with their fingers.
The bhikṣus who were versed in the twelve dharmas went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:

"If a bhikṣu, while in meditative concentration, startles another by poking them with his finger, and the other yawns; if he then pokes the person's mouth with his finger, he commits a pācittiya offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus were sitting in meditation in their quiet chambers; as the weather was extremely hot, they each felt drowsy.
The bhikṣus sprinkled water on one another to startle the bhikṣu who was in meditation.
The bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu sprinkles water upon another to startle one who is in meditative concentration, he commits an offense of falling.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Anuruddha was observing the rains retreat in the realm of Kosala. Having completed the retreat, he donned his robes, took up his bowl, and set out for Śrāvastī.
On the way, he passed through a village and asked the people there, "May I stay the night here?"
The people pointed out the house of a certain widow,
saying, "You may stay here.
Venerable Anuruddha then went to that house and spoke to her.
“Elder sister! Can you stay here? Ānanda’s face was pure and white;
when the woman saw him, lustful thoughts arose within her, and she replied:
"Welcome," he said.
He immediately swept the room clean, spread out a bed for him to sit upon inside, and prepared various kinds of food and drink.
As the sun was already setting, he brought water for him to wash his hands and then brought the food.
"Śramaṇa, you may eat.
Anuruddha replied, "I now eat but one meal; I do not take a meal toward evening."
The woman then thought to herself:
"Although he does not eat now, he will surely lie with me at night.
She prepared a more comfortable bed for him to sleep upon.
After the woman had finished eating, she lit an oil lamp.
Then, standing at the head of the bed, she pulled at Aniruddha’s robes, desiring to engage in unchaste conduct.
Anuruddha replied:
“The holy life is pure; it cannot be according to your wishes.

The World-Honored One has taught through countless skillful means that sexual desire is impure: turning toward sexual desire, dwelling on sexual desire, and the mind’s passion for sexual desire becoming intense.”
The woman disturbed Anuruddha throughout the entire night.
She then thought to herself:
"This must surely be a pure śramaṇa; he is not an impure person."
Her mind was immediately opened and her understanding clarified as she turned toward Anuruddha.
Anuruddha expounded various profound teachings for her; at that very moment, the woman destroyed two billion evils, attained the stage of Srotāpanna, and realized the fruit of seeing the Truths.
She immediately rose from her seat, prostrated herself with her head at the feet of Aniruddha, and said:
"From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. Please accept me as an upāsikā; for the rest of my life, I shall refrain from taking life."
"May the Venerable Aniruddha accept my invitation to eat here.
Aniruddha accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
The woman entered her home to prepare various kinds of food; she served pure water and personally presented the food with her own hands.
Having finished eating, he offered water for rinsing the mouth, knelt before Āniruddha, and said to him:
"For the rest of my life, please accept from me robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicine for illness and infirmity."
Anuruddha accepted the invitation in silence.

Having preached the Dharma for them, he rose from his seat and departed, traveling to Śrāvastī to the place where the World-Honored One was. There, he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
The Buddha asked Ānanda:
"During the summer retreat, have you lacked for nothing?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
“There was nothing lacking.
Then Āniruddha reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told him:
"Anuruddha! It is as if four venomous snakes were dwelling in the same room; it would be better to dwell with those evil serpents than to sit on the same bed with a woman."
It is like a wise man whom a king commands, saying:
"Guard these four snakes; do not fail them in their food and drink at the proper times.
If even one snake becomes angry, it will kill you without a doubt."
He said to this man,
"Do as you see fit. Thereupon,
the man departed, only to encounter five bandits with drawn swords who intended to kill him.
"What do you think, Anuruddha!
This man, having escaped the fear of the four snakes, encountered five bandits;
having barely managed to avoid them, he encountered six enemies who constantly watch for an opportunity, and now they have met him face-to-face—they will kill him without a doubt."

Having escaped once more, he approached an empty house intending to enter it for concealment; seeing that the house was vacant and devoid of anything, he felt along its four walls and found that all the jars and vessels were empty.
A certain person came and said to him, "A thief is coming now; you should flee at once.
Just as he stepped out the door, he encountered the thief.

Having escaped that [peril], he encountered ahead a mountain torrent flowing with great rapidity; countless people had fallen into the water and perished. At his current location, there were also wolves and tigers wishing to harm him.
Desiring to cross the river but finding no boat, he thought to himself: "By what means can I cross this water?"

He immediately gathered grass and wood to bind them into a raft, waded through the water with his hands and feet, and reached the other shore. Thus he escaped the four snakes, the five thieves, the six enemies, and the robbers in the empty house; he crossed over the tigers and wolves of the mountain waters, and the Brahmin was saved.
The Buddha told Aniruddha:
"As for the reason I have employed this analogy, you should understand its meaning:
that which the snake inhabits is used as a metaphor for this body."
The body is plump, white, and handsome; it grows by means of its parents, yet this too is impermanent and subject to decay.

As for the "four snakes," these are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*): the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element. When each of these increases, death will undoubtedly follow.
The five thieves are a metaphor for the five aggregates (*skandhas*): form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The six enemies are a metaphor for the six sense bases (*āyatanas*).
The empty village is a metaphor for the six faculties (*indriyas*), namely the spheres of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
One contemplates the eye as empty of the eye; one contemplates the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind as empty of the mind.
"Leaving the gate and seeing a thief" refers to the six external sense objects (*bāhyaviṣaya*).

"Mountains and waters" refers to the four underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): the tendency toward desire in the realm of desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*), the tendency toward aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), the tendency toward ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*), and the tendency toward views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*).
The river waters are the three cravings: craving for sense-pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless.
The tigers and wolves dwelling therein refer to the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.
"Crossing to the other shore" refers to *nirvāṇa*.
"The raft" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.
"Using hands and feet to propel through the water" refers to valorous diligence.
“The Brahmin who attains life is one who is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The Buddha told Anuruddha:
“I and you all have studied the Path with diligent effort; it is precisely as you have said.”
"For this reason, forest-dwellers should always remain under trees or in open spaces, practicing meditation without slackening.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu stays overnight in the same room as a woman, he commits an offense of defeat (pārājika)."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Mount Śvetaśaila. At midnight, the Buddha rose and walked back and forth in front of his chamber.
At that time, the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra, son of Kṛkī, having been seized and bound, came to frighten the World-Honored One, saying:
"I am a great deity of heaven and earth; you must avoid me and depart!"
The World-Honored One said:
"When eighteen billion Māras came to terrify me, they could not move even a single hair; how then could I fear being captured and brought here from afar to terrify me?"
At dawn the next day, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu causes himself to be terrified, or causes another to be terrified, he commits an offense of falling (pārājika).
While the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took the robes and bowls of the group of seventeen bhikṣus and hid them. When the gong was struck and the community of bhikṣus entered to take their seats, the group of seventeen bhikṣus searched for their robes and bowls but did not know where they were.
When the assembly of bhikṣus had concluded, they returned his robes and bowl.
The seventeen groups of bhikṣus said to him, "You are a śramaṇa; why did you steal another's robes and bowl?"
The group of six bhikṣus replied, “We were merely playing; we did not steal.
When the other bhikṣus heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:

"If a bhikṣu, for the sake of sport, hides his robe, bowl, door-key, needle-case, leather sandals, or various other items—whether hiding them himself or instructing another to hide them—he commits an offense of falling."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda sold a robe to a bhikṣuṇī on credit and later borrowed it back from her to wear.
Once his robe was worn out, he further demanded its price from the other.
When the bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas heard of this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu sells a robe on credit to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, and they subsequently borrow it back to wear."
"If one has already put on a robe that is damaged and then demands its price back, one falls [into an offense].
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila came from the kingdom of Kośala to Śrāvastī; on the way, he stayed overnight in another village.
At that time, a husband and wife in a village were quarreling, and the wife fled.
In the early morning, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila put on his robes, took up his bowl, and departed from this village for Śrāvastī;
on the road, he encountered this woman and asked, "Sramaṇa, where do you wish to go?"
He replied, "I am going to Śrāvastī.
The woman said to the śramaṇa:
"Accompanied by Greed, he went to Śrāvastī.
He replied, "As you wish."
At that time, the husband sought his wife but did not know her whereabouts. Encountering a man coming along the road, he immediately asked the traveler:
"Have you seen a woman traveling westward?"
The traveler replied,
"A woman went westward together with a śramaṇa.
He immediately pursued them in a rage and seized the śramaṇa.
“You are a bhikṣu; taking my wife, where do you intend to go?
At that time, the bhikṣu replied:
“I am not taking her along; she is walking on the road by herself.”
He then beat the śramaṇa severely and released him to depart.
Upon reaching Śrāvastī, he recounted the matter to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu travels along the same road with a woman from one village to another, he commits a pācittiya offense.
While the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
The bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra repeatedly accused the Venerable Sudatta of committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
When the other bhikṣus heard this, they went and informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha and, endowed with the ten merits, the Buddha established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu makes a claim of having committed the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense without foundation, it is a *pāyattika*.
While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
There was a bhikṣu traveling from Kosala to Śrāvastī who, on the way, arrived at the Caitra Garden and encountered a band of thieves.
He immediately asked the thieves, "Where are you going?"
He replied, "I am going to Śrāvastī. The śramaṇa said:
"Let us be companions through mutual desire.
They then became companions.
Upon reaching Śrāvastī, the thieves did not travel along the main road and were captured by the rāṣṭrapālas.
The people of Rājagṛha said to the bandits,
"Does this śramaṇa also commit robbery? They replied:
"He was also a thief and served as their chief leader.
They then went to the elders and reported the circumstances in detail.
The elders, who were fond of virtue and the Way, said:
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, will never again commit theft; let him go, and do not do this again.
This bhikṣu went to the kingdom of Śrāvastī and told the bhikṣus there.
The bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One declared:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that he is traveling together with a band of robbers from one village to another, commits an offense of defeat."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was ordaining some ten or more youths from within the city of Rājagṛha as his disciples. He gathered seventy or eighty young śrāmaṇeras who were under twenty years of age and conferred the full precepts upon them in succession.
Outside the gate of the Bamboo Grove, several novice monks were weak from hunger and cried out, begging for food.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, asked Ānanda:
"Who is it that is crying out and weeping?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha:
"The Venerable Maudgalyāyana was outside conferring full ordination upon seventy or eighty śrāmaṇeras.
Being hungry, they could not obtain food; for this reason, they were crying out."
The World-Honored One, knowing [the situation], asked Maudgalyāyana:
“Did you confer full ordination upon one whose age was not yet twenty?
He replied:
"It is so, Blessed One! The Blessed One said:
"Those who have not yet reached twenty years of age cannot endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, nor are they capable of practicing the Path.
Those who have reached twenty years of age can endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and are further able to practice the Path."
If a bhikṣu confers full ordination upon a śrāmaṇera who is less than twenty years of age, he commits an offense of transgression.
If the full ordination is conferred, the recipient does not obtain the precepts, and the conferring bhikṣus commit an offense of shamelessness.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were digging the earth with their own hands and also instructing others to dig the earth.
When the householders saw this, they said to one another:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, dig the earth with their own hands and further instruct others to dig the earth?
How are they any different from plowmen?"
When the Bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hands, or instructs another to dig it, saying 'place it here,' he commits a pācittiya offense."
The Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

A certain householder invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for the four-month summer retreat, providing them with offerings of robes, food, drink, and medicinal requisites for the sick and infirm.

The bhikṣus went to the householders and requested that they provide them with summer retreats for four months, including medicine for their ailments and emaciation; some bhikṣus even requested periods longer than four months.
When the householders saw this, they said to one another, "We have granted the bhikṣus a limit of only four months; there shall be no further provisions."
When the Bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:

"If a bhikṣu, having accepted the invitation for the four-month summer retreat, goes to request robes, medicine for illness or weakness—excluding those that are long-term invitations, or occasional separate invitations, or invitations for a single day—if it concerns items from a long-term invitation, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya)."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
On the fifteenth day, the ghaṇṭā was struck, and the community of bhikṣus assembled for the recitation of the precepts.
The Venerable Channa said to the bhikṣus:
"I will not train in this precept.
I shall first question a learned Vinaya master to ask what the meaning of this precept is."
The bhikṣus did not know how they should answer, so they went and informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One told them:
"If a bhikṣu, on the day of the recitation of the precepts, should speak thus:"
"If one says, 'I will not train in this precept;
I shall first ask a learned Vinaya master what the meaning of this precept is,' one falls [into an offense]."
The World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:
"If one does not understand the precepts, one should study under a bhikṣu who is learned and a master of the Vinaya; in this case, there is no offense."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma monastery in Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the monks of Kauśāmbī were fond of quarreling, disputing, arguing, reviling, and slandering one another.
Then the group of six bhikṣus said to one another:
"These bhikṣus revile and slander us; we shall recite [the scriptures] and speak of them to them tomorrow.
When the bhikṣus who uphold the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Blessed One said:
"If a bhikṣu, while engaged in a dispute, recites [the scriptures] in silence and then speaks of them to others the following day, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya).
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling at Kuśinārā in the Gosiṅga Grove.
At that time, the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī assembled a group of twenty monks to perform repentance among them.
Then the group of six bhikṣus said to one another,
"Let us depart in silence so that they cannot perform their repentance."
He then rose from his seat and departed.
The monks who observe the twelve dharmas went to inform the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said to them:

"If a bhikṣu, while the legal proceedings of the Saṃgha of bhikṣus have not yet concluded, rises and departs in silence without having entrusted his seat to a neighboring bhikṣu, he commits an offense of transgression.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus raised their voices and shouted loudly in the midst of the great assembly, causing disturbance to the Saṃgha.
When the bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
“If a bhikṣu raises his voice and shouts loudly to disturb others,
he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya).”
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Sāgara traveled from Kosala to the country of Caṇpā.
Not far from the country of Caṇpā, there lived a nāga named Amatiktu.
It is so fierce and cruel that no human can reach its place; neither elephants, horses, camels, oxen, nor donkeys may go there, and even birds cannot fly above it.
At dawn, the Venerable Khaṇḍadravya donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the kingdom of Khaṇḍita to beg for alms.

He heard that not far from the city there was a dragon named Amratitthu, who was fierce, cruel, and tyrannical; no person could go to that place, nor could elephants, horses, camels, oxen, or donkeys reach it, and even birds could not fly over it.
Having finished his almsround, he returned out of the city; he took up his robe and bowl, washed his feet, folded his sitting mat, placed it upon his shoulder, and went to where the dragon was.
Under the tree, he first caused it to tremble three times, spread out his *niṣīdana* mat, and sat down cross-legged.
When the dragon king Amratituka smelled the odor of the *kāṣāya*, he became greatly incensed and came forth.
The Venerable Sāgara immediately entered *samādhi*.

At that time, the dragon unleashed thunder, rain, and lightning; the Venerable One then transformed the rain and lightning into *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses by means of his verse-mantra.

Then the dragon again rained down snakes, scorpions, turtles, and tortoises; the Venerable Aśvajit transformed the snakes into blue lotus garlands, the scorpions into campaka flower wreaths, and the turtles and tortoises into wreaths of hundred-petaled flowers.
The dragon again rained down spears, swords, and halberds; the sea was transformed into sugarcane, rock honey, and grapes, which [the man] took and ate.
At that time, the dragon thought to himself:
"This must be a great divine person who has come to sit here for the sake of delivering me."

At that time, the dragon’s mind opened and his thoughts were liberated; no longer harboring anger, he cast off his form and transformed into a brahmin. He came before the sea, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, joined his palms, and said:
"I take refuge in you."
Sāgara replied, "Do not take refuge in me; rather, as I have taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus, you should follow my example.

Then the Nāga joined his palms and accepted the instruction: "I shall indeed take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. Grant that I become an upāsaka; from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from taking life."

At that time, when the people within the borders of the kingdom heard that the ocean had sent down this evil dragon, the elders and brahmins heard of it and vied with one another to come and make offerings.
The community of bhikṣus gradually arrived at Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
There was a female lay follower who, having heard that Piṇḍola had arrived, invited him separately for a day’s meal.
At dawn, Piṇḍola put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the house of this female lay follower.
When the upāsikā saw that they were seated, she prostrated with her head at their feet, served them pure water,
and personally portioned out various foods. Sāgara said to the upāsikā, “Sister!
"Having traveled here, I am thirsty; do you have any water or juice?
The upāsikā then thought to herself:
"If I were to give her black stone honey, grape juice, or sour wine, I fear it might cause wind in her belly."
He then filled the cup with wine that appeared like water and tasted like water.
At that time, Kātyāyana drank it without noticing its flavor.
When the upāsikā had finished serving the water, she sat before him to listen to the Dharma.
Having preached the Dharma in verse, he departed.

Upon reaching the space between two gates of the Jeta Grove, the scent of alcohol began to permeate him; being intoxicated, he could not proceed further and lay down by the side of the road. His three robes, alms bowl, bowl pouch, and mendicant’s staff were each lying in a different place.
The Buddha, knowing this, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Put on your robes and come; let us go together out of the Jetavana to observe.

Then the World-Honored One took Ānanda out through the gate of the Jetavana and saw from afar the drunkard Caṅgī lying asleep by the roadside, with his three robes, alms bowl, bowl-bag, and mendicant’s staff each lying in a different place.
The World-Honored One, knowing [the answer], asked Ānanda: "Who is this person?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"Venerable Vāgīśa. The World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"Return to the Jetavana and tell all the bhikṣus to come and assemble here."
Then Ānanda, respectfully receiving the Buddha’s instruction, immediately entered the Jetavana to invite the bhikṣus and led them to the gate.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“What do you think, bhikṣus?”
"Have you seen, heard, or learned of the bhikṣu Khaṇḍadravya subduing the evil nāga?
Those who had seen him said they had seen him; those who had heard of him said they had heard of it.
The World-Honored One said:
“Monks, how is this? Can this man now subdue even a single frog,
let alone a wicked dragon?”
The bhikṣus replied: “We cannot,
World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One said:
"It is so, bhikṣu! This is a great fault of drinking alcohol."
"O Bhikṣus! From this day forward, you must not drink alcohol or taste alcohol.
Whoever drinks or tastes alcohol commits an offense of falling (pārājika)."
There are eight kinds of syrups:
grape syrup, sugarcane syrup, persimmon syrup, pear syrup, jujube syrup, malted barley syrup, fermented yeast syrup (bitter wine), and flower syrup.
To state the essential point: regarding those fermented drinks that resemble liquor, have the flavor of liquor, and cause intoxication when drunk—the World-Honored One said these must not be drunk.
Regarding those fermented drinks that resemble liquor, have the flavor of liquor, but do not cause intoxication when drunk—the World-Honored One said these may be drunk.
If a fermented drink does not resemble liquor in appearance nor taste like liquor, yet one becomes intoxicated by drinking it, the World-Honored One said that it must not be drunk.
If a fermented drink does not resemble liquor in appearance nor taste like liquor, and one does not become intoxicated by drinking it, the World-Honored One said that it may be drunk.

"Eight types of fermented drinks may all be consumed before midday; among them, there are those that may be consumed after midday. While the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he [spoke thus].
At that time, Kālodāyin, having attained the path of Arhatship, thought to himself:
"When I had not yet attained the Path, I was with these six groups of bhikṣus in this city of Śrāvastī, where we greatly troubled the families of the elders and committed many transgressions."
"I shall now go forth to teach and transform others to atone for my former transgressions.
Thereupon, in Śrāvastī, he taught and transformed nine hundred and ninety-nine households, falling short of one by less than a thousand.
Those whose wives attain the Way while their husbands do not are not counted;
those whose husbands attain the Way while their wives do not are likewise not counted;
only those where both husband and wife attain it together are counted.
There was a certain brāhmaṇa whose husband and wife were destined to attain the Way through Kālodāyin.
At dawn, Kālodāyin dressed, took up his bowl, and entered Śrāvastī; proceeding through the city of Bhindivaddha without missing his proper sequence, he arrived at the house of this brāhmaṇa.
At that time, the brahmin was away on a journey. The brahmin’s wife had closed the door and remained inside preparing food.
Kāḷodāyin then entered into samādhi and emerged from the ground in front of the hearth.
When the brahmin’s wife saw him, she thought to herself:
"He must surely be begging for alms from me;
if he hangs upside down in mid-air, I will not give him food."
Kāḷudāyin immediately hung upside down in mid-air.
The brahmin woman thought again:
"His eyes are as large as the mouth of a cauldron; I will not give him food."
At that moment, Kāḷudāyin’s eyes became as large as the mouth of a cauldron.
The brahmin woman thought again:
“If he turns his mouth upward toward his forehead, I will not give him food.”
Then Kāḷodāyin immediately turned his mouth toward her forehead.
The Brahmin woman thought again:
"Even if he were to die right here before me, I would still not give him food."
Kālodayin died right before her eyes.
The brahmin woman was greatly terrified and said, "This śramaṇa son of the Śākyas is widely known; he is a good friend of King Prasenajit and the preceptor of Queen Mallikā."
"If it were known that he died in this brahmin's house, my entire clan would be executed.
Since he is now to live, I shall grant whatever he seeks from his heart and will not oppose his wishes."
Then, as Kāḷodāyin rose after stretching his limbs slightly, the Brahmin woman saw him rise and thought again:
"I shall give him the rice that has scorched in the cauldron to eat."
She immediately began scooping with the ladle, but in the end she could not find any scorched rice; instead, she found only fine rice, as the rice from the cauldron flowed toward her bowl.
When the Brahmin’s wife witnessed this miraculous transformation, her mind was opened and her understanding awakened:
“This great divine being who has come here intends only to deliver me; he has not come to seek food.”
He then held out his alms bowl and offered the food to Udāyin.
Udāyin replied, "Sister!..."
"Do not eat this rice;
you may take it and give it as an offering to the community of bhikṣus.
This Brahmin woman had previously planted roots of merit under former Buddhas, and she said to Kālodāyin:
"Let us go together.
I wish to take this pot of rice and offer it entirely to the community of bhikṣus. Udāyin said:
"As you wish. Then the Brahmin’s wife, carrying this pot of rice, went to the Jetavana, struck the *gandī* to assemble the community of bhikṣus, and offered the rice as alms to the bhikṣu-saṃgha.
He prostrated with his head at Kāḷudāyin’s feet and sat to one side.
Udāyin then preached various teachings to him, whereby he destroyed twenty koṭis of evil and attained the fruit of srotāpanna.
At that time, this woman, having attained the vision of the Truths, prostrated herself with her head at Udāyin’s feet and said:
“From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; please accept me as a laywoman (upāsikā), and for the rest of my life, I shall refrain from taking life.”
Then the woman prostrated herself at the feet of Kālodāyin and departed.
Returning home, she said to the brāhmaṇa:
"The Venerable Kālodāyin came here for alms and performed various miraculous transformations; I immediately offered him rice from my cauldron."
"The community of bhikṣus has taught me the Dharma, and I have attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Now is the time for you; you should go quickly to listen to the Dharma.

At that time, the brahmin, having planted roots of goodness under previous Buddhas, immediately went to where Kālodāyin was, prostrated himself at his feet with his head and face touching them, and sat to one side.
Kāḷodāyin preached the Dharma for him, whereby he destroyed twenty koṭis of evil and attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
At that time, the brahmin realized the Truth; rising from his seat, he prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet and said:
“From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. Please accept me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*); for the rest of my life, I shall refrain from taking life.”
When the upāsaka had heard this teaching of the Dharma, he rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, and departed.
Upon arriving at his home, he said to his wife:
"Kāḷodāyin is our most excellent spiritual friend; he has severed the root of our birth and death, closed the gates to hell, and enabled us to cross to the further shore."
"Whatever robes, food, medicine for the sick, or provisions you require, have them brought here.
Then the wife said to the brahmin,
"You go and request them."
He immediately went and prostrated himself at the feet of Kāḷudāyin, and standing before him, said:
"Whatever robes, food, bedding, or medicinal requisites for the sick you may require, please come to my home to take them; do not hesitate or find it difficult."
Kālodāyin accepted this in silence, and whenever he required anything, he would regularly go there to take it.
This brahmin had only one son; he then gave him a wife and, calling both the son and his wife before him, instructed his son, saying:
"After we, husband and wife, have passed away, you must look after Kālodāyin just as you did when I was alive."
The child knelt and replied,
"I shall follow your instructions.
Subsequently, his parents gradually passed away.
After seven days, having bathed and put on his robes, he went to where Kāḷudāyin was, prostrated himself at his feet, sat to one side, and said to Udāyin:
"Kāḷudāyin is as my own father and mother; whatever clothing, bedding, food, drink, or medicine for illness I require, please take it from my house."
Kālodāyin was in need of certain things and would regularly go there to take them.
At that time, the son of this brahmin was away on a journey. Meanwhile, five hundred bandits, having plundered people outside, were bringing their loot into the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, among the bandits there was a leader who was peerlessly handsome.
From atop the roof, the Brahmin’s daughter-in-law saw him from afar and immediately sent a maidservant to say:
"Please deign to visit my humble home for a moment."
He went straight to her house and engaged in unchaste conduct with the Brahmin’s daughter-in-law.
Shortly thereafter, Venerable Kāḷudāyin also arrived at the house; he took his seat, whereupon they offered him pure water and served various kinds of food.
When the meal was finished, he again provided pure water for washing; [the Buddha] sat to one side and listened to the teaching of the Dharma.
He spoke of the foul impurities of lust, how violating the precepts leads to falling into evil realms, and how upholding the precepts results in rebirth in heaven.
The Brahmin’s wife then thought to herself:
“This śramaṇa arrived late and spoke of the impurity of sexual desire and how observing the precepts leads to rebirth in heaven; he must surely suspect me of unchaste conduct.”
"Furthermore, he is most intimate with my husband; if he were to speak of this matter, my offense would not be small.
After Kālodayin had departed, she said to that wicked teacher:
"That śramaṇa arrived later and spoke only of sexual matters; he must have intended to see me engage in impure conduct."
"Furthermore, she was most intimate with my husband; if she were to report this matter, my punishment would not be slight.
The bandit asked, "What should be done?"
The Brahmin’s wife said,
“You should seize and kill him.
The bandit replied:
"You must not kill. The woman asked,
"For what reason may I not kill?"
The bandits replied, "This is the son of a great lineage; he is a spiritual friend to King Prasenajit and the teacher of Queen Mallikā.
Therefore, he must not be killed."
The wife said, "We must employ a skillful means.
She then feigned illness and sent a messenger to summon him.
After his meal, Kāḷudāyin dressed, took up his bowl, and came to this house; he prostrated himself at their feet and sat to one side.
Kāḷudāyin preached the Dharma to them, and having finished preaching, he wished to depart.
The Brahmin’s wife said, “Please stay a little longer and do not go; I am eager to hear Dhāyī preach the Dharma, and my illness has slightly improved.
Kāḷodāyin then once again preached the profound Dharma.
At sunset, this thief seized a sharp blade and struck off his head from behind, ending his life immediately; he then hid the body beneath the horse dung behind the house.

That day was the fifteenth, the day for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*; the *gaṇḍī* was struck to assemble the Saṃgha for the recitation, and the voting sticks (*śalākā*) were distributed, with one stick remaining long.
Pavarana asked, "Who has not entered for the recitation of the precepts?
Those sitting nearby replied:
"Venerable Kāḷudāyin has not come. Pāṭaliputra then asked,
"Was there someone who gave him instructions?"
He replied, "There is none. At that time,
Piṅgala did not know what he should do and went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"O bhikṣus, let us simply recite the precepts; Kālodāyin has already entered parinirvāṇa, so we are one short of the full number of five hundred.
Thus spoke the World-Honored One.
“Kāḷudāyin has always been my good friend; today we part.
Then, at dawn, the World-Honored One dressed, took his bowl, and together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, entered the city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to the place where the horse dung was piled.

By the power of the Buddha, Kāḷudāyin’s body leaped up seven fathoms above the ground; the bhikṣus supported him with a bed held aloft, and he immediately lay down upon it as they carried him outside the city walls.

They went to the cemetery, making offerings of various flowers and incense, surrounding the site with banners and canopies, performing various musical entertainments, pouring fragrant oil over the body, cremating it, and erecting a stūpa.

When King Prasenajit heard that the Venerable Kālodāyin had been killed by a certain Brahmin, he immediately executed the Brahmin’s family; eighteen households on his left and right were also executed, and five hundred bandits were captured, their hands and feet severed, and cast into the moat surrounding the Jetavana.
On account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha, endowed with the ten merits, and the Buddha established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without having informed the bhikṣus nearby, it is a pāyattika."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"What evil did the Venerable Kālodāyin commit in the past that, despite having now attained arhatship, he was killed by this brahmin family?"
The World-Honored One said:
"In the distant past, Kālodāyin was the presiding priest of a celestial sacrifice.
There were five hundred bands of bandits who, having plundered goods, brought them into the kingdom of Śrāvastī."
A band of five hundred thieves cut off the four legs of a sheep and brought it to sacrifice to the gods.
The presiding priest of the temple then took the life of this sheep.
Those who were the band of five hundred thieves that cut off the sheep's four legs at that time are the very same five hundred thieves currently within the moat of the Jeta Grove.
The one who was the master of the deva-shrine and slaughtered the sheep at that time is now Kāḷudāyin.
Although he has attained arhatship, he cannot escape his past retribution.
The sheep of that time is now the brahmin’s wife.
At that time, the World-Honored One recounted the past experiences of Kālodāyin. Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced, paid their respects, and departed.
