The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went to the house where they had been invited to stay with the Buddha and the Saṃgha of bhikṣus; having arrived there at dawn, they sat down and amused themselves by fondling a small child.
At that time, the weather was extremely hot; the women of the household removed their garments to prepare food offerings for the community of bhikṣus.
When the group of six bhikṣus saw this, the householders said to one another:
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, has no sense of propriety; he arrived here first before the community of monks had come and sat down, obstructing others from preparing the food.
When the bhikṣus who uphold the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One declared:

"If a bhikṣu, having been invited to a morning meal or a midday meal, arrives there first and sits down, yet plays with small children in front of the great assembly, he commits an offense of downfall."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, relying on their status as sons of noble families, entered the palace before the roosters had crowed.
When the householders saw this, they said among themselves,
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, relying on their own status as members of a royal family, enter the palace before the cock has even crowed.
When the bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:

"If a bhikṣu, before dawn has broken and before treasures have been put away, or before the king has donned his robes, should pass through the threshold of a city gate—except when summoned by an official on urgent business—the offender commits a pācittiya offense."
There are ten matters for which one must not enter the royal palace:
if a bhikṣu enters the inner court and the king’s first consort comes out, smiles, and pays homage to the śramaṇa, the bhikṣu shall also smile back.
Upon seeing him, the king immediately conceived an evil thought:
"This śramaṇa must have had illicit relations with my wife.
This is the first reason one should not enter a royal household.
At one time, the king had spent the night with his consort, but later forgot that he had done so, and the consort became pregnant.
When a bhikṣu entered the palace, the king conceived an evil thought:
"This śramaṇa comes to the palace frequently; he must surely have had illicit relations with my wife."
"This is the second reason a bhikṣu must not enter a royal household.
Suppose at some time the royal household loses precious jewels; if the bhikṣu enters the palace, the king will immediately conceive an evil thought:
'This śramaṇa enters the palace repeatedly; perhaps he has stolen these precious jewels and departed.'"
"This is the third reason a bhikṣu must not enter a royal household:
it may happen that the king is deliberating on how to kill the crown prince and his kinsmen, and before the king has given the order, the matter leaks out."
When a bhikṣu enters the palace, the king immediately conceives an evil thought:
"There is no one else; it must be this bhikṣu who has transmitted this matter.
This is the fourth reason a bhikṣu must not enter the royal household.
At one time, the Crown Prince intended to plot the king’s murder. A bhikṣu entered the palace and sat and conversed with the prince.
The king then conceived an evil thought:
"This bhikṣu frequently visits the prince's quarters; he must surely be conspiring with him."
"This is the fifth reason a bhikṣu must not enter the royal palace.
Suppose at some time the king intends to execute a high minister; before the king has even given the order, the sound [of the execution] leaks out.
If the bhikṣu enters the palace, the king will immediately conceive an evil thought:"
"There is no one else; this must have been leaked by a bhikṣu.
This is the sixth reason a bhikṣu shall not enter the royal household.
Or, at times, the king may wish to appoint a low-born person as a minister; before the king has given his command, the word leaks out.
When a bhikṣu enters the palace, the king immediately conceives an evil thought:
"This bhikṣu has leaked this word.
This is the seventh reason a bhikṣu may not enter the royal household.
At another time, when the king wished to launch a military expedition against another country, non-human yakṣas transmitted these words.
When a bhikṣu entered the palace, the king immediately conceived an evil thought:
"This must be the bhikṣu who has leaked this word."
This is the eighth reason why a bhikṣu must not enter the royal palace:
at times, the king’s ministers and attendants may be displeased at the sight of a bhikṣu; if the bhikṣu enters the palace, the ministers will be displeased at the sight of him.
This is the bhikṣu’s ninth [precept]: he must not enter the royal palace.
Or, if a bhikṣu enters the palace repeatedly and remains there overnight without being able to leave, it will hinder him from practicing dhyāna, reciting sūtras, or receiving instruction.
"This bhikṣu is the tenth who shall not enter the royal palace.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
On the fifteenth day, the *gandī* was struck, and the bhikṣus assembled for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).
At that time, the bhikṣu Channa himself made this statement:
"I have fully memorized and recited all the instructions from memory.
The other bhikṣus then addressed the bhikṣu Channa as "the one who recites the precepts from memory."
The bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
The Blessed One told them:
"If a bhikṣu, when the precepts are being recited, speaks as follows:..."
"I know this Dharma; it is recited every half-month as the Prātimokṣa. I understand this Dharma.

When the bhikṣus perceive that such a bhikṣu has come frequently to listen, or has previously heard these precepts, or has heard them here and there, they should instruct him to repent according to the Dharma and then direct him to listen to the precepts with a single-minded focus.
"If a bhikṣu claims to understand what he does not understand, he falls [into an offense].
While the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park,
the bhikṣus were making needle cases out of ivory, bone, and horn.
When the householders saw this, they said to one another,
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, does not refrain from desiring fine things.
How can he take ivory, bone, or horn to make a needle case?"
When the Bhikṣus who follow the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu makes a needle case from ivory, bone, or horn, he commits an offense of falling (pācittiya)."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
The bhikṣus did not know how to make beds; they made beds with high legs.
When the bhikṣus who uphold the twelve dharmas heard of this, they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a bhikṣu makes a bed, the legs shall be eight finger-breadths high, excluding the space occupied by the frame.
Should they exceed this, it is an offense of falling."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus collected cotton from trees and reed mats to use as bedding; however, after only a few days, worms began to breed within them.
The Bhikṣus of the Twelve Dharmas went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu takes cotton from trees or *pū* grass to use as stuffing for bedding, he commits an offense."

"Tree-cotton" refers to wild silkworm cotton. At one time, when the Blessed One was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus made rain-cloaks (vassikasāṭikā) without knowing their proper length.
The twelve-group of bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha told them:
"If a bhikṣu makes a rain-cloak, it shall be six cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width."
"One who transgresses this shall fall [into sin].
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the bhikṣus’ robes were thin and insufficient; the World-Honored One permitted them to wear the *kaṇṭhaka-cīvara*, the *saṃkakṣikā*, and the *nivāsana* as undergarments to cover their loose robes.
The bhikṣus did not know how they should proceed, so they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu makes a *khaṭvāṅga* (staff), it should be four cubits long and two cubits wide."
"One who exceeds this limit falls into an offense.
While the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he permitted the making of *niṣadanas*.
The bhikṣus did not know how they should make them, so they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:

"If a bhikṣu makes a sitting mat (niṣīdana), it shall be two cubits in length and one and a half cubits in width, excluding the border. Should it exceed these dimensions, it constitutes an offense of falling."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the bhikṣu Nanda was the World-Honored One’s younger brother and the son of his maternal aunt; he was peerlessly handsome, possessing thirty of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man that the Buddha possessed.
The robes worn by the World-Honored One were the same as those worn by Nanda.
When the elder bhikṣus saw Nanda approaching from afar, they thought he was the Tathāgata and all rose from their seats to welcome him.
When Nanda arrived and met them, they realized he was Nanda and not the Buddha; feeling ashamed, they all returned to their seats.
The monks who observed the twelve dharmas went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One assembled the harmonious Saṃgha, endowed with the ten merits, and the Buddha established a precept for the śramaṇas:
"If a bhikṣu makes the three robes equal in size to those of the Tathāgata, it is a pāyattika."
"The Tathāgata’s robe is nine cubits in length and six cubits in width;
this is the Tathāgata’s robe. [The Buddha said:

"A bhikṣu uses his own cubit; it is three cubits wide and five cubits long. (The ninety cases of *pātideśanīya* are concluded. Regarding the *pātideśanīya*: While the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a drought and grain was expensive; it was difficult to obtain alms, and the bhikṣus appeared haggard and emaciated.
The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī was widely known and well-regarded; whatever she requested was granted according to her wishes, as the elders did not oppose her.
Seeing that the bhikṣus were haggard and emaciated, he gave away all the food he had received to them and remained hungry, refusing to eat himself.
After not eating for three or four consecutive days, at dawn he intended to enter the city; having reached the city gate, he lay prostrate by the roadside.
A certain upāsaka saw her from afar and immediately went into his house and sent a maidservant, saying:
"Go and assist that bhikṣuṇī and bring her here.
At that time, the maidservant went and assisted the bhikṣuṇī, bringing her to the house, where she then cooked gruel and rice for the bhikṣuṇī.
The upāsaka asked: "Auntie!
What affliction or suffering do you have that you lie by the side of the road?"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī recounted these matters in detail.

When the elders heard this, they said to one another, "These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know contentment; they have even caused the bhikṣuṇī Tiśya to go without food for three or four days—how truly distressing!"
When the bhikṣus who observed the twelve dharmas heard this, they went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
“If a bhikṣu, not being ill, enters a village and takes cooked rice with his own hand from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative.”
This bhikṣu should confess his transgression to a virtuous bhikṣu, saying:
"I have acted shamefully; I repent according to the Dharma.
This is the method for confession.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
A certain householder prepared pure food and invited a great assembly of bhikṣus.
The bhikṣuṇī Tullanandā also ate at that house, calling out loudly in her desire for gain.
When the elders saw this, they said to one another,
"Why does this bhikṣuṇī call out so loudly in the midst of the great assembly?"
When the bhikṣus who uphold the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"If a bhikṣu is eating while seated, and a bhikṣuṇī shouts out loudly in the midst of the assembly demanding food..."
The bhikṣus shall not eat, but should remain silent.
The bhikṣus should say to the bhikṣuṇīs: "Sisters!..."
"Wait a moment;
you must wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating.
If there is not a single bhikṣu among that assembly who says to the bhikṣuṇī, "Wait a moment," this bhikṣu should confess his transgression before the bhikṣus:
"I am ashamed; I repent according to the Dharma.
This is the method for repentance.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a minister of King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī named Śreṇika. He possessed immeasurable wealth and vast estates; he was observant of the precepts, diligent, wise, and intelligent. Having seen the truths and attained the fruits [of the path], he invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to provide them with clothing, food, bedding, and medicinal requisites for the sick, practicing generosity and cultivating merit.
Having performed meritorious deeds without ceasing, he later gradually became poor; his wife, children, and servants were so poorly clothed that their bodies could not even be covered.
When the elders saw this, they said to one another:

"This śramaṇa son of the Śākyas knows no contentment; he comes frequently to the house of Śrīkaṇṭha, seizing his wife and children to divide them as food for the bhikṣus, leaving the wife and children to walk about naked."
When the bhikṣus who observed the twelve dharmas heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"Knowing that you have been invited by a family of those who have realized the Truths, you must not remain for a long time at that house to eat."

If a bhikṣu, having previously accepted an invitation at a family where the Truth has been realized, stays for more than one night, and then goes there and takes food or drink with his own hand, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression to a virtuous bhikṣu, saying:
"I have acted shamefully; I confess according to the Dharma."
"This is the method for repentance. While the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, was staying at the Nyagrodha Park of the Śākyas in Kapilavastu,
the Śākyas of Kapilavastu would always set aside a portion of food and drink specifically for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus before they ate themselves.
At that time, women of the Śākya clan were carrying food and drink as they approached, when they were robbed by bandits.
When the group of six bhikṣus heard that the Śākya women had been robbed by bandits, they said to one another,
"Let us go together to meet them and mock them."
He immediately went to the woman and said,
"Where are the food and drink?
Give me a little to eat."
All the women lost their garments and, feeling ashamed, replied,
"We have been plundered by bandits.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, asked Ānanda:
"What kind of people outside the garden are making such loud clamor?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
"Women of the Śākya clan have come carrying food and drink, and they have been plundered by bandits."
"Furthermore, the group of six bhikṣus went there and mocked him; that is why his voice is so loud.
The World-Honored One said to Ānanda, "Go and fetch a long, white cotton cloth and give it to him so that he may wrap himself in it and come here."
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately took a white cotton cloth and gave it to the messenger to bring back.

The women of the Śākya clan who had come before then wrapped themselves in the white cotton cloth and approached the place where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the women; having finished preaching, he remained silent.
Seeing that the Buddha was silent, the women rose, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the women had not gone far, assembled the harmonious Saṃgha on account of this matter. Endowed with the ten merits, the Buddha established a precept for the śramaṇas:
“The dwelling places of forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka) are remote; the roads are perilous and difficult, and there are many bandits.”
If a bhikṣu knows that the dwelling place of a forest-dweller (*āraṇyaka*) is distant, with roads that are rugged and difficult, and infested with many bandits;

yet, if the community of bhikṣus has not previously been dispatched outside the monastery grounds to provide food within the grounds, and [the forest-dweller] goes outside to seek food and drink again.
This bhikṣu should confess his transgression to a virtuous bhikṣu, saying:
"I am ashamed; I repent according to the Dharma.
This is the method for confession.

Regarding the *śikṣāpada*, the *śikṣāpada*: When the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the group of six bhikṣus wore their inner robes (*nirvāṇasaṅghāṭī*) trailing on the ground.
When the various elders saw this, they said to one another,
"How does this śramaṇa son of the Śākyas differ from a woman, wearing his inner robe (nirvāṇasaṅghāṭī) trailing on the ground?
The bhikṣus who observed the twelve dharmas went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"When wearing the nivāsana, one must not let it trail on the ground.
If it trails on the ground, it constitutes an offense of *śaikṣa-dharmas*."
Those six groups of bhikṣus again wore their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarments) too high.
When the householders saw this, they said to one another, "How is it that these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, wear their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* so high? How are they any different from women?"
The Bhikṣus of the Twelve Dharmas went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"You must not wear the nivāsana (undergarment) too high."
"If it is worn too high, it is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
Those six groups of bhikṣus then pulled one corner of their nivāsana robes down to one side.
When the laypeople saw this, they said to one another:
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, wears his nivāsana robe by trailing one corner.
The World-Honored One said,
"When wearing the nivāsana robe, one must not trail one corner."
"It is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts to drag one corner [of the robe] unevenly.
Those bhikṣus of the group of six wore their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* with the belt tied tightly so that it hung down above and below like the blade of an axe.
When the various householders saw this, they said to one another,
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, wears his inner robe (nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī) with its belt tied so tightly that it hangs down both above and below.
The World-Honored One said:
"When putting on the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, one must not gather the upper and lower edges too tightly.
If the upper and lower parts hang down excessively, it is contrary to the rules of conduct.
Those monks of the group of six wore their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭīs* with many tree leaves tucked inside.
When the elders saw this, they said to one another,
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, wear their inner robes like the leaves of a tala tree.
The World-Honored One said:
"One should not wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* like a *tālaka* tree leaf;
one who wears it like a *tālaka* tree leaf does not accord with the practice of the precepts.
Those bhikṣus of the group of six wore their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* like the trunk of an elephant.
When the householders saw this, they said to one another,
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, wears his inner robe like the trunk of an elephant.
The World-Honored One said:
6. "When putting on the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, it must not be like an elephant's trunk.
To wear it like an elephant's trunk is contrary to the rules of conduct.
At that time, those six groups of bhikṣus placed lumps of wheat porridge inside their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭīs*. One corner was left hanging down in front.
When the various householders saw this, they said to one another,
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, wears his inner robe like a lump of barley meal.
The World-Honored One told them:
"When putting on the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, it must not be like a lump of wheat porridge.
To wear it like a lump of wheat porridge is contrary to the rules of conduct.
They tucked up one corner and pinned it over the shoulder; this was how the six groups of bhikṣus, including Kailāsa, wore their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭīs* without fastening the straps.
When the householders saw this, they said to one another,
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, wear their inner robes (nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī) like kāśika cloth.
The World-Honored One said:
"When putting on the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, one must not do so like a *kairāva*.
To do so like a *kairāva* is contrary to the practice of the precepts.

8. [The Buddha said: "When folding the upper robe tightly, it should be like a bundle of grass; 'bundle' (*kairāva*) is the foreign word for this. Those bhikṣus of the group of six rolled up their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭīs* to make them shiny as they wore them."
When the various householders saw this, they said to one another,
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have polished their saṃghāṭī robes until they shine like ornaments.
The World-Honored One told them:
"When putting on the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment), one must not iron it to make it shiny.
One who irons it to make it shiny does not conform to the practice of the precepts.
Those bhikṣus of the group of six wore their *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭīs* with the necks tucked up.
When the various elders saw this, they said to one another,
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, has tucked up his head while wearing his inner robe (nirvāṇasaṅghāṭī).
The World-Honored One told them:
"One must not bunch the head of the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment).
To bunch the head of it is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Those monks of the group of six wore *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭīs* made of fine thread.
When the various elders saw this, they said to one another,
"This śramaṇa son of the Śākyas is wearing a saṃghāṭī robe with fine thread.
The World-Honored One told them:
"One must not wear a *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) with fine thread.
Whoever wears one thus shall not be in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
Thus the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus.
"One should wear the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* neatly;
one who wears it untidily does not conform to the practice of the precepts.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One, while he was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus let one corner of their triple robe trail on the ground. Seeing this, the World-Honored One said to them:
"You must not let one corner of the triple robe trail on the ground."
"If one drags them down, it is not in accordance with the rules of conduct.
The World-Honored One saw those six groups of bhikṣus wearing their three robes high and said to them,
"One must not wear the three robes high."
"Those who wear their robes high should not practice the precepts.
Seeing the group of six bhikṣus letting the front corners of their triple-robes hang down, the World-Honored One saw them and said:
"One must not wear the triple-robe with its front corners hanging down."
"It is not proper for a wearer to wear it in such a manner.
When [the robe] was not tucked over the shoulder but hung down from the upper arm above the elbow, the World-Honored One said: "O Bhikṣus!"
"One should wear the three robes in a neat and orderly manner;
one who wears them untidily does not conform to the practice of the precepts.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One, while he was traveling through Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered a room without maintaining silence. Seeing this, the World-Honored One said to them:
"One should enter a room maintaining silence.
To enter without maintaining silence is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus entered their rooms and sat down without being tranquil. Seeing this, the World-Honored One said to them:
"One should enter one's room and sit in tranquility.
To enter one's room and sit without being tranquil is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus entered their rooms without looking carefully. When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to them:
"One should enter one's room while looking carefully.
For one who does not look carefully, it is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus entered the room and sat down without looking carefully. When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to them:
"One should enter the room and sit down after looking carefully.
To sit down without looking carefully is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus entered a room with their eyes wide open; the World-Honored One saw them and said, "One must not enter a room with one's eyes wide open."
"If one enters a room with eyes wide open, it is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
When the group of six bhikṣus entered a room and sat down with their eyes wide open, the World-Honored One saw them and said:
"One must not enter a room and sit with eyes wide open."
"One who enters a room while staring with wide-open eyes does not act in accordance with the precepts.
When the World-Honored One saw those six groups of bhikṣus scolding people as they entered rooms, he said to them:
"One must not scold people as they enter a room."
"To enter a room while scolding others is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
This act of looking up with the intent to scold is the same as the former. When those six groups of bhikṣus entered a room and sat down while scolding others, the World-Honored One saw them and said:
"One must not enter a room and sit while scolding others."
"One who scolds others before entering a room and sitting down should not act as if they are haughty in their observance of the precepts.
When the World-Honored One saw those bhikṣus of the group of six entering a room while shouting and calling out, he told them:
"One must not enter a room while shouting and calling out."
"To call out while entering a room is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
Seeing those six groups of bhikṣus calling out as they entered a room and sat down, the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not enter a room and sit down while calling out."
"To call out loudly as one enters a room and sits down is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Seeing the group of six bhikṣus entering a room while shouting at the top of their voices, the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not enter a room shouting at the top of one's voice."
"To enter a room while shouting loudly is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
Regarding this, when the group of six bhikṣus entered a room and sat down while shouting loudly, the World-Honored One saw them and said:
"One must not enter a room and sit down while shouting loudly."
"To enter a room while shouting loudly and sitting down is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
When the World-Honored One saw the group of six bhikṣus entering a room while squatting, he said to them:
"One must not enter a room while squatting."
"To enter a room walking on one's heels is not in accordance with the rules of conduct.
Seeing the group of six bhikṣus entering a room and sitting while walking on their heels, the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not enter a room and sit while walking on one's heels."
"To enter a room while walking on tiptoe and sitting down [immediately] is not in accordance with the precepts.
When the World-Honored One saw the group of six bhikṣus entering a room while walking with their three robes covering their heads, he said to them:
"One must not enter a room while walking with one's three robes covering one's head."
"To enter a room while walking with one's head covered by the three robes is contrary to the rules of conduct.
When the World-Honored One saw those six groups of bhikṣus entering a room and sitting down while walking with their heads covered by the three robes, he said to them:
"One must not enter a room and sit down while walking with one's head covered by the three robes."
"To enter a room and sit with one's head covered by the three robes is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
When the World-Honored One saw the group of six bhikṣus entering a room with their heads wrapped in the three robes, he said to them:
"One must not enter a room with one's head wrapped in the three robes."
"It is not in accordance with the precepts for one who enters a room while walking with their head wrapped in the three robes.
Seeing the group of six bhikṣus entering a room and sitting down with their heads wrapped in the three robes,
the World-Honored One saw them and said:
"One must not enter a room and sit with the three robes wrapped around one's head.
To enter a room and sit with the three robes wrapped around one's head is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Those bhikṣus of the group of six, having put on the three robes, entered a room walking with their chests bared and their breasts exposed.
The World-Honored One saw him and said:
"One must not enter a dwelling with the chest exposed and the breast revealed.
To enter a dwelling with the chest exposed and the breast revealed is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus, having put on their three robes, entered a room and sat down with their chests bared and their breasts exposed.
When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to them:
"You must not enter a room and sit with your chests bared and your breasts exposed."
"To enter a room and sit with one's chest exposed and breast revealed is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
When the World-Honored One saw the group of six bhikṣus walking into a room with their triple robes hanging down to cover their feet, he said to them:
"One must not walk into a room with the triple robe hanging down to cover the feet."
"To enter a room with the three robes hanging down to cover the feet is contrary to the rules of conduct.
Those monks of the group of six entered a room and sat down with their three robes hanging down to cover their feet.
The World-Honored One saw this and said:

"One must not enter a room and sit with the three robes draped over the feet; for one who enters a room and sits with the three robes draped over the feet does not accord with the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus, wearing their three robes, tucked them up on both sides of their arms and entered a room.
When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to them:
"One must not enter a room wearing the three robes tucked up on both sides of the arms."
"To enter a room with the three robes tucked under both arms and worn upon the upper arms is not in accordance with the rules of conduct.
Yet those bhikṣus of the group of six, having put on the three robes, entered a room and sat down with them tucked under both arms and worn upon their upper arms.
The World-Honored One saw this and said:
"One must not enter a room and sit with the three robes draped over both arms.
To enter a room and sit with the three robes draped over both arms is contrary to the rules of conduct."
Those six groups of bhikṣus entered a room with their three robes draped over their left shoulders.
When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to them:
"You must not enter a room with your three robes draped over your left shoulders."
"To enter a room with one's three robes draped over the left shoulder is contrary to the rules of conduct.
Yet those monks of the group of six entered a room and sat down with their three robes draped over their left shoulders.
The World-Honored One saw him and said:
"One must not enter a room and sit with the three robes draped over the left shoulder.
To enter a room and sit with them draped over the left shoulder is contrary to the rules of conduct."
The minor precepts are on the right. Those six groups of bhikṣus entered a room while swinging their left and right arms within their three robes.
Seeing this, the World-Honored One said to them:
"You must not enter a room while swinging your left and right arms within your three robes."
"To enter a room swinging one's left and right arms is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
Thus, those six groups of bhikṣus entered rooms and sat down while swinging their left and right arms within their three robes.
The World-Honored One saw this and told them:
"One must not enter a room and sit with one's left and right arms dangling inside the three robes.
To enter a room and sit with one's left and right arms dangling is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus entered the dwellings shaking their hands.
When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to them:
"You must not enter the dwellings shaking your hands."
"To enter a room swaying one's hands is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
Seeing the group of six bhikṣus entering a room and sitting down while swaying their hands,
the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not enter a room and sit with swinging one's arms.
To enter a room and sit while swinging one's arms is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Regarding this many precepts, those bhikṣus of the group of six entered rooms walking with their elbows swinging.
The World-Honored One saw this and said:
"One must not enter a dwelling room while swinging one's elbows.
To enter a dwelling room while swinging one's elbows is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus entered a room and sat down shaking their elbows.
When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to them:
"You must not enter a room and sit shaking your elbows."
"To enter a room while swinging one's elbows is not in accordance with the precepts.
Seeing those six groups of bhikṣus entering rooms while swaying their shoulders,
the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not enter a room walking with the shoulders shaking.
To enter a room walking with the shoulders shaking is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Yet those bhikṣus of the group of six entered a room and sat down while walking with their shoulders shaking.
The World-Honored One saw this and said:
"One must not enter a room and sit with the shoulders shaking.
To enter a room and sit with the shoulders shaking is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six group-of-six bhikṣus entered a room while shaking their heads.
The World-Honored One saw them and said,
"One must not enter a room while shaking one's head."
"One who enters a room shaking their head does not act in accordance with the precepts.
Seeing those six groups of bhikṣus entering a room and sitting while shaking their heads,
the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not enter a room and sit while shaking one's head;
for one who enters a room and sits while shaking their head does not accord with the practice of the precepts.
Those bhikṣus of the group of six entered the room walking while swaying their bodies.
The World-Honored One saw him and said:
"One must not enter a room walking with the body swaying.
To enter a room walking with the body swaying is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus entered a room and sat down while swaying their bodies.
The World-Honored One saw them and said:
"One must not enter a room and sit while swaying the body."
"To enter a room while swaying the body and then sit down is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
Seeing the group of six bhikṣus entering a room walking hand-in-hand,
the World-Honored One saw them and said:
"One must not enter a room walking hand-in-hand.
To enter a room walking hand-in-hand is contrary to the code of conduct.
Yet those bhikṣus of the group of six entered the room and sat down while walking hand-in-hand.
The World-Honored One saw them and said:
"One must not enter a room and sit with hands joined together.
For those who enter a room and sit with hands joined together, it is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts."
Linking arms, they blocked the road with their carriages and horses, while the group of six bhikṣus leaped along with one foot raised as they entered the room.
Seeing this, the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not enter a room walking with one foot raised."
"To enter a room walking on one foot is not in accordance with the rules of conduct.
Seeing the group of six bhikṣus entering a room and sitting down while standing on one foot,
the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not enter a room and sit with one leg raised.
To enter a room and sit with one leg raised is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Those monks of the group of six entered a room walking on their tiptoes.
The World-Honored One saw this and said:
"One must not enter a room by hopping on both feet; for one who enters a room by hopping on both feet, it is not in accordance with the precepts.
Yet those six groups of bhikṣus continued to enter and sit in rooms by hopping on both feet.
The World-Honored One saw him and said:
"One must not enter a room and sit down by hopping on both feet.
To enter a room and sit down by hopping on both feet is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus sat with their legs crossed inside a room.
When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to them:
"One must not sit with legs crossed inside a room."
"To sit cross-legged with feet overlapping in the dwelling is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
When the World-Honored One saw those six groups of bhikṣus sitting with their legs crossed in the dwelling, he addressed them, saying:
"One must not sit with legs crossed in the dwelling.
To sit with legs crossed in the dwelling is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Yet those monks of the group of six sat in the dwelling propping their cheeks against their hands, laughing at one another.
The World-Honored One saw them and said:
"You must not sit in the hall with your cheeks propped up, laughing at one another.
Laughing at one another is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
A certain householder invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.

Once the Buddha and the bhikṣus were seated, the householder personally provided water for washing and laid out various kinds of food and drink; the householder’s women all came forward to serve the meal.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus looked up at the women of the householders; consequently, the food and drink fell out and did not enter their bowls.
When the householders saw this, they said to one another, "How can these śramaṇas gaze at the countenances of women while their food and drink do not even enter their bowls?"
The twelve-group monks went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
“You should receive food with focused attention and direct gaze.”
"To receive food without careful and upright observation is not in accordance with the precepts.
The World-Honored One addressed the group of six bhikṣus who were receiving soup and vegetables without careful and upright observation:
"One should receive soup and vegetables with focused attention;
for one who lacks focused attention does not correspond to the practice of the precepts.
Those bhikṣus of the group of six received rice until their bowls overflowed.
The World-Honored One said:
"One should receive rice in a bowl that is level.
To receive rice until it overflows is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus ate by picking out morsels from the center of their bowls.
The World-Honored One saw this and said to them:
"You must not eat by picking out morsels from the center of your bowls."
"Eating with one's hand while holding the bowl is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
When those six groups of bhikṣus pressed their thumbs into the bowl and ate from the rice,
the World-Honored One said:
"One must not hold the bowl with the thumb and eat by inserting the thumb into the rice.
To hold the bowl with the thumb and eat by inserting the thumb into the rice is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Those monks of the group of six then began to knead the rice while eating.
The World-Honored One said:
"One must not take morsels of food.
To take morsels of food is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus ate by picking up morsels of food here and there.
When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to them:
"You must not eat by picking up morsels of food here and there."
"Eating by picking up morsels of food from here and there is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
When the World-Honored One saw the group of six bhikṣus eating with their noses scrunched up, he said to them:
"One must not eat with a snubbed nose.
To eat with a snubbed nose is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Those bhikṣus of the group of six ate while shaking their hands.
The World-Honored One saw this and said:
"One must not eat while shaking one's hand.
To eat while shaking one's hand is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus made sucking sounds while eating their rice.
The World-Honored One saw this and said to them:
"One must not make sucking sounds while eating rice."
"Eating by gulping down food is not in accordance with the rules of conduct.
Seeing that group of six bhikṣus licking their hands while eating,
the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not lick one's hands while eating.
To lick one's hands while eating is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Yet those six groups of bhikṣus licked their food by wiping their bowls with their fingers.
The World-Honored One saw this and said to him:
"One must not lick food from the bowl by using a curved finger to wipe it.
To lick food from the bowl by using a curved finger to wipe it is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus ate with their tongues protruding.
When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to them:
"You must not eat with your tongues protruding."
"Eating with the tongue protruding is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
Seeing that the group of six bhikṣus were swallowing their food without chewing,
the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not swallow food without chewing it;
to swallow food without chewing it is contrary to the precepts.
Those bhikṣus of the group of six took their gruel with their thumbs, which were soiled and greasy, while holding their bowls.
The World-Honored One saw this and said:
"One must not take the gruel with a thumb that is soiled and greasy.
To take gruel with a thumb that is soiled and greasy is contrary to the rules of conduct."
Those six group-of-six bhikṣus took large mouthfuls of rice, pressing them into their mouths with their palms.
Seeing this, the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not take large mouthfuls of rice, pressing them into the mouth with the palm."
"To take a large mouthful of rice that fills the palm and thrusts it into the mouth is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
The World-Honored One said this to the group of six bhikṣus who were taking mouthfuls of rice exceeding the width of four fingers.
"One must not take morsels of food larger than the width of four finger-joints.
To exceed the width of four finger-joints is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Yet those bhikṣus of the group of six opened their mouths wide to eat.
The World-Honored One saw this and said:
"One must not eat with the mouth wide open.
To eat with the mouth wide open is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus opened their mouths wide in anticipation before the morsel of food had even reached them.
Seeing this, the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not open one's mouth wide in anticipation before the morsel of food has arrived."
"To wait with the mouth wide open is not in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
Seeing that the group of six bhikṣus were speaking while holding food in their mouths,
the World-Honored One said to them:
"One must not speak with food in one's mouth.
To speak with food in one's mouth is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Those bhikṣus of the group of six, though not ill, were invited to receive rice and soup.
The World-Honored One saw him and said:
"One who is not ill should not request rice and soup.
To request rice and soup is not in accordance with the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus covered their soup with rice and then asked for more soup.
When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to them:
"One must not cover one's soup with rice and then ask for more soup."
"One who covers their soup with rice and then asks for more soup does not act in accordance with the precepts.
Those six groups of bhikṣus looked around at the amount of rice in the bowls of those sitting beside them.
The World-Honored One saw this and said:
"One must not look left and right to observe the quantity of food in the bowls of those sitting nearby.
To look left and right to observe the quantity of food in the bowls of those sitting nearby is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus ate without looking at their bowls.
When the World-Honored One saw this, he said to them:
"One must not eat without looking at one's bowl."
"To eat without looking at one's bowl is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Seeing that the group of six bhikṣus were receiving food by selecting specific individuals,
the World-Honored One saw them and said:
"One must not accept offerings by discriminating among people;
to accept offerings by discriminating among people is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Those six groups of bhikṣus discarded the food remaining after they had washed their bowls without informing the donor.
The World-Honored One saw this and said:
"Regarding the food remaining in the alms bowl, if the host does not permit it to be discarded, one must not discard it.
To discard it would be contrary to the practice of the precepts."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
King Prasenajit made a vow for himself:
“For as long as I live, while the Buddha remains at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, I shall personally go each day to pay my respects to the World-Honored One.”
"If I do not go, the ministers will fine me five hundred taels of gold.
He said to the ministers:
"Sweep and sprinkle the Jetavana; today I wish to go and pay my respects to the World-Honored One."
The ministers heard the king’s command but did not obey it.
The king repeated his words to the ministers two or three times:
“Sweep and sprinkle the Jetavana; today I wish to go there to pay my respects and visit the World-Honored One.”
When the ministers heard these instructions, they did not comply with the command.
King Prasenajit became enraged and said to his great ministers, "I have ordered you to sweep and sprinkle the Jetavana;
why do you not follow my instructions and fail to sweep the Jetavana?"
"Those who do not follow my instructions and do not sweep the Jetavana shall have their heads decapitated.
Their heads shall then be placed upon the road, and you shall tread upon them with your feet all the way to the gate of the Jetavana.
When the ministers heard these words, they said to one another:
"This king is cruel and lacks any compassion; he is capable of seizing us for that very reason.
Having said this, they went to sweep and sprinkle the Jetavana monastery.
They then returned and informed the king:
“Having finished sweeping and sprinkling water, Great King,
now is the time.”
King Prasenajit then commanded his charioteer:
"Go and prepare the precious peacock-chariot; I now wish to go and pay my respects to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the charioteer immediately went to prepare the carriage, which was stationed outside the gate, and returned to inform the king.
"The carriage is prepared,
Great King! Now is the very time."

At that time, King Prasenajit, riding in a carriage adorned with precious feathers, traveled from Śrāvastī to the gate of the Jeta Grove. There he alighted from his chariot and set aside his five royal insignia: he removed his parasol, took off his crown, laid aside his pearl-handled fly-whisk, cast off his carved sandals, and unsheathed his sword. Accompanied by his footmen, he proceeded to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

King Prasenajit heard a fragrance unlike that of the human world; however, as the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the king, it did not enter his mind, for his attention remained fixed solely upon the fragrance.
Knowing this, the World-Honored One asked King Prasenajit:
"Why does Your Majesty not listen to the Dharma with full attention today, but instead harbor a divided mind?"
King Prasenajit addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Since my youth, I have been raised within the inner palace; at the age of eight, I took charge of state affairs.
Throughout the treasuries, there are all kinds of incenses—agallochum, *candana*, sandalwood, *mṛṇāla*, and *kakkola*—and upon smelling their fragrance, I recognize them all."
"Never before have we heard of such a fragrance as this, which is not of the human realm.
Whose fragrance is this?
We pray that the World-Honored One will tell us."
The World-Honored One said,
“Great King, do you wish to see this incense? [The King replied,] “Indeed, I wish to see it.”

Then the World-Honored One extended his right arm, adorned with the hundred marks, and pressed it against the earth. Thereupon, skeletons emerged, five *zhang* long—each about six or seven feet in height—and ascended into the void. They sat, lay down, and flew through the air; some entered into *samādhi*, emitting various rays of light—blue, yellow, red, white, or the color of lapis lazuli. They surged up from the east and sank down in the west, and did likewise in all four directions. From the lower part of their bodies water issued forth while fire issued from the upper parts; from the lower part of their bodies fire issued forth while water issued from the upper parts. Having performed these manifold transformations, they vanished back into the earth.
While at Jetavana, having heard the fragrance of these remains,
King Prasenajit asked the Buddha,
"Whose remains are these?"
The World-Honored One told the king:
"This is the bone of a Pratyekabuddha.
The king addressed the World-Honored One:
"What meritorious deeds did this person perform to possess such a wondrous fragrance?
The World-Honored One replied:

"In the distant past, incalculable kalpas ago, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there appeared in the world the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa. He extensively preached the Dharma for sentient beings and entered parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder."

At that time, there was a king named Kṣemaka (transliterated as Zhíbī, with the second character pronounced *pú* and *mí*), who carried incense, flowers, banners, canopies, standards, and pennants, along with conchs, drums, and various musical performances, making diverse offerings as he performed the cremation.
At that time, King Kṛkin thought to himself:
"I wish to construct a stūpa for the Tathāgata Kāśyapa.
Which would be more excellent?"

At that time, within the four city gates, there were four great dragon kings who emerged from the water and transformed themselves into the forms of brahmins. They came before the king, joined their palms in greeting, and sat down to one side, asking:
"We wonder, Great King, what kind of stūpa are you constructing for Kāśyapa?"
The King replied,
"It shall be constructed by piling up earth.
Then the four men said to the King:
"Ordinary people, when they die, have earthen mounds built as their tombs; how much more so for this World-Honored One—should not an earthen mound be built for him?
The King asked the four men, "How do you wish it to be made?"
The four men replied,
"It was made from the four precious substances. Then the king said:
"Even if one were to offer all of Jambudvīpa for sale, not a single jewel could be obtained, much less four jewels.
At that time, the four men thought to themselves:
"The King surely does not know that we are dragon kings."
He then addressed the king, saying:
"I am a dragon king, not an ordinary mortal.
I dwell within the four gates of this city, and my palaces are made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal."

The king dispatched skilled craftsmen to construct moats within the four city gates; those that were made of gold became golden moats, while those made of silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli likewise became moats of silver, crystal, and lapis lazuli.

At that time, the king immediately dispatched men to construct moats within the four cities; these were all completed as moats made of the four kinds of precious substances. He constructed a stūpa for Kāśyapa, one yojana in length, one yojana in width, and one yojana in height. At its summit was a *kṣatriya* [finial], and above the *kṣatriya* canopy and the dew-receptacle (*candraśālā*), the pinnacle rose to a height of one *krośa*, which is eight thousand *chi*; thus, the four sides measured one yojana.
When the construction of the Kāśyapa stūpa was completed, he intended to drive stakes into the ground at night to mark the boundaries with mud.
The King dispatched men into the city to ring a bell, commanding all those who sold flowers to come to the palace gate.
"I shall give you the payment.
There was a son of a wealthy householder who frequently visited a certain courtesan.
At that time, this woman commanded a maidservant:
"Open the gate for that son of a householder who comes bringing flowers;
if he has no flowers, do not open the gate.
At that time, the son of a householder came to this gate.
The maidservant asked, "Who is this? He replied:
"This is the son of the elder.
The maidservant asked:
"Did he bring any flowers?"
He replied, "There are no flowers. [The other said,] "If there are no flowers, you may not enter."
At that time, the son of the elder thought to himself:
"The flowers in this city are very precious and cannot be obtained;
however, the flowers for the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha are easy to obtain."
He immediately went into the stūpa of Kāśyapa, filled it with white cotton flowers, and returned.
As the sun had already set and the city gates were closed, he entered through a water drain and knocked on the door of the Mātaṅga family.
The maidservant then asked, "Who is it? He replied:
"Son of a householder," the maid asked again,
"Have you brought any flowers?"
He replied, "There are flowers.
He opened the door and called him forward; he immediately entered, took the flowers, and gave them to the wife of the man of the lecherous caste.

Having engaged in sexual intercourse during the middle of the night, by dawn his entire body breaks out in sores like mustard seeds; these gradually grow as large as cowpeas, then as large as soybeans, then as large as *āmalaka* fruits, then as large as *vibhītaka* fruits, and finally like small hundred-seed gourds, with pus and black blood flowing from them.
Then this courtesan immediately commanded her maidservant to throw her into a pit.
The maidservant said,
"I cannot do this."
"You should inform his father.
Thereupon, the maidservant went at once and said to his father, "My worthy son is ill; you should go to see him."
The father immediately came, and the four of them together carried him back home.
He summoned various skilled physicians and said to them, "This boy suffers from this affliction; how should he be treated?"
The physicians replied,
"One requires nine *tolas* of gośīrṣa sandalwood.
His father asked:
"What do you intend to do with it?
The physician replied,
"Three ounces shall be used to anoint the body, three ounces shall be taken as medicine, and three ounces shall be used to fumigate the clothes."
His father then thought to himself:
"All my wealth has been spent at the courtesan's house.
Sandalwood from the ox-head mountain is extremely expensive; I fear I shall not be able to afford it."
He said to his kinsmen and relatives,
"Prepare a small amount for me," and immediately obtained nine *liang* of ox-head sandalwood (*gośīrṣa-candana*).
He ground it upon a stone in front of the patient.
The patient asked,
"What do you intend to do?"
His father replied,
"To apply it to a wound.
The son said to his father:
"The transgression I have committed is grave;
though you lay me within a grove of sandalwood, you still cannot cure my illness.
His parents asked:
"What is this grave offense?
The son reported the matter to him in full detail, saying,
"I pray that you grant me these nine *liang* of sandalwood."
He immediately took the sandalwood and gave it to them, saying, "I pray that my parents will carry me to the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha.
Then four men carried him there; holding two or three pieces of ox-head sandalwood, he spoke these words:
"Take this incense as payment for the *Kāśyapa-buddha-puṣpa* you recently took;
as for the remaining six *liang*, I offer them to Kāśyapa Buddha.
He then made this aspiration:

"By virtue of these merits, may you not fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals; instead, may you be born only among gods and humans, until finally attaining the state of a Pratyekabuddha and entering Parinirvāṇa."
Immediately his bodily sores were healed; whereas he had previously traveled by carriage, upon returning he walked on foot.
Later, when his life ended, he was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
On the day of his birth, there were none among the devas who did not smell the fragrance of his sandalwood.

When his life in the heavens came to an end, he was reborn in this human world; every single pore emitted the fragrance of sandalwood. He left the household life to study the Way, attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha, and entered Parinirvāṇa in the Nirvana without remainder.

Since his parinirvāṇa until this day, five hundred years have passed; his remains have not decayed, and thus there is this fragrance unlike any in the world, causing the entire Jetavana to be filled with its scent.
When these words were spoken, tens of millions of people conceived the aspiration for the state of a pratyekabuddha. "Great King!
The son of the elder at that time is now these very skeletal remains of a pratyekabuddha."
The World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the king; having finished preaching, he remained silent.
Then King Prasenajit rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, and departed. He mounted a carriage adorned with feathered jewels and returned to the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus preached the Dharma while the king was riding in his carriage.
When the bhikṣus who observe the twelve dharmas saw this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"One must not preach the Dharma to those traveling by carriage;
he who preaches the Dharma to those traveling by carriage does not accord with the practice of the precepts.
Yet those bhikṣus of the group of six preached the Dharma while the king was in front and they were behind him.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a person is in front and you are behind, you should not preach the Dharma to them.
One who preaches the Dharma should not fail to observe the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus stood outside the road while the king was on the road and preached the Dharma for him.
The World-Honored One said:
"One should not preach the Dharma to someone who is on the road while one is outside the road."
"One who preaches the Dharma should not fail to observe proper conduct.
Those six groups of bhikṣus preached the Dharma while standing, even though the king was seated.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"If a person is seated and a bhikkhu is standing, he should not preach the Dharma to them;
one who preaches the Dharma in such a manner does not act in accordance with the training rules.
Yet those bhikkhus of the group of six, while sitting on low seats themselves, preached the Dharma to the king as he sat on a high seat.
The World-Honored One said:
"If one is seated on a low seat while another person is seated on a high seat, one should not preach the Dharma to them.
One who preaches the Dharma should not violate this rule of conduct, except in the case of illness."
Those six groups of bhikṣus preached the Dharma to the king while his head was covered.
The World-Honored One said:
"One should not preach the Dharma to a person whose head is covered."
"One who preaches the Dharma should not [preach] to one whose conduct does not accord with the precepts.
To those six groups of bhikṣus who preached the Dharma to the king while his head was wrapped in a turban,
the World-Honored One said:
"One should not preach the Dharma to a person with their head wrapped.
One who preaches the Dharma should not violate the rules of conduct.
Yet those bhikṣus of the group of six preached the Dharma to people who had tucked up their three robes on both sides.
The World-Honored One said:
"One should not preach the Dharma to a person who has both shoulders covered by their three robes.
One who preaches the Dharma in such a manner does not act in accordance with the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus preached the Dharma to people who were dragging one corner of their three robes.
The World-Honored One said:
"One should not preach the Dharma to those who are dragging one corner of their three robes."
"One who preaches the Dharma should not [behave] contrary to the rules of conduct.
Those six groups of bhikṣus preached the Dharma while letting one corner of their upper robe hang down to one side, exposing their chests.
The World-Honored One said:
"One must not preach the Dharma to a person who has draped the upper corners of their three robes over one shoulder.
Such preaching does not accord with the precepts, except in cases of illness."
Those six groups of bhikṣus preached the Dharma to people who had turned their three robes over and placed them upon their shoulders.
The World-Honored One said:
"One should not preach the Dharma to those who have turned their three robes over and placed them upon their shoulders."
"To preach the Dharma while violating the precepts, except in cases of illness.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were swinging their two arms inside another person's three robes while preaching the Dharma.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"One should not preach the Dharma to a person who is swinging both arms inside their three robes;
one who preaches the Dharma in such a manner does not act in accordance with the precepts.
Yet those bhikṣus of the group of six sat while the person lay down, and they preached the Dharma to them.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a person is lying down and a bhikṣu is sitting, one should not preach the Dharma to them.
One who preaches the Dharma in such a manner does not act in accordance with the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus preached the Dharma to people who were wearing leather sandals.
The World-Honored One said to them:
"One should not preach the Dharma to those who are wearing leather sandals."
"One who preaches the Dharma should not [preach to] one who does not observe the rules of conduct.
Those six groups of bhikṣus preached the Dharma to people wearing wooden clogs.
The World-Honored One said:
"One should not preach the Dharma to a person wearing wooden clogs;
one who preaches the Dharma should not fail to observe this precept.
Yet those Bhikṣus of the group of six preached the Dharma to a person whose body was covered by a parasol.
The World-Honored One said:
"One should not preach the Dharma to a person who holds a parasol over their body.
One who preaches the Dharma in such a manner does not act in accordance with the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus preached the Dharma to people who were leaning on staffs.
The World-Honored One told them:
"One should not preach the Dharma to those who are leaning on staffs."
"One who preaches the Dharma should not preach it to one who is not observing the precepts.
To those six groups of bhikṣus who preached the Dharma to people carrying knives,
the World-Honored One said:
"If a person is holding a knife, one must not preach the Dharma to them at all.
One who preaches the Dharma should not violate the rules of conduct.
Yet those Bhikṣus of the group of six preached the Dharma to a person carrying a sickle.
The World-Honored One said:
"If a person carries a *gāthā* (verse), one must not preach the Dharma to them.
To preach the Dharma to such a person is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus preached the Dharma to people who were holding axes.
The World-Honored One told them:
"One should not preach the Dharma to people who are holding axes."
"One who preaches the Dharma should not violate their conduct.
Both Yuè and Chándài said "Āyùhē," a sound similar to that of the group of six bhikṣus who voided excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva in a clean vegetable garden.
The World-Honored One said:
"One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate upon clean vegetables or grass.
To defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate there is contrary to the practice of the precepts."
Those six groups of bhikṣus urinated, defecated, sneezed, and spat into the water that the householder was using for drinking.
The World-Honored One told them:
"One must not urinate, defecate, sneeze, or spit into pure water."
"To discharge feces, urine, nasal mucus, or saliva while standing is contrary to the practice of the precepts.

When the six groups of bhikṣus urinated while standing, the householders saw them and said to one another, "These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, urinate while standing; how are they any different from the Nirgranthas?"
He went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"One must not urinate while standing."
"Standing to urinate is not in accordance with the rules of conduct, except in cases of illness.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One, while he was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
A certain householder invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.

The group of six bhikṣus and the group of seventeen bhikṣus were on duty to remain behind as guards. They consulted among themselves and settled upon having the group of seventeen bhikṣus stay to guard the residence, while the group of six bhikṣus went out to request their share of the offerings.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went halfway along the road and said to one another:
"If we obtain food, we shall follow behind the community of bhikṣus at a leisurely pace; once midday has passed, we shall take the food and go."
When the community of bhikṣus had finished eating, he gave him his share of the meal.
Following behind the bhikṣus, he walked slowly to the gate of Jetavana, or perhaps to the foot of the city wall, or beneath a tree, where he wandered about without entering.

At that time, the seventeen groups of young bhikṣus could not endure the hunger; they went outside the gate and looked, but could not see them. They then climbed a large tree to look and saw that they were all sitting beneath trees at the foot of the city wall.
When the elders saw [the monks] climbing trees, they came and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told them:
"One must not climb a tree with more than one person."
"To climb a tree higher than the height of one person is contrary to the practice of the precepts, except when it is to remove the fear of tigers, wolves, or bandits.
Thus spoke the Buddha, the World-Honored One, while he was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Sgū who delighted in quarreling and did not avoid those of high or low status; he provoked others and reviled the various bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus of the Twelve Dharmas went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"Forgive this bhikṣu as you would forgive a fool.
There are seven methods for the expiation of transgressions."
First, when someone commits a transgression, one should immediately instruct them to repent;
this is the first point. Second, rectify their mental intentions so that no further errors occur.
Third, if a fool commits a transgression, instruct them to remain silent.
Fourth, for those who do not know the Dharma, one instructs them so that they may come to know it.

Fifth, when there is an offense committed, one should repent within the community of bhikṣus by spreading the grass upon the ground (*tṛṇastāraka*) and repenting with great earnestness, as is the practice of spreading out four pieces of sheepskin.
Now, there are five methods for admonishing and reprimanding bhikṣus:
first, one must be free of flaws oneself before reproaching others.
If one is not pure oneself, one cannot purify others.
First purify yourself, and then purify others.
When admonishing a bhikṣu, first rectify your own mind and thoughts according to this primary dharma; only then should you admonish another—this is the first point.
That monk who rebukes others speaks impurity with his mouth; his own mouth is impure, and he cannot purify himself.
He should first purify himself, and only then purify others.
Second, when a bhikkhu who reproves others does so with his mind upright and one-pointed regarding these two dharmas, he is a bhikkhu who reproves others.
However, if that bhikkhu who reproves others has an impure mind and cannot purify himself, [he is not a true reprover].
First purify your own mind, and only then purify others.
When admonishing a bhikṣu, you must first bring these three factors to a state of focused and single-minded attention, and only then admonish those three in him.
He rebuked the bhikṣus for coming and going without restraint and being unable to self-control.
"First purify yourself, and only then instruct others.
He rebuked the bhikṣus to first rectify their own minds and intentions regarding these four dharmas, and only then instruct others in those same four.
When admonishing a bhikṣu who is not learned, lacks intelligence, and has no prior training,
one should first diligently study oneself and only then teach others.
When admonishing a bhikṣu, one should first rectify one’s own mind and thoughts regarding these five dharmas, and only then admonish those five in him.
Furthermore, one should train in five things:
reverence for the World-Honored One, the Dharma, the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, the precepts, and pure conduct.
These are the five things.
If a transgression has been committed, a senior bhikṣu should confess it to a junior bhikṣu, and a junior bhikṣu should confess it to a senior bhikṣu.
You should forgive one another’s faults; you must not fail to repent until the night has passed.
If one does not repent of an offense after it has passed one night, one will not attain the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharma from the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharma.

When the minds of the bhikṣus are no longer virtuous due to having committed an offense, the senior bhikṣus and junior bhikṣus should together perform confession; thus, regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharma, they shall attain the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharma, and the bhikṣus will then be able to dwell in peace and practice the Path.
The Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"To have transgressions and not repent them is contrary to the practice of the precepts.
Regarding the seven dharmas of the precepts, there are two matters concerning the senior and junior elders, as well as the young.

That person takes the latter two sets of five matters as seven; within the latter five, they repent of the upper and lower parts facing each other, thereby completing it. Regarding the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*, the rules for the Vinaya and the *Śīla* differ; the two Vinayas state:
"Gather its upper edge tightly."
The precepts state: "Finely gather the head of the wheat-rice. *Chuǎn* means to fold back.

Among the three robes, the first four are identical to the precepts; the latter six concern the practice of placing one corner over the right shoulder during the Dharma teaching, while sitting on a low seat when the interlocutor is on a high seat. Regarding the shaking of the hand at the time of eating, the *Vinaya* frequently mentions shaking the hand; there are two pairs concerning the two feet.

Regarding the many rules for dwelling in sudden mindfulness while receiving food, they are summarized as follows: eating with the mouth wide open, holding the bowl with the fingers, inserting the thumb into the rice, swallowing without chewing, taking large mouthfuls, and pushing the food with the palm.

One should refrain from shaking [the bowl], pointing with the finger, stuffing food into the throat, or making a smacking sound while eating. Regarding the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*, it states that one must not stare with wide eyes, scold, or call out loudly inside the monastery.
One should also refrain from being self-important or looking up haughtily; this is as stated in the *Naiyāya* (Sifen lü), Scroll Ten.
